catholic-christianity-practices.title: Catholic Social Teaching: Loving Our Neighbour
catholic-christianity-practices.description: Catholic Social Teaching, Gaudium et Spes, justice and peace, and the work of CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio.
catholic-christianity-practices.content_html:
Loving Our Neighbour: A Catholic Imperative

When Jesus was asked which commandment was the greatest, he gave two: love God and love your neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). He illustrated the second with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), making clear that “neighbour” crosses ethnic, religious and social boundaries. For Catholics, the duty to love the neighbour is not optional — it is integral to what it means to follow Christ. This duty is expressed locally (in parish communities), nationally (through Catholic charities and advocacy) and globally (through international agencies such as CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio).

Catholic Social Teaching (CST) is the name given to the set of principles and commitments that the Church has developed for applying the Gospel to the structures of society. It emerged in its modern form in 1891 with Pope Leo XIII’s letter on the condition of workers, and has been developed by every subsequent Pope. Its core principles include the dignity of the human person, the common good, solidarity, subsidiarity (decisions made at the lowest appropriate level), a preferential option for the poor, and care for creation.

Key Fact

Core principles of Catholic Social Teaching: (1) Dignity of the human person — every person is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); (2) The common good — the conditions of social life that allow all people to flourish; (3) Preferential option for the poor — the poor and vulnerable have a claim on society’s first resources; (4) Solidarity — we are all members of the human family, responsible for one another.

Gaudium et Spes: Joy and Hope

Gaudium et Spes (“Joy and Hope”) was one of the four constitutions produced by the Second Vatican Council (Vatican II), published in 1965. It is a landmark document that turned the Church’s gaze outward to the world. Paragraph 26 is specifically named in the GCSE specification: it describes the social order as something that must be built on truth, justice and love, and insists that the development of institutions serving the common good is a Christian duty. The document teaches that the joys and griefs of humanity are the joys and griefs of the Church too — the famous opening line is: “The joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the people of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted, these too are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.”

Before Vatican II, some Catholics understood the Church’s role as primarily sacramental and otherworldly. Gaudium et Spes explicitly rejected this separation: the Church is not above or outside the world but within it, sharing humanity’s struggles and called to transform unjust social structures. This commitment to engaging with the world on questions of poverty, war, human dignity and economic justice remains central to Catholic identity today.

Justice, Peace and Reconciliation

Catholic teaching on justice holds that justice is not merely a legal concept but a moral one rooted in the equal dignity of all human beings. The Catholic Bishops of England and Wales have consistently called for a “just wage” for workers, fair housing, and the protection of asylum seekers — all flowing from the Church’s Social Teaching. The Prophet Amos’s demand “let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:24) is often quoted in Catholic social action contexts.

Peace in Catholic teaching is not merely the absence of war but the fruit of justice (a phrase from the Latin opus iustitiae pax — the work of justice is peace). The Church calls Catholics to be peacemakers — echoing the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Reconciliation — the restoration of broken relationships between individuals, communities and nations — is understood as a practical expression of the Gospel command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales. Founded in 1962, it works in more than forty countries, responding to humanitarian crises and supporting long-term development. CAFOD’s work is grounded explicitly in Catholic Social Teaching: its campaigns address climate justice, food security, fair trade and the rights of workers. Each year CAFOD’s fast-day fundraiser engages millions of Catholics in England and Wales in practical solidarity with the world’s poorest communities.

Trocaire is the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland (the name means “mercy” in Irish). Like CAFOD, it works to address structural poverty and injustice rather than simply providing emergency relief. Missio is the pontifical mission society of the Catholic Church, supporting the Church’s evangelising work (spreading the faith) alongside practical support for education and healthcare in mission territories. Together these three agencies represent the global reach of Catholic social action: local parish fundraising connects directly to international justice work.

The Gospel Call to Global Solidarity

The Catholic commitment to global solidarity is anchored in the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–46), in which Jesus identifies himself with the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” For Catholics, serving the poor is not a supplement to faith but an expression of it. Pope Francis’s description of a “Church of the poor” draws directly on this tradition.

At a parish level in Britain today, Catholic Social Teaching shapes a wide range of activities: parish food banks, collections for CAFOD, campaigns against human trafficking (supported by groups like CSAN — Catholic Social Action Network), and parish twinning with communities in the developing world. The GCSE specification names specific agencies — CAFOD, Trocaire, Missio — because they are the institutional expression of this teaching, translating theological principles into concrete action for millions of the world’s poorest people.

Secular humanist approaches to global justice share some goals with Catholic Social Teaching — reducing poverty, promoting equality, protecting human rights — but ground them differently. Secular humanists appeal to human reason, the shared humanity of all people, and to frameworks such as the UN Declaration of Human Rights (1948) rather than to scripture or Church authority. They may argue that poverty relief and justice work are more effective when separated from religious motivations and missionary agendas.

Some critics argue that Missio, because it combines charitable work with evangelisation (spreading the Catholic faith), has a complex relationship with the communities it serves: development and conversion can become entangled in ways that complicate the purely humanitarian dimension. Catholic Social Teaching responds that authentic human development includes the spiritual dimension — it is not possible to fully serve a person while ignoring their soul. This tension is a useful contrasting perspective in a 12-mark Evaluate question.

Key Fact

CAFOD (England and Wales): overseas development and relief, grounded in CST; over forty countries. Trocaire (Ireland): poverty and injustice; the name means ‘mercy’ in Irish. Missio: pontifical mission society; supports evangelisation, education and healthcare in mission territories. All three translate the Gospel call to “love your neighbour” (Matthew 22:39) into global structural action.
catholic-christianity-practices.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on Catholic Social Teaching or the work of a named agency, cite at least one source. Strong choices: Matthew 22:39 (love your neighbour), Matthew 25:40 (whatever you did for the least), Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 (the social order must be built on truth, justice and love), or Genesis 1:27 (imago Dei — the foundation of human dignity). Name the source AND explain how it supports the reason — a bare quotation earns fewer marks than a quotation plus development.

For the 12-mark Evaluate on Catholic Social Teaching (e.g. “The Catholic Church does more good through its social action than through its worship”), arguments FOR will use the work of CAFOD, Trocaire, Missio, and Matthew 25; arguments AGAINST will emphasise that the Mass and the sacraments are the ‘source and summit’ of Catholic life and that social action flows from worship. A non-religious view might argue secular charities do equivalent or better work without a religious mission. Your JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION must state which side is stronger and WHY.
catholic-christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic Social Teaching (CST) applies Gospel values to the structures of society, with core principles including human dignity (imago Dei), the common good, solidarity and a preferential option for the poor. Gaudium et Spes (Vatican II, 1965) is the foundational modern document, declaring that the Church shares the joys and griefs of humanity and is committed to justice and peace in the world.
  • Justice and peace in Catholic teaching are not abstract ideals but practical imperatives: justice is the fair distribution of goods and rights required by human dignity; peace is the fruit of justice. Catholics are called to be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9) and to serve the poorest (Matthew 25:40) as an expression of their faith.
  • CAFOD (England and Wales), Trocaire (Ireland) and Missio (pontifical mission society) are the main institutional expressions of Catholic global social action. Each translates the Gospel command to “love your neighbour” (Matthew 22:39) into concrete development, relief and evangelisation work in the world’s poorest communities.

practice_questions.text:
Which Second Vatican Council document (1965) named in the GCSE specification describes the Church's commitment to the common good and the social order built on truth, justice and love?
A) Humanae Vitae
B) Laudato Si'
C) Gaudium et Spes
D) Lumen Gentium
practice_questions.marks: C) Gaudium et Spes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks: CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholic Social Teaching influences the work of CAFOD or a similar Catholic agency.
For each way, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- CAFOD's work is grounded in the CST principle of the preferential option for the poor — this means it prioritises the world's most vulnerable communities, because Catholic teaching holds that the poor have a special claim on the resources and attention of the Church and society.
- The CST principle of solidarity — that all people are members of one human family — is expressed in CAFOD's global reach: a parish in Birmingham raising money for a community in Sudan is a practical expression of the conviction that poverty anywhere is the concern of all people.
- Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 grounds the work: the social order must be built on truth, justice and love, not just on charity — CAFOD therefore works on structural issues like trade justice and climate policy, not just emergency relief.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the command to 'love your neighbour' is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; named source integrated (e.g. Matthew 22:37-39, Matthew 25:40, Luke 10:25-37, Gaudium et Spes 26); both reasons clearly linked to significance for Catholic life and action.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- Jesus himself names love of neighbour as the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-39), making it inseparable from love of God; for Catholics, this means that a devout Catholic cannot ignore the suffering of others — service to the poor is service to God.
- The parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:40) makes the command concrete: 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me'; this means helping the poor, the hungry and the stranger is not optional charity but a direct encounter with Christ himself.
- Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 grounds the command in the social order: the Church is committed to building a world in which the dignity of every person is respected, requiring Catholics to work not only for individual acts of charity but for structural justice.

practice_questions.text:
'The Catholic Church does more good in the world through its social action (like CAFOD) than through its worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; social action vs worship comparison developed accurately; Catholic teaching on the Eucharist as 'source and summit'; work of CAFOD/Trocaire/Missio cited; Matthew 25 and Matthew 22 used; non-religious view on secular vs religious charity; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- CAFOD works in over forty countries, responding to famine, conflict and climate disaster; Trocaire and Missio extend this reach globally; millions of people's lives are materially improved by the Church's social action in ways that cannot be attributed to worship.
- Matthew 25:40 makes social action the criterion of judgement: 'Whatever you did for the least of these...'; a non-believer cannot do this but a society can measure material improvements in wellbeing.
- Some would argue that the Church's global development work is its most compelling argument for its relevance in the modern world — it translates faith into action that crosses religious boundaries.

Arguments against:
- Catholic theology insists that the Eucharist is 'the source and summit of Christian life' — social action flows from and returns to worship; without the Mass, CAFOD would have no theological foundation for what it does.
- Secular charities such as Oxfam and Save the Children do comparable development work without a religious mandate; the distinctively Catholic contribution is not development work per se but the theological conviction that grounds it in the Gospel.
- Prayer, the sacraments and the worship life of the Church are the means by which Catholics receive the grace to sustain their social action; without spiritual nourishment, the motivation for justice work would diminish.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that for Catholic theology the distinction is false — worship and social action are inseparable, each nourishing the other; but if forced to choose, the candidate can argue that social action has more measurable global impact, or that worship is the deeper foundation without which social action loses its distinctive character.

practice_questions.text: A Catholic parish in Newcastle is organising its annual CAFOD Fast Day collection. Give two reasons why this is important for Catholics.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- It expresses practical solidarity with the world's poorest people, fulfilling the Gospel command to love the neighbour (Matthew 22:39).
- It connects local parish life to the global mission of the Church and its commitment to justice (Catholic Social Teaching).
- It expresses the preferential option for the poor — a core principle of CST — in a practical and accessible way.
- It gives Catholics a way to apply the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:40) in their daily lives.

catholic-christianity-practices.title: Mission, Evangelism and Catholic Charities
catholic-christianity-practices.description: Mission and evangelism for Catholics today, the aims of the SVP, and the work of either Corrymeela or Pax Christi.
catholic-christianity-practices.content_html:
What Is Mission?

Mission is the task given by the risen Jesus to his followers: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20). This command, known as the Great Commission, is foundational to Catholic identity. The Catholic Church understands itself as a missionary Church — not in the sense of imposing its beliefs on others, but in the sense that it has something of great importance to offer: the Good News of God’s love and the invitation to share in the life of Christ.

Evangelism (or evangelisation) is the process of sharing the Good News. For Catholics today in Britain, evangelism takes many forms: inviting friends and neighbours to Mass, running faith exploration courses (such as RCIA — the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults), speaking openly about faith in workplaces and schools, and engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths. Pope Francis has consistently urged Catholics to be a “missionary Church” — one that reaches out rather than waiting for people to come to it.

Key Fact

The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20): Jesus commands his disciples to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” This is the foundation of Catholic mission: the Gospel is not private property but a gift to be shared with everyone. Catholics in Britain today engage in evangelism through faith courses, parish outreach and community service.

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP)

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP) was founded in Paris in 1833 by a group of young Catholic university students led by Frédéric Ozanam. It is named after St Vincent de Paul (1581–1660), a French priest who dedicated his life to the service of the poor and who reformed the training of priests and the care of the sick and orphaned in seventeenth-century France.

The SVP is an international lay organisation operating in 153 countries. Its members — called Vincentians — visit people in their homes, hospitals and care homes, offer practical help (food parcels, clothing, furniture), befriend the lonely and isolated, and run projects for the homeless, the unemployed and those in financial difficulty. The SVP operates through local parish conferences (groups), making it one of the most locally embedded Catholic charitable organisations in Britain. Its motto is “Serviens in Spe” — “Serving in Hope.”

What distinguishes the SVP from purely secular charities is its emphasis on the personal relationship: Vincentians do not simply deliver goods, they sit with the people they serve, treating each person as Christ. The theological grounding is Matthew 25:40: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” In a Catholic parish in Liverpool, for example, the local SVP conference might visit elderly parishioners who cannot attend Mass, bring Holy Communion to the housebound, run a lunch club for the lonely, and collect food for a local food bank.

Pax Christi (Latin: “Peace of Christ”) is an international Catholic peace movement founded in 1945, initially as a movement of Franco-German reconciliation after the Second World War. It now works in over forty countries, campaigning for disarmament (including opposition to nuclear weapons), challenging militarism, and promoting reconciliation between enemies as a concrete expression of the Gospel.

Pax Christi’s theological foundation is the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9) and the Catholic commitment to the “just war” tradition alongside its increasingly strong pacifist strand. In Britain, Pax Christi UK campaigns against the Trident nuclear weapons programme, works with schools on peace education, and runs interfaith peace-building initiatives. The organisation sees disarmament not as political preference but as a moral requirement flowing from the sanctity of human life and the command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

The Corrymeela Community is an ecumenical Christian reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, founded in 1965 by Ray Davey — a Presbyterian minister who had been a prisoner of war and had witnessed the destruction of Dresden. Located at a residential centre on the Antrim coast, Corrymeela brings together Catholics and Protestants divided by the violence of the Troubles, young people from different communities, and families affected by conflict, to work together on healing and understanding.

Corrymeela is notable for being explicitly Christian but ecumenical — it does not belong to one denomination. Its work is grounded in the conviction that the Gospel calls all Christians to reconciliation, drawing on Paul’s letter to the Corinthians: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). While primarily Protestant in origin, the GCSE specification names Corrymeela alongside Pax Christi as an example of Catholic-engaged peace-building, because it works across the Catholic-Protestant divide and many Catholics participate in its work.

Catholics in Great Britain: Mission Today

There are approximately five million Catholics in England and Wales, making Catholicism the largest single Christian denomination. Catholics in Britain today engage in mission in a context very different from earlier centuries: a secular, pluralist society in which faith is often treated as a private matter. The challenge of Catholic mission in Britain is therefore not primarily overseas but local: how to share the Gospel with a society that is largely unchurched, and how to demonstrate the relevance of Catholic teaching and practice to contemporary life.

This local mission takes many forms. Westminster Cathedral in London hosts regular public events, concerts, lectures and open days to engage people who might not otherwise encounter Catholicism. Individual parishes run Alpha and RCIA courses for people exploring the faith. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales speaks publicly on issues of justice, education and family life, acting as a public voice for Catholic Social Teaching in national debate. For Catholics, none of this is separate from the central command: “Love the Lord your God… and love your neighbour as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–39).

Key Fact

SVP: international lay organisation visiting and serving the poor person-to-person in 153 countries, grounded in Matthew 25:40 (“Whatever you did for the least…”). Pax Christi: international Catholic peace movement working for disarmament and nonviolent conflict resolution, grounded in the Beatitude (Matthew 5:9). Corrymeela: ecumenical reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, bringing Catholics and Protestants together, grounded in 2 Corinthians 5:18.
catholic-christianity-practices.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question about mission or the work of a named Catholic organisation, always name the organisation AND explain its theological grounding. For the SVP: cite Matthew 25:40. For Pax Christi: cite Matthew 5:9 (“Blessed are the peacemakers”). For Corrymeela: cite 2 Corinthians 5:18 (ministry of reconciliation). A source without development earns partial marks; a source with a full explanation of how it motivates the organisation earns top-band marks.

For the 12-mark Evaluate (e.g. “Mission is the most important Catholic activity today”), you need arguments on both sides. Arguments FOR mission: the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19); Catholic identity is inherently missionary. Arguments AGAINST: the Eucharist is ‘source and summit’; social action (CAFOD, SVP) may do more immediate good; non-religious view that proselytisation interferes with individual freedom of belief. Your JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION must choose a side and explain why.
catholic-christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mission is the task given by Jesus in Matthew 28:19–20 (the Great Commission) to share the Gospel with all nations. Catholics in Britain today engage in evangelism through faith courses, parish outreach and community service. The challenge in a secular society is to share the faith winsmomely without coercion.
  • The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP) is a lay Catholic organisation present in 153 countries, providing direct person-to-person service of the poor based on Matthew 25:40. Local parish conferences visit the elderly, housebound and isolated, embodying the Catholic conviction that serving the poor is serving Christ.
  • Pax Christi is an international Catholic peace movement working for disarmament and nonviolent conflict resolution, grounded in Matthew 5:9. Corrymeela is an ecumenical reconciliation community in Northern Ireland that has brought Catholic and Protestant communities together since 1965, grounded in 2 Corinthians 5:18 (the ministry of reconciliation).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholics in Britain today carry out mission and evangelism.
For each way, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholics run faith exploration courses such as RCIA (Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults) or Alpha — these invite people who are not Catholic or who are returning to faith to explore Christianity in a welcoming setting, responding to Jesus's command to 'go and make disciples' (Matthew 28:19).
- Through the work of organisations like the SVP, Catholics embody the Gospel by serving the poor and marginalised in their local communities; this demonstrates the faith in action rather than just in words, and can draw people toward the Church.
- Individual Catholics may speak openly about their faith in workplaces and schools, or invite friends to Mass — a form of personal evangelism that many parish missions encourage.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the work of Pax Christi or Corrymeela is important for Catholics.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons for either Pax Christi or Corrymeela (or one each); named source integrated and developed (e.g. Matthew 5:9, Matthew 5:44, 2 Corinthians 5:18, Gaudium et Spes); both reasons clearly connected to Catholic belief or practice.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points for Pax Christi:
- Pax Christi works for disarmament because Catholic teaching holds that nuclear weapons threaten the God-given dignity of all human life; Jesus's Beatitude 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9) gives Catholics a clear mandate to oppose warfare and militarism.
- Pax Christi's campaigns also draw on the just war tradition: Catholic theology has always held that war must meet strict conditions to be morally justified; nuclear weapons, which cannot discriminate between combatants and civilians, fail to meet these conditions.

Acceptable points for Corrymeela:
- Corrymeela has brought Catholic and Protestant communities in Northern Ireland together since 1965, building relationships across a divide that has resulted in violence and death; this expresses the Catholic commitment to reconciliation as a practical Gospel imperative — 'God gave us the ministry of reconciliation' (2 Corinthians 5:18).
- The willingness of Catholics to work alongside Protestants in Corrymeela reflects the Catholic teaching on ecumenism (work for Christian unity) and on the dignity of every person, regardless of denomination.

practice_questions.text:
'Mission and evangelism is the most important task of Catholics in Britain today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; Catholic teaching on mission (Matthew 28:19), the Eucharist as source and summit, social action (SVP, CAFOD); non-religious view on evangelism as interference; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) is Jesus's final command to his disciples — it is the last thing he said before the Ascension; if Catholics take the words of Christ seriously, mission must be a high priority.
- Without mission, the Church would decline and eventually disappear; Catholics have a duty to share the Good News they have received so others can experience the grace and salvation Jesus offers.
- Pope Francis has consistently called for a 'missionary Church' that goes out to the margins — this is the Pope's own stated priority for the Church in the twenty-first century.

Arguments against:
- Catholic theology insists that the Eucharist is 'the source and summit of Christian life'; without worship, sacramental life and prayer, mission has no foundation — the most important task may be maintaining the community of faith.
- The work of the SVP, CAFOD and Pax Christi arguably does more immediate good for the world's poor and suffering than evangelism; many Catholics today see social action as their primary vocation.
- From a non-religious perspective, evangelism that aims to convert others may interfere with their freedom of belief and conscience; in a pluralist society, building peace and justice across religious boundaries (as Corrymeela does) may be more important than denominational expansion.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that for Catholic theology, mission, worship and social action are inseparable — each nourishes the others — but that the Great Commission gives mission a foundational importance that cannot be set aside without abandoning a core Gospel imperative.

christianity-practices.title: Worship & Prayer
christianity-practices.description: Forms of worship, the role of prayer, and the significance of the Lord's Prayer.
christianity-practices.content_html:
Why Do Christians Worship?

Worship is how Christians express their love and devotion to God. The word comes from the Old English ‘worthship’ — recognising that God is worthy of praise. Christians worship for many reasons: to thank God for creation and blessings, to ask for forgiveness, to seek guidance, and to strengthen their relationship with God. The Bible teaches, “Come, let us bow down in worship, let us kneel before the Lord our Maker” (Psalm 95:6).

Key Fact

Christians worship in four main ways — liturgical, non-liturgical, informal and private. Each serves the same purpose of honouring God but differs in structure and style.

Liturgical Worship

Liturgical worship follows the same set pattern every time. It is led by a priest or minister who guides the congregation through prayers, Bible readings, a sermon and symbolic actions such as the Eucharist. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches use liturgical worship.

Supporters value its familiarity — worshippers know what to expect. It connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides the same structure in churches worldwide. The use of the Bible is central: readings follow a set lectionary so that all congregations hear the same passages on the same day.

Non-Liturgical Worship

Non-liturgical worship has no fixed order. Hymns, Bible readings and a sermon may be included, but the service is flexible and can change from week to week. It is commonly practised in Methodist, Baptist and United Reformed churches. The focus is on the word of God in the Bible, and services often respond directly to the needs of the congregation.

Informal worship includes charismatic worship, which is free-flowing and may include dance, clapping, calling out, speaking in tongues and modern music. Pentecostal and evangelical churches commonly practise this form. It is seen as more relevant to modern life and allows worshippers to express their faith spontaneously.

Quaker worship is another form of informal worship. There is no leader and no set structure. Worshippers sit in a circle in silent reflection and may speak when they feel moved by the Holy Spirit. This allows God to communicate directly with individuals.

Private Worship

Private worship is when a Christian praises God alone. It may include personal prayer, Bible reading, meditation, or using worship aids such as the rosary or icons. Jesus encouraged private worship: “When you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen” (Matthew 6:6). Private worship can use set prayers or the Christian’s own words.

Private worship gives Christians personal time with God away from the pressures of everyday life. Many believers set aside a regular time each day for personal devotion — reading a passage of Scripture, reflecting on its meaning and praying about their daily concerns. Some Christians use structured devotional guides, while others simply open the Bible and read. The advantage of private worship is that it allows a deeply personal relationship with God that communal services may not always provide.

Prayer

Prayer is communication with God. It can be silent or spoken, individual or communal. Christians pray for many reasons, remembered by the acronym STOP: Sorry (confession), Thank (gratitude), Others (intercession) and Please (petition). Jesus taught, “Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours” (Mark 11:24).

Set prayers are written down and used repeatedly by many Christians. They provide unity and tradition and are central to liturgical worship. An example is the Catholic grace before meals.

Informal prayer uses the Christian’s own words. It allows believers to express their personal emotions and concerns freely. Most Christians use informal prayers in private worship — these might be as simple as “Help me, God” or “Thank you, God.”

The Lord’s Prayer

When Jesus’s disciples asked how to pray, he taught them the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13). It is a model of good prayer because it combines praise of God with submission to His will, requests for daily needs, forgiveness and protection from evil.

“Our Father in heaven” — God is the Father of all people. “Hallowed be your name” — God’s name is holy and should be treated with reverence. “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” — Christians pray for God’s rule to be established. “Give us today our daily bread” — asking God to provide what is needed. “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us” — forgiveness must be both received and given. “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” — asking for God’s protection.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer teaches Christians that prayer should include praise (“hallowed be your name”), submission to God’s will, requests for daily needs, and forgiveness. It is said at worship, baptisms, marriages and funerals, uniting all Christian denominations.
christianity-practices.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark ‘Explain similarities and differences’ question, make sure your two examples are genuinely different — for example, contrast liturgical worship (set structure, Catholic Mass) with charismatic worship (free-flowing, Pentecostal). For 6-mark questions, you must refer to a source of Christian teaching such as Matthew 6:6 or the Lord’s Prayer. For 12-mark evaluations, always give arguments for and against, include specific Christian teachings, and reach a justified conclusion.
christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians worship in four main forms — liturgical (set structure), non-liturgical (flexible), informal/charismatic (free-flowing) and private (individual) — each serving the purpose of honouring God.
  • Prayer is communication with God and can be set (written, repeated) or informal (own words). The STOP acronym covers the main reasons: Sorry, Thank, Others, Please.
  • The Lord’s Prayer, taught by Jesus in Matthew 6:9–13, is the model for all Christian prayer — combining praise, submission, daily needs, forgiveness and protection.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar or different ways in which Christians worship.
In your answer you must refer to two Christian traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Liturgical worship follows a set structure with set responses and is led by a priest (e.g. Catholic Mass, Anglican service) — it provides familiarity, tradition and connects Christians worldwide.
• Non-liturgical worship has no set order and can change from week to week (e.g. Baptist, Methodist) — it places emphasis on the Bible and allows services to respond to the congregation's needs.
• Charismatic worship is free-flowing with modern music, dance and clapping (e.g. Pentecostal) — contrasting with Quaker worship which is silent with no leader.
• Private worship is individual devotion through prayer and Bible reading — available to all Christians regardless of denomination.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian beliefs about the importance of prayer.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prayer strengthens a Christian's relationship with God — through prayer, believers feel God's presence and guidance. Jesus taught 'Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours' (Mark 11:24).
• Prayer provides comfort and strength in difficult times — Christians believe God listens and responds to prayer. Jesus encouraged private prayer: 'Go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen' (Matthew 6:6).
• Prayer allows Christians to praise and thank God for His creation and blessings — Psalm 95:6 says 'Come, let us bow down in worship.'
• Prayer helps Christians seek forgiveness — the Lord's Prayer teaches 'Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.'
[6 marks — 3 marks per belief: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text:
'Private worship is more important than communal worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus encouraged private prayer in Matthew 6:6 — 'go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen' — suggesting a personal relationship with God is valued.
• Private worship allows Christians to express personal concerns and emotions freely without the pressure of a congregation.
• It can take place anywhere and at any time, making it more accessible than attending a church service.
• The quality of prayer may be deeper when a Christian is alone and undistracted.

Arguments against:
• Communal worship unites believers and creates a sense of community — Jesus said 'Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them' (Matthew 18:20).
• Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a structured encounter with God through sacraments like the Eucharist.
• The Bible instructs Christians not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25).
• Communal worship provides support, teaching and accountability that private worship cannot.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Lord's Prayer is used in Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Lord's Prayer is said during Sunday services in liturgical worship — it is part of the set structure of Catholic Mass, Anglican services and other denominations, uniting the congregation in a prayer taught by Jesus himself.
• It is used in private worship — individual Christians say it as part of their daily devotion, using it as a model for their own prayers.
• It is used at key ceremonies such as baptisms, marriages and funerals — marking important life events with the words Jesus taught.
• It is taught in Church schools — helping young Christians learn how to pray.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

christianity-practices.title: Sacraments: Baptism & Holy Communion
christianity-practices.description: The meaning of sacrament, infant and believers' baptism, and Holy Communion.
christianity-practices.content_html:
What Is a Sacrament?

A sacrament is a sacred ritual through which Christians believe they receive God’s grace. The word comes from the Latin ‘sacramentum’, meaning a solemn oath. Sacraments are outward, visible signs of an inward, spiritual blessing. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestant churches recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion. These two were specifically commanded by Jesus in the Gospels.

Key Fact

A sacrament is an outward sign of inward grace. Roman Catholics recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestants recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion — because only these were directly instituted by Jesus.

Infant Baptism

Infant baptism is practised by Roman Catholic, Anglican and Methodist churches. During the ceremony, a priest or minister pours water over the baby’s head three times in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Parents and godparents make promises on the child’s behalf to reject evil and turn to Christ.

For Catholics, infant baptism removes original sin — the sinful state inherited from Adam and Eve. The baby receives a white garment symbolising purity and a candle symbolising the light of Christ. Other Christians see it as a way of welcoming the child into the Church community and dedicating them to God. Jesus himself said, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Mark 10:14).

Believers’ baptism is practised by Baptist and Pentecostal churches. It involves the full immersion of a person who is old enough to make their own declaration of faith. The person is submerged completely under water and then raised up — symbolising dying to their old sinful life and being raised to new life in Christ, mirroring Jesus’s death and resurrection.

Baptists argue that babies cannot understand the commitment being made. They point to the example of Jesus, who was baptised as an adult by John the Baptist in the River Jordan (Matthew 3:13–17). Believers’ baptism is a personal choice and a public declaration of faith, making the commitment more meaningful.

Different Beliefs About Baptism

Christians hold different views on which form of baptism is correct. Those who practise infant baptism believe that God’s grace should be available to everyone from birth and that parents can make promises on a child’s behalf. Those who practise believers’ baptism argue that faith requires a conscious, personal decision and that Jesus was baptised as an adult. Some Christians, such as the Salvation Army and Quakers, do not practise baptism at all — they believe the inward spiritual change matters more than the outward ritual.

Key Fact

Infant baptism and believers’ baptism share the same purpose — entry into the Christian faith — but differ in method and timing. Infant baptism uses pouring of water and relies on parents’ promises; believers’ baptism uses full immersion and requires a personal declaration of faith.

Holy Communion / The Eucharist

Holy Communion (also called the Eucharist, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) remembers the Last Supper, the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his crucifixion. At this meal, Jesus took bread and said, “This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me,” and took wine saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:19–20).

In the Roman Catholic Church, the Mass is the central act of worship. Catholics believe in transubstantiation — that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ during the service. Only a priest can celebrate Mass, and the service follows a strict liturgical structure.

In Orthodox churches, the Divine Liturgy is a highly elaborate and symbolic celebration. The bread and wine are also believed to become the body and blood of Christ, though the Orthodox Church does not use the term transubstantiation.

In Protestant churches, Holy Communion is generally seen as a symbolic act of remembrance rather than a literal transformation. Anglicans vary in their interpretation — some lean towards the Catholic view, others see it as symbolic. Methodists and Baptists see the bread and wine as symbols of Jesus’s body and blood, taken in remembrance of his sacrifice.

The Salvation Army and Quakers do not celebrate Holy Communion. They believe that the spiritual reality of Christ’s presence does not depend on physical elements and that every meal can be sacred.

Holy Communion is important to Christians for several reasons. It obeys Jesus’s direct command to “do this in remembrance of me.” It brings Christians closer to God and to one another through a shared sacred meal. It reminds believers of Jesus’s sacrifice on the cross and the promise of salvation. For Catholics, receiving the Eucharist is considered essential for spiritual nourishment — Jesus said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53).

Key Fact

The biggest difference in Holy Communion is between Catholics, who believe the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and most Protestants, who see it as a symbolic remembrance of Jesus’s sacrifice at the Last Supper.
christianity-practices.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on the sacraments, always name the specific denomination you are writing about. For a 4-mark ‘Explain similarities and differences’ question on baptism, clearly contrast infant baptism (Catholic/Anglican — water poured, parents’ promises) with believers’ baptism (Baptist/Pentecostal — full immersion, personal choice). For 12-mark evaluations on Holy Communion, use the technical term ‘transubstantiation’ and explain what it means — this shows the examiner you understand the key theological difference.
christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sacrament is an outward sign of inward grace — Catholics recognise seven, most Protestants recognise two (baptism and Holy Communion).
  • Infant baptism (water poured, parents’ promises, removes original sin) contrasts with believers’ baptism (full immersion, personal declaration of faith, mirrors Jesus’s baptism).
  • Holy Communion remembers Jesus’s Last Supper — Catholics believe in transubstantiation (literal change), while most Protestants see it as symbolic remembrance.

• Most Christian denominations worldwide (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Methodist) practise infant baptism — it has centuries of tradition behind it.

christianity-practices.title: Pilgrimage & Festivals
christianity-practices.description: The role of pilgrimage to Lourdes and Iona, and the significance of Christmas and Easter.
christianity-practices.content_html:
What Is Pilgrimage?

A pilgrimage is a journey to a place of special religious significance. Christians go on pilgrimages to deepen their faith, seek healing, do penance, experience God in a special way, or feel a connection to important events in Christian history. Some Christians believe that visiting a sacred place brings them closer to God. Others see the journey itself as a spiritual act — a time for prayer, reflection and personal growth.

Not all Christians agree that pilgrimage is necessary. Some argue that God is everywhere and can be worshipped anywhere. Others believe the money spent on travel could be better used to help the poor. However, many Christians value pilgrimage as a powerful expression of faith that has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity.

Key Fact

You need to know two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage: Lourdes (Roman Catholic, focus on healing) and Iona (ecumenical, focus on community and simplicity). Be ready to explain why Christians visit each and how they differ.

Lourdes

Lourdes is a town in south-west France. In 1858, a 14-year-old girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported 18 visions of the Virgin Mary in a grotto near the river. During one vision, Mary told Bernadette to dig in the ground, and a spring of water appeared. This water is believed by many Catholics to have miraculous healing properties.

Today, around six million pilgrims visit Lourdes each year, making it one of the most visited Christian pilgrimage sites in the world. Pilgrims bathe in or drink the spring water, hoping for physical or spiritual healing. The site includes the Grotto of Massabielle (where the visions occurred), the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, and hospitals and care facilities for the sick. Over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.

Christians visit Lourdes to seek physical healing by bathing in or drinking the spring water. They also go to seek spiritual renewal and forgiveness through prayer and confession. Many go to pray for others who are sick, to feel closer to God in a place associated with the Virgin Mary, or to serve as volunteers caring for the sick and disabled. The sense of community at Lourdes — with millions of believers gathering together — strengthens faith and provides support for those who are suffering.

Iona

Iona is a small island off the west coast of Scotland. In 563 CE, an Irish monk named St Columba founded a monastery there, which became a centre for spreading Christianity across Scotland and northern England. Today, the Iona Community is an ecumenical Christian community that welcomes people of all denominations and none.

Pilgrims visit Iona for its simplicity, peace and sense of spiritual renewal. The community emphasises justice, peace and the integrity of creation. Visitors share in communal worship, manual work and discussion. Unlike Lourdes, Iona does not focus on miracles or healing — instead, it offers a retreat from modern life and an opportunity to live in a simple, prayerful community.

Christmas

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — the belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. Christians celebrate Christmas on 25 December (though Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January). The festival recalls the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as described in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.

Christmas is important because it marks the moment God entered the world as a human being to save humanity from sin. The angel told the shepherds, “Today in the town of David a Saviour has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Christians celebrate through special church services (including Midnight Mass and carol services), nativity plays, gift-giving (symbolising the gifts of the Magi) and acts of charity.

For Christians in Great Britain today, Christmas remains the most widely celebrated religious festival. It brings families and communities together. Churches hold special services, including Advent services in the weeks leading up to Christmas, Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve, and Christmas Day worship. Many Christians also see it as a time to help those in need — through charity appeals, food drives and volunteering.

Some Christians are concerned that the religious meaning of Christmas has been overshadowed by commercialism and consumerism. They argue that the focus should be on Jesus’s birth and its theological significance, not on shopping and materialism.

Easter

Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar. It celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, three days after his crucifixion. The events of Easter are central to the Christian faith: without the resurrection, there would be no Christianity. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Palm Sunday remembers Jesus’s triumphal entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna!” Maundy Thursday recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and shared bread and wine. Good Friday marks the crucifixion and death of Jesus — many churches hold sombre services, and some Christians fast or walk the Stations of the Cross. Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection — churches hold joyful services with hymns, flowers and the lighting of the Paschal candle.

Key Fact

Easter is the most important Christian festival because it celebrates the resurrection — the foundation of the entire Christian faith. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no hope of salvation or eternal life.
christianity-practices.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on pilgrimage, always identify the specific site (Lourdes or Iona) and explain why Christians visit it — don’t just describe what happens there. For questions on festivals, explain the theological significance (Christmas = Incarnation; Easter = Resurrection) rather than just describing how they are celebrated. For 12-mark evaluations, consider whether pilgrimage or festivals are essential to being a good Christian, and include counter-arguments.
christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lourdes (Catholic, healing-focused, France) and Iona (ecumenical, community-focused, Scotland) are two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage — both deepen faith but in different ways.
  • Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. Easter celebrates the Resurrection — Jesus rising from the dead, which is the foundation of Christian faith.
  • Easter is the most important Christian festival because without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no salvation (1 Corinthians 15:17).

• Both sites offer spiritual renewal — Lourdes through prayer, confession and the healing waters, Iona through shared worship, manual work and reflection in a peaceful island setting.
• Lourdes attracts around six million pilgrims per year and is associated with miraculous cures. Iona is much smaller and offers a retreat from modern life.

• The resurrection proves that Jesus is the Son of God and has power over death — it gives Christians hope of eternal life. Jesus said 'I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die' (John 11:25).
• Easter shows that God's plan of salvation was fulfilled — Jesus's death on Good Friday paid the price for human sin, and his resurrection on Easter Sunday proved that sin and death had been defeated.

practice_questions.text:
'Pilgrimage is essential for all Christians.'

• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Pilgrimage has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity — it deepens faith and brings believers closer to God.
• Sites like Lourdes offer healing and spiritual renewal — over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.
• Jesus himself made pilgrimages to Jerusalem for Jewish festivals.
• Pilgrimage to places like Iona builds community and provides time for prayer and reflection away from daily life.

Arguments against:
• God is omnipresent — present everywhere — so He can be worshipped anywhere. There is no need to travel to a special place.
• Jesus taught that what matters is the quality of your faith, not where you worship: 'God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth' (John 4:24).
• Money spent on pilgrimage could be better used to help the poor — Jesus said 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me' (Matthew 25:40).
• Some Christians (e.g. many Protestants) do not practise pilgrimage at all and do not consider it necessary for salvation.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

• Christians give gifts to one another — symbolising the gifts brought by the Magi to the baby Jesus. Many also give to charity, helping those in need through food drives and volunteering, reflecting Jesus's teaching to love one's neighbour.
• Churches hold nativity plays and carol services during Advent — these retell the story of Jesus's birth and bring communities together in celebration.

christianity-practices.title: Mission, Evangelism & the Worldwide Church
christianity-practices.description: The Church's role in local communities, mission and evangelism, and worldwide Christian work.
christianity-practices.content_html:
The Church in the Local Community

The Church is not just a building — it is the community of believers who follow Jesus’s teachings. Christians believe they have a duty to help others in their local area. Jesus taught, “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31), and the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) shows that ‘neighbour’ means anyone in need, regardless of background.

Many churches are active in their communities, running projects that support vulnerable people. Two important examples of local church action are food banks and street pastors.

Key Fact

You need to know about the Church’s role in the local community, including food banks and street pastors. These are practical examples of Christians putting Jesus’s teaching about loving your neighbour into action.

Food Banks

Food banks collect donated food and distribute it to people in crisis — those who cannot afford to feed themselves or their families. The Trussell Trust, founded on Christian principles, runs over 1,400 food bank centres across the UK. People are referred to food banks by professionals such as doctors, social workers or schools, and receive an emergency food parcel lasting three days.

Christians support food banks because Jesus taught that helping others is the same as serving God: “For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35). Churches provide volunteers, collection points and premises for food banks, putting their faith into practical action.

Street Pastors

Street pastors are trained Christian volunteers who patrol town and city centres at night, usually on Friday and Saturday evenings. They care for vulnerable people — offering water, flip-flops to those in bare feet, warm clothing, and a listening ear. They help people who are drunk, distressed or at risk of harm, and liaise with police and ambulance services when needed.

The Street Pastors movement was founded in London in 2003 by Reverend Les Isaac. It now operates in over 300 locations across the UK. Street pastors do not preach or try to convert people — they simply demonstrate Christian love through practical care. Their presence has been shown to reduce crime and antisocial behaviour in many areas.

Mission is the broader calling of the Church to carry out God’s work in the world. This includes preaching the gospel, caring for the poor, promoting justice and working for peace. Evangelism is the specific act of spreading the Christian faith — sharing the good news of Jesus Christ with non-believers.

Jesus commanded his followers to evangelise: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). This is known as the Great Commission. Christians carry out evangelism in many ways — through preaching, missionary work overseas, Alpha courses, social media and personal example. Church growth depends on both evangelism (reaching new people) and nurturing existing believers.

The Worldwide Church

The Church operates on a global scale. Christians believe they have a responsibility not just to their local community but to the whole world. The worldwide Church works for reconciliation (bringing peace between conflicting groups), responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty and injustice.

Reconciliation is central to Christian teaching. Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). The worldwide Church works to bring peace in areas of conflict — for example, the role of churches in the peace process in Northern Ireland and in post-apartheid South Africa, where Archbishop Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Many Christians around the world face persecution for their faith. In some countries, Christians are imprisoned, attacked or even killed for practising their religion. Churches respond by praying for persecuted Christians, raising awareness, campaigning for religious freedom and providing practical support. Jesus warned his followers that persecution would come: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency For Overseas Development) is the official Catholic aid agency for England and Wales. It works in over 40 countries, providing emergency relief after disasters, funding long-term development projects (clean water, education, healthcare) and campaigning for justice. CAFOD is funded mainly by Catholic parishes.

Christian Aid works with communities of all faiths and none in around 37 countries. It tackles poverty through emergency response, long-term development and advocacy for policy change. Christian Aid Week, held every May, raises millions of pounds through door-to-door collections and fundraising events across UK churches.

Tearfund is an evangelical Christian charity that works in over 50 countries. It partners with local churches to address poverty, provide disaster relief, and support communities in building sustainable livelihoods. Tearfund’s distinctive approach is to work through local church networks, believing that churches are uniquely placed to understand and serve their communities.

All three organisations are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour and care for the poor. Jesus said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Key Fact

The specification requires knowledge of the work of one of CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund. All three are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour (Mark 12:31) and serve the poor (Matthew 25:40), but they differ in their denominational links and methods.
christianity-practices.exam_tip_html: For questions on the Church in the community, always link your examples to a specific Christian teaching — “Love your neighbour” (Mark 12:31) and “I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35) are the two most useful quotations. For 12-mark evaluations, consider whether practical action (food banks, charity work) is more important than worship and prayer, and include arguments from both perspectives.
christianity-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Church serves the local community through practical projects such as food banks (emergency food for those in crisis) and street pastors (night-time care for vulnerable people).
  • Mission is the Church’s broader calling to do God’s work; evangelism is specifically spreading the faith. Jesus commanded both in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19).
  • The worldwide Church works for reconciliation, responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty through agencies such as CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund.

Arguments against:

• Without evangelism, the Church would eventually die out — new believers are needed for the faith to survive and grow.
• Spreading the faith addresses people's spiritual needs, which Christians believe are even more important than physical needs — Jesus said 'What good is it for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul?' (Mark 8:36).
• The best approach combines both — mission includes both practical help AND sharing the gospel.

judaism-beliefs.title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
judaism-beliefs.description: God as One, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge — loving and merciful — and the divine presence (Shekhinah).
judaism-beliefs.content_html:
God as One: The Foundation of Jewish Belief

At the heart of Judaism lies the declaration that God is absolutely, uniquely One. Every morning and evening, observant Jews recite the Shema — a single sentence that anchors the entire tradition: “Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). This is not simply a statement of arithmetic oneness but a declaration of God’s incomparable nature. There is nothing comparable to God; no partner, no rival, no image can capture the divine reality.

This belief in monotheism distinguishes Judaism from polytheistic religions and shapes every aspect of Jewish life and practice. Because God is One, all of creation flows from a single source of will, wisdom and moral law. Jewish thinkers throughout history have emphasised that God has no body and no physical form — any description of God using human terms (such as “God’s hand” or “God’s voice”) is understood as metaphor, not literal description.

Key Fact

The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is recited twice daily by observant Jews and is the declaration of God’s absolute oneness. It is also traditionally said on the deathbed, making it both a daily affirmation and a final act of faith.

God as Creator

Jewish teaching holds that God is the Creator of all that exists. The opening words of the Torah — “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) — establish God’s role as the ultimate originator of the universe. Creation is not a distant, mechanical event; God is intimately involved in the world God has made. Jewish theology describes God as bringing the world into existence through divine speech: “And God said, let there be light, and there was light.”

The creation narrative in Genesis 1 also establishes human dignity. Because humanity is created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim), every human being possesses inherent worth and equality. This principle underpins many of Judaism’s ethical teachings, including the sanctity of human life and the duty to protect the vulnerable.

God as Law-Giver and Judge

Judaism understands God as the ultimate source of moral law. God is not merely a powerful force but a personal God who cares how human beings treat one another. The mitzvot (commandments) — 613 of them in the Torah — represent God’s will for human conduct. These cover every area of life: prayer, food, business dealings, care for the poor, treatment of animals, and the celebration of holy days.

Jewish teaching holds that God is also the Judge of all human actions. On Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year), it is taught that God reviews the deeds of every person and writes their fate in the Book of Life. The ten days ending with Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) are a time of deep reflection, repentance and prayer for forgiveness. Yet this God of judgement is also understood as deeply merciful: Jewish liturgy emphasises that God is “slow to anger and abounding in loving kindness.”

Jewish theology holds two divine qualities in careful balance: tzedek (justice) and chesed (loving kindness). God demands moral accountability — wrongdoing has consequences — but God also extends compassion and offers forgiveness to those who repent sincerely. The High Holy Day liturgy (the prayers of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur) is rich with both themes: God as King and Judge, and God as Father and Shepherd who does not wish anyone to be lost. This is not a contradiction but a complex portrait of a God who holds humanity to a high standard precisely because God loves humanity deeply.

The Shekhinah: The Divine Presence

One of the most distinctive and beautiful concepts in Jewish theology is the Shekhinah — the immanent presence or “indwelling” of God. The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to dwell.” While God is transcendent (beyond and above all creation), the Shekhinah expresses God’s nearness, the sense that God is present with and among the Jewish people.

In ancient times, the Shekhinah was associated with the Tabernacle in the desert and later with the Temple in Jerusalem. After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, Jewish thinkers taught that the Shekhinah went with the Jewish people into exile — God was not distant from those who suffered, but accompanied them. Today, the Shekhinah is described as present whenever Jews study Torah, engage in prayer, or perform acts of justice and charity.

Students sometimes confuse the Shekhinah with a separate divine being or a lesser manifestation of God. In Jewish teaching, this is not the case. The Shekhinah is not a separate entity but a way of describing how the one, indivisible God is experienced as present and near. Jewish monotheism remains absolute: there is one God, and the Shekhinah is one way of speaking about how that single God is experienced in the world and in human life. The Shema’s declaration — “the Lord is One” — is never compromised by the concept of the Shekhinah.

Maimonides and the Principles of Faith

The medieval Jewish philosopher Maimonides (also known as the Rambam) formulated Thirteen Principles of Faith that have become widely accepted across Jewish communities. The first five concern the nature of God: that God exists, that God is one, that God has no body, that God is eternal, and that God alone is worthy of worship. These principles are summarised in a hymn called the Yigdal, sung at many synagogue services to this day.

It is worth noting that while Maimonides’ principles are widely respected, they do not function in Judaism as a formal creed in the same way the Nicene Creed functions in Catholic Christianity. Orthodox Judaism tends to treat them with great weight; Reform and Liberal Jewish thinkers may engage with them more critically, emphasising that Judaism is primarily a way of life and action rather than a system of required doctrinal belief. This reflects the broader diversity within British Jewish communities today.

Key Fact

Jewish teaching describes God as: One (echad — the Shema); Creator (borei — author of all that exists, Genesis 1:1); Law-Giver and Judge (source of the 613 mitzvot; the moral examiner on Rosh Hashanah); Loving and Merciful (chesed and rachamim in the liturgy); and Present (the Shekhinah, God’s indwelling presence among the Jewish people).
judaism-beliefs.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about the nature of God in Judaism, the most common error is failing to name a source of authority. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) and Genesis 1:1 are your two strongest sources here — name them and connect them to the specific attribute you are explaining. For example: “Jewish teaching holds that God is Creator because Genesis 1:1 states that God created the heavens and the earth; this means that God is the ultimate source of all existence and that creation reflects God’s will and wisdom.” Two reasons, each developed, with at least one named source: that is the top-band structure.

On 12-mark Evaluate questions, make sure your conclusion is justified and explicit. Simply listing arguments for and against without a final reasoned judgement will cap you mid-band. End with a sentence such as: “Overall, I believe [the statement] is [supported / not supported] because [the stronger argument] and [named religious source], although those who disagree would point to [counter-argument].”
judaism-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish teaching holds that God is absolutely One (the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4), the Creator of all existence (Genesis 1:1), and the Law-Giver who revealed the 613 mitzvot through Moses at Sinai.
  • God is both Judge (holding humanity accountable, especially at Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur) and deeply loving and merciful (chesed), holding justice and compassion in balance.
  • The Shekhinah describes God’s immanent presence among the Jewish people — not a separate being but God’s nearness, experienced in prayer, study and acts of justice.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important teaching in Judaism is that God is One.'
Evaluate this statement.

- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is recited twice daily and at the point of death — its centrality signals that monotheism is the foundation of all Jewish belief and practice. Maimonides lists the oneness of God as the second of his Thirteen Principles, after only God's existence. All other Jewish teachings — the covenant, the mitzvot, prayer — rest on the premise that there is one God. Arguments against: Some Jewish thinkers and communities emphasise that Judaism is fundamentally a way of life rather than a set of beliefs; observing the mitzvot (practical commandments) may be more central than any creedal statement. Others might argue that the covenant with Abraham or Moses is more foundational because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people — not merely who God is, but how God acts in history. Non-religious perspectives: A humanist might argue that ethical teachings (justice, tzedakah, Pikuach Nefesh) are more important than any theological claim, since they produce measurable good in the world. Justified conclusion required: e.g. 'The oneness of God is the most important teaching because without it every other belief loses its foundation, although the covenant and the mitzvot show how that oneness is expressed in lived Jewish experience.' Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments for and against; religious sources cited on both sides; justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments on both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided or limited development; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic points, listing, no conclusion.

The Shekhinah encourages communal worship and Torah study — knowing that God's presence is found where Jews gather motivates regular attendance at the synagogue and engagement with sacred texts.
