judaism-beliefs.title: Life After Death and the Messiah
judaism-beliefs.description: Olam ha-ba, resurrection and judgement; the Messiah in Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.
judaism-beliefs.content_html:
Jewish Beliefs About Life After Death

Unlike some other religious traditions, Judaism does not place enormous emphasis on detailed doctrines about life after death. The Tenakh focuses primarily on this world — on how to live justly, on the covenant relationship with God, and on the communal life of the Jewish people. Nevertheless, Jewish teaching does hold that this life is not all there is, and several important concepts address what lies beyond death.

The most significant term is olam ha-ba — “the world to come.” This refers to a future state of existence in which the soul continues after the death of the body. Some Jewish thinkers describe it as a realm of pure spiritual existence; others connect it to a future messianic age when the world is restored and the dead are resurrected. In the Talmud, the world to come is described as the place where righteous souls experience closeness to God.

Key Fact

Jewish teaching on life after death centres on three ideas: the soul’s continued existence in olam ha-ba (the world to come); judgement by God according to deeds in this life; and, in many traditions, a future resurrection of the body when the Messiah comes. These beliefs vary across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Judgement and Resurrection

Jewish teaching holds that God judges human beings according to their deeds. The annual pattern of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur mirrors this: on Rosh Hashanah, God opens the Book of Life and reviews the deeds of every person; on Yom Kippur, the judgement is sealed. The idea of judgement motivates ethical living — knowing that actions matter to God and have consequences beyond this life.

Belief in the resurrection of the body is held particularly strongly within Orthodox Judaism. Maimonides included belief in resurrection as one of his Thirteen Principles of Faith. The resurrection is understood as God’s ultimate vindication of the righteous: those who suffered unjustly in this world will be restored. Orthodox Jewish morning prayers include the declaration “Blessed are You, Lord our God, who restores life to the dead.”

Orthodox Judaism affirms both the existence of the soul in olam ha-ba and the physical resurrection of the body. These are held as literal beliefs, supported by Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles and traditional prayer texts. Orthodox communities regard resurrection as a core tenet.

Reform Judaism tends to emphasise the immortality of the soul rather than physical resurrection. Some Reform thinkers interpret resurrection metaphorically — as the enduring influence of a good life rather than a literal bodily rising. Reform prayer books have sometimes modified traditional resurrection language to speak instead of spiritual continuity. The focus in Reform communities is often on creating a just world in this life (tikkun olam) rather than detailed beliefs about the next.

Liberal Judaism (particularly the UK Liberal movement, founded 1902) generally takes a more open and questioning approach. Many Liberal Jews understand afterlife concepts symbolically, emphasising that goodness and righteousness have their own reward and that the details of olam ha-ba are beyond human certainty. What matters is living ethically and in accordance with Jewish values now.

The Messiah (Moshiach)

The concept of the Moshiach (Messiah) is one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish belief. The Jewish understanding of the Messiah is significantly different from the Christian one: in Jewish teaching, the Messiah is not a divine being but a human leader — a great king descended from the line of King David — who will usher in an era of universal peace, justice and the knowledge of God.

The Hebrew prophets — especially Isaiah — describe a future age in which swords will be turned into ploughshares, the nations will live in peace, and the Jewish people will return to the land of Israel. The Messiah is the agent through whom God will bring about this transformation. Maimonides lists belief in the eventual coming of the Messiah as his twelfth Principle of Faith, stating that even if the Messiah delays, one must wait for his arrival.

Orthodox Judaism awaits the coming of a personal Messiah — a specific individual who will fulfil all the biblical criteria: rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem, gathering all Jews to the land of Israel, and bringing an era of universal peace. This is understood literally and is a central hope in Orthodox prayer and liturgy.

Reform Judaism has generally reinterpreted the concept, moving away from the idea of a personal Messiah towards a “messianic age” — a future era of justice, peace and human flourishing that the entire Jewish people (and indeed all humanity) helps to bring about. Rather than waiting for one individual, the responsibility lies with all people to pursue justice and repair the world (tikkun olam).

Liberal Judaism similarly tends to understand the Messiah symbolically — as a vision of a better world that inspires ethical action now, rather than a prophetic prediction of a single future individual. Both Reform and Liberal traditions emphasise that Judaism’s deepest calling is to work for justice in the present world.

Key Fact

Orthodox Judaism awaits a personal moshiach (Messiah) descended from King David, who will rebuild the Temple and bring universal peace. Reform and Liberal Judaism tend to reinterpret this as a “messianic age” brought about through human action and tikkun olam — rather than through one individual.
judaism-beliefs.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about Jewish beliefs on life after death or the Messiah, you must name a sacred source. Strong choices are: the Tenakh (e.g. the Psalms, the prophets Isaiah or Ezekiel on resurrection); Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles of Faith (twelfth principle — belief in the Messiah; thirteenth — belief in resurrection); or the Talmud’s description of olam ha-ba. You also need to name the sub-tradition: Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism hold different views, and the mark scheme rewards this contrast. A top-band answer might read: “Orthodox Judaism holds that belief in the resurrection of the body is a core tenet, as stated by Maimonides in his Thirteen Principles of Faith; this means that death is not the end but that God will restore the righteous at the end of days.”

On 12-mark Evaluate questions about the Messiah, remember: the arguments ‘for’ a personal Messiah are Orthodox in nature; the arguments ‘against’ may draw on Reform/Liberal reinterpretation AND on non-religious/humanist views that reject any supernatural intervention in history. Your justified conclusion must say which argument is stronger and WHY — not just describe both sides.
judaism-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish teaching on life after death centres on olam ha-ba (the world to come), divine judgement, and (in Orthodox tradition) physical resurrection; Reform and Liberal Judaism emphasise the soul’s immortality and ethical living now over detailed afterlife doctrines.
  • The Messiah (moshiach) in Jewish teaching is a future human leader descended from King David, who will bring universal peace and justice — not a divine figure; Orthodox Judaism awaits a personal Messiah; Reform and Liberal traditions focus on a messianic age achieved through tikkun olam.
  • These contrasts between Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism are exactly what the exam rewards — always name the sub-tradition when explaining Jewish views on afterlife and the Messiah.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs, each with a clear explanation and a named source. practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the coming of the Messiah is the most important Jewish belief.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Maimonides lists belief in the Messiah as his twelfth Principle of Faith, stating that one must wait for the Messiah even if he delays — indicating its centrality to Orthodox Jewish theology. The messianic hope runs through the entire Hebrew prophetic tradition (Isaiah, Ezekiel) and through daily Orthodox prayer. It provides hope and direction for the entire Jewish people. Arguments against: Judaism is primarily a way of life and action rather than a system of beliefs; observing the mitzvot, keeping Shabbat, upholding tikkun olam may be more central to Jewish identity than any particular theological doctrine. Reform and Liberal Jews re-interpret or de-emphasise the personal Messiah — yet they are fully committed Jews. The Shema's declaration of God's oneness might be argued as the single most important belief. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that the concept of a Messiah is a human projection of the desire for a better world, and that the real work of repair is the responsibility of each individual, not a future leader. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced arguments for and against, Jewish sources on both sides, non-religious view included, justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic, listing, no conclusion.

judaism-beliefs.title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
judaism-beliefs.description: The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3), the Covenant at Sinai, Moses and the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17).
judaism-beliefs.content_html:
What Is a Covenant?

A covenant is not a simple contract. It is a solemn, binding relationship — in the Jewish context, an agreement between God and the Jewish people that carries profound obligations and promises on both sides. The covenants at the heart of Jewish theology are not merely ancient historical events; Jewish teaching holds that they remain active and binding today. They define who the Jewish people are in relation to God and what God expects of them.

Two covenants stand at the foundation of Jewish belief: the covenant with Abraham (recorded in Genesis 12 and 17) and the covenant at Sinai (recorded in Exodus 20), sealed through the giving of the Torah and the Ten Commandments.

The Covenant With Abraham

In Genesis 12:1-3, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a land that God will show him. The promise is threefold: land (“the promised land”), descendants (a great nation), and blessing (through Abraham’s descendants, all the families of the earth will be blessed). This is one of the most important passages in the Tenakh because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people and holds out a universal vision — Abraham’s family becoming a source of blessing for the entire world.

The covenant with Abraham was renewed and developed in Genesis 17, where God gives Abraham the sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) as the physical mark of the covenant. Every Jewish male circumcised at eight days old carries the sign of this covenant in his body — making it an embodied, communal identity marker across all generations.

Key Fact

The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) contains three promises: a land (Canaan, the “promised land”); descendants (a great nation); and blessing to all peoples of the earth through Abraham’s family. These promises form the bedrock of Jewish identity and hope.

Moses and the Covenant at Sinai

Moses is the most significant human figure in the Torah. After leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, Moses ascended Mount Sinai and received God’s revelation. The covenant made at Sinai is qualitatively different from the covenant with Abraham: at Sinai, the entire Israelite people — not just one individual and his family — entered into a binding agreement with God. They would be God’s people; God would be their God. In return, they accepted the Torah and its commandments as their way of life.

The significance of Moses cannot be overstated. He is described in the Torah as the greatest of all prophets — the only person who spoke with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jewish teaching holds that no prophet would arise in Israel greater than Moses, and his role as the transmitter of the Torah — both written and oral — makes him the founding teacher of the Jewish tradition.

The Ten Commandments

The Ten Commandments (Decalogue) recorded in Exodus 20:1-17 are the most prominent and widely recognised part of the Sinai revelation. They divide into two groups: the first four concern the relationship between humanity and God (no other gods; no idols; not taking God’s name in vain; keeping Shabbat holy), and the remaining six concern the relationship between people (honour your parents; do not murder; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not give false witness; do not covet).

Jewish tradition teaches that the full covenant at Sinai involved not just the Ten Commandments but the complete Torah — 613 commandments covering every aspect of life. The Ten Commandments are understood as a summary or foundational statement rather than the entirety of divine law. In synagogue services, the Ten Commandments are recited on certain occasions, and many synagogues display them on plaques near the ark.

The Torah divides the 613 mitzvot into two broad categories. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l’Makom) include prayer, observing Shabbat and festivals, keeping dietary laws, and daily rituals of study and gratitude. These sanctify the individual’s relationship with the divine. Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l’chavero) include not stealing, not lying, caring for the poor, and treating every person with dignity. These sanctify communal life. Jewish teaching holds that, for the mitzvot between man and man, God’s forgiveness on Yom Kippur cannot substitute for making direct amends to the person wronged.

The “promised land” (Eretz Yisrael) has remained a central element in Jewish consciousness throughout history, even during centuries of exile. Orthodox communities typically understand the promise of the land as literal and ongoing. Some Orthodox Jews make aliyah (immigration to Israel) as a religious act, fulfilling the covenant. Reform and Liberal communities hold more varied views: many affirm a spiritual or cultural connection to the land of Israel without prioritising physical settlement as a religious obligation. It is important to note that these are internal Jewish theological debates — the exam expects you to describe what different Jewish traditions teach, not to adjudicate the political dimensions.

Key Fact

Two foundational covenants: (1) Abraham — Genesis 12:1-3: land, descendants, blessing for all peoples. Sign: Brit Milah (circumcision). (2) Sinai — Exodus 20:1-17: the entire Israelite people accept God’s Torah and commandments; God becomes their God. Moses is the mediator. Together these covenants define Jewish identity and obligation.
judaism-beliefs.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about the covenant, you have two excellent sources ready: Genesis 12:1-3 (the covenant with Abraham) and Exodus 20:1-17 (the Ten Commandments at Sinai). Use them precisely. For example: “The Covenant with Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3 is important because God promised Abraham both land and descendants, meaning that Jewish identity is tied to a specific people and a specific place, giving Jews a sense of purpose and mission across all generations.” Two developed reasons, at least one named source: that is top-band structure.

On 12-mark Evaluate questions about the relative importance of the two covenants, remember: ‘which is more important’ arguments need to weigh them against each other. The Abraham covenant is more personal and promises; the Sinai covenant is more communal and demands. Both sides should use named sources. Your conclusion must explain WHY one side is stronger.
judaism-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) promises land, descendants and blessing for all peoples; the physical sign is Brit Milah (circumcision). It establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people.
  • The Covenant at Sinai (Exodus 20:1-17) extends the covenant to the entire Israelite people, through Moses; the Ten Commandments and the full Torah are accepted as God's law for all of Jewish life.
  • The 613 mitzvot divide into duties to God (bein adam l'Makom) and duties to other people (bein adam l'chavero); both categories are considered binding obligations, not optional guidelines.

practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Abraham Covenant is the oldest and most foundational — it establishes the identity of the Jewish people as God's chosen people and promises them a land and a future (Genesis 12:1-3). Without Abraham there is no Sinai — the covenant with Abraham creates the people who will later receive the Torah. The physical sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) makes it an embodied, lifelong commitment. Arguments against: The Sinai covenant encompasses the whole people, not just one individual and his family; it gives the Jewish people their entire way of life through the Torah and the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17). Jewish daily life is structured around the Sinai covenant — prayer, Shabbat, festivals, dietary laws all flow from it. Moses — the mediator of the Sinai covenant — is the greatest of all Jewish prophets. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that neither covenant is literally true but that the ethical teachings they generated (justice, care for the poor, respect for life) are what matter. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source present, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l'chavero) govern relationships with other people — e.g. not stealing, caring for the poor, honesty — sanctifying communal life (2 marks).

judaism-beliefs.title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
judaism-beliefs.description: Justice, tikkun olam, tzedakah and chesed; the sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh; the 613 mitzvot and free will.
judaism-beliefs.content_html:
Jewish Moral Principles: An Overview

Judaism is often described as a religion of action. Beliefs matter deeply, but what Jewish teaching emphasises above all else is how people treat one another and how they respond to God’s call to live justly. The mitzvot are not experienced by most Jews as burdensome restrictions but as a framework of sanctity — a way of bringing holiness into every moment of daily life. Jewish tradition teaches that no mitzvah is too small to matter: even feeding a hungry person or speaking honestly in a business deal is an act of worship.

Four core moral principles run through Jewish ethical teaching and appear explicitly in the Torah and the prophetic tradition: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity) and chesed (loving kindness). These four principles operate together and are reflected in countless practical mitzvot.

Tzedek: Justice

The Hebrew word tzedek means both “justice” and “righteousness.” The Torah commands, “Justice, justice shall you pursue” (Deuteronomy 16:20) — the double repetition of the word signals its urgency. Jewish courts (batei din) have a long tradition of applying Torah law to resolve disputes fairly. The prophets of the Tenakh — particularly Amos, Micah and Isaiah — repeatedly challenged the wealthy and powerful to treat the poor justly, warning that God is not satisfied with ritual worship when justice is absent from public life. “Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Tzedakah: Charity as Obligation

Tzedakah is often translated as “charity” but the Hebrew root is tzedek (justice) — giving to the poor is understood not as an act of generosity but as an act of justice. The poor have a right to a portion of the community’s resources; the wealthy have an obligation to give. Many Jewish communities have a tzedakah box (pushke) in the home into which small amounts are placed regularly, making giving a habitual part of daily life. Organisations such as World Jewish Relief operate from this principle, providing aid to vulnerable people across the world regardless of religion.

A common error is to describe the 613 mitzvot as “rules Jews have to follow.” Jewish teaching frames the mitzvot very differently: they are not restrictions imposed from outside but a gift from God — a detailed guide to living a sanctified life. Observant Jews describe the sense of meaning and structure the mitzvot bring to daily life. Keeping Shabbat is not experienced as a ban on work; it is experienced as a weekly gift of rest and family togetherness. This is the texture the exam rewards: mitzvot as joyful duties and expressions of the covenant, not as arbitrary rules.

Tikkun Olam: Healing the World

The concept of tikkun olam — repair or healing of the world — has become one of the most widely cited principles of Jewish ethics in the modern period, particularly in Reform and Liberal communities. It expresses the idea that the world as it is is not as it should be: there is suffering, injustice and brokenness. Every act of justice, every act of tzedakah, every act of chesed is a stitch in the repair of the world. Modern Jewish organisations that campaign for human rights, environmental justice or refugee support often invoke tikkun olam as their motivating principle. Jewish Care and HIAS (the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society) are examples in Britain and internationally.

The Sanctity of Human Life and Pikuach Nefesh

One of the most distinctive and powerful teachings in Judaism is Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving human life takes precedence over almost all of the commandments. The Talmud teaches that to save a single life is as if one has saved an entire world (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This remarkable teaching reflects the absolute sanctity of every human being, created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim).

In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that if a life is at risk, a Jew is obligated to break Shabbat rules, eat non-kosher food, or disregard almost any other commandment in order to save that life. Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews all affirm this principle, though they may apply it differently in edge cases. Medical professionals in the Jewish community may work on Shabbat; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive to save a life. The principle shows that the mitzvot serve human life — they are never more important than life itself.

Key Fact

Pikuach Nefesh: preserving human life overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot. Rooted in the teaching that every person is created in God’s image (tzelem Elohim) and that “one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world” (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This principle is accepted across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Free Will and the Mitzvot

Jewish teaching holds that God gave human beings genuine free will. The mitzvot are binding obligations, but no one is compelled to observe them. The Torah presents the choice explicitly: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). The fact that God requires observance of the mitzvot but does not compel it makes every act of obedience or disobedience morally significant.

The tension between free will and divine commandment is one that Jewish thinkers have explored across the centuries. If God knows in advance what each person will choose, how is that choice truly free? Maimonides wrote that “free will is given to every human being” and that God’s foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility — a teaching maintained across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism today.

Chesed — loving kindness — is expressed in countless ways in British Jewish community life. A large Reform synagogue in north-west London runs a weekly food bank and visits housebound elderly members; the young people’s group at a Manchester Reform synagogue organises clothing collections for asylum seekers. These acts are understood not simply as “volunteering” but as performing a mitzvah — fulfilling a divine commandment to show kindness to others. The distinction matters: chesed is not optional generosity but a religious obligation rooted in the covenant relationship with God.

Key Fact

The four core Jewish moral principles: Tzedek (justice — pursue fair treatment for all); Tikkun olam (repair the world — act to reduce suffering and injustice); Tzedakah (charity — giving as a moral obligation, not optional generosity); Chesed (loving kindness — showing compassion to all, especially the vulnerable).
judaism-beliefs.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about Jewish moral principles, your most powerful sources are: Deuteronomy 16:20 (“Justice, justice shall you pursue”) for tzedek; Talmud Sanhedrin 37a (“one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world”) for Pikuach Nefesh; and Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) for free will. You must name at least one of these and develop your reason around it.

A very common error is describing tzedakah as “voluntary charity.” Always clarify that tzedakah is a mitzvah — a moral obligation, not optional generosity. The Hebrew root of tzedakah is tzedek (justice): giving to the poor is not above-and-beyond kindness but what justice requires. This distinction often marks the difference between Developing and Mastering band answers.
judaism-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish moral life is structured around four core principles: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity as a moral obligation, not optional), and chesed (loving kindness).
  • Pikuach Nefesh — preserving human life — overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot; rooted in the Talmudic teaching that saving one life is equivalent to saving an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a).
  • The mitzvot are understood not as restrictive rules but as a framework of holiness; God gave human beings free will, making every act of obedience or kindness morally meaningful.

islam-practices.title: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts & Shahadah
islam-practices.description: The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam, Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi'a Islam, and the Shahadah.
islam-practices.content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core duties known as the Five Pillars. Just as the pillars of a building hold up its roof, these five duties hold up the entire faith. If a Muslim neglects any one of them, their spiritual life is weakened. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Islam is built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari).

Key Fact

The Five Pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer five times daily), Zakah (charitable giving of 2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime).

The Five Pillars are not optional — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. They give Muslims a shared identity across the world, uniting the global ummah through common acts of worship, charity and devotion. Whether a Muslim lives in London, Jakarta or Cairo, these duties connect them to every other believer.

Each pillar addresses a different aspect of devotion. The Shahadah establishes belief, Salah maintains daily contact with God, Zakah ensures social responsibility, Sawm builds spiritual discipline, and Hajj connects Muslims to the origins of their faith. Together they form a complete framework for living according to Allah’s will. Neglecting any pillar is considered sinful because each one supports the others.

The Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims — particularly Twelver Shi’a — follow the Ten Obligatory Acts. These include all of the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj and Jihad) plus five additional duties that reflect Shi’a theological priorities.

The ten duties are: Salah (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakah (almsgiving), Hajj (pilgrimage), Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of God), Amr bil ma’ruf (commanding what is good), Nahi anil munkar (forbidding what is evil), Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt — the Prophet’s family), and Tabarra (dissociating from the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt).

The additional duties reflect Shi’a emphasis on social justice, the authority of the Prophet’s family, and the responsibility of every Muslim to actively promote good and resist evil in society. Khums is particularly important because the money is partly given to the descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi’a community.

Key Fact

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share the core duties of prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage. The key difference is that Shi’a Muslims have additional obligations including Khums (20% tax) and duties related to social justice and loyalty to the Prophet’s family.

The Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the first and most fundamental of the Five Pillars. It is a single sentence that captures the entire foundation of Muslim belief:

Key Fact

“La ilaha illa Allah wa-Muhammad rasul Allah” — “There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.”

The first half of the Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the oneness of God. This rejects any form of Shirk (associating anything with God). The second half acknowledges Muhammad as God’s final messenger, meaning Muslims accept the authority of his teachings and the Qur’an.

The Shahadah in Daily Life

The Shahadah is woven into every stage of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered into the ear of a newborn baby so it is the first thing the child hears. It is recited during every set of daily prayers. Muslims hope it will be the last words they speak before death. Sincerely reciting the Shahadah before Muslim witnesses is the only requirement for converting to Islam — once spoken with genuine belief, a person becomes part of the ummah.

Shi’a Muslims add a third clause to the Shahadah: “and Ali is the friend of God.” This reflects their belief that Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, was divinely appointed as Muhammad’s successor. By including Ali in the declaration of faith, Shi’a Muslims affirm the authority of the Imamate — the line of twelve Imams descended from Ali who they believe are the rightful leaders of Islam.

Why is the Shahadah the Most Important Pillar?

The Shahadah is placed first among the Five Pillars because it is the foundation for everything else. Without sincere belief in one God and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other pillars — prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage — would have no meaning. The Qur’an declares: “Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” (Qur’an 2:163). Every act of Islamic worship flows from this declaration.

Tawhid is not just a belief — it shapes every aspect of a Muslim’s life. If Allah is the only God, then only He deserves worship, obedience and devotion. This means Muslims should not place anything — money, status, other people — above God. Surah 112 states: “He is Allah, the One, Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” The Shahadah is how Muslims publicly commit themselves to this belief every single day.
islam-practices.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark “Explain Similarities & Differences” questions on the Five Pillars, always compare Sunni and Shi’a perspectives — for example, both follow the core duties but Shi’a Muslims have additional obligations like Khums. For 12-mark evaluation questions, use Qur’anic references (such as Surah 112 or Surah 2:163) to support your arguments. Always give arguments on both sides before reaching a justified conclusion.
islam-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Five Pillars (Shahadah, Salah, Zakah, Sawm, Hajj) are compulsory duties for all Muslims. Shi’a Muslims also follow the Ten Obligatory Acts, which include additional duties like Khums and commanding good.
  • The Shahadah is the declaration of faith and the foundation for all other pillars — it affirms Tawhid (God’s oneness) and Muhammad’s prophethood. Shi’a Muslims add a reference to Ali.
  • The Shahadah is recited at birth, during daily prayers, and at death — it defines a Muslim’s entire life and is the only requirement for converting to Islam.

islam-practices.title: Salah & Sawm
islam-practices.description: How and why Muslims pray, the rituals of Salah, and fasting during Ramadan.
islam-practices.content_html:
Salah — The Second Pillar

Salah is the second of the Five Pillars and the most regular act of worship in a Muslim’s life. It is not simply asking God for things — it is a structured, formal act of submission to Allah that involves the whole body and mind. The Qur’an commands: “Establish prayer for My remembrance” (Qur’an 20:14).

The Five Daily Prayers

Sunni Muslims pray at five set times each day, calculated from the position of the sun. The times shift slightly throughout the year. This constant rhythm of prayer is designed to keep Allah at the centre of a Muslim’s day, no matter what else they are doing.

Key Fact

The five daily prayers are: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (just after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (just after sunset), and Isha (night). Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine Zuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha, praying three times a day.

Preparing for Prayer — Wudu

Before praying, Muslims must perform wudu — a ritual washing that prepares the body and mind for standing in God’s presence. Wudu involves washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, forearms up to the elbows, wiping the head and ears, and washing the feet up to the ankles. The Qur’an instructs: “You who believe, when you are about to pray, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, wash your feet up to the ankles” (Qur’an 5:6). If water is unavailable, Muslims may use clean earth or sand in a practice called tayammum.

Direction, Movements and Recitations

All Muslims face the direction of the Ka’aba in Makkah when they pray. In a mosque, the mihrab shows this direction. Each prayer consists of a set number of rak’ah — cycles of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, accompanied by recitations from the Qur’an in Arabic. The physical act of prostration — placing the forehead on the ground — symbolises total submission to Allah.

Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean — at home, at work, or outdoors. However, praying in the mosque is considered more meritorious, especially for men. Muhammad said that prayer in congregation is “twenty-seven times more rewarding than prayer performed individually” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). In the mosque, an imam leads the prayer, and worshippers stand in rows facing the mihrab. Women may pray in a separate area or at home. At home, Muslims use a prayer mat and a compass to find the direction of Makkah.

Jummah is the Friday congregational prayer, held at the mosque just after midday. It replaces the normal Zuhr prayer. All adult male Muslims are expected to attend, and women may also attend. The imam delivers a khutbah (sermon) covering religious guidance, moral teaching and community matters. The Qur’an instructs: “Believers! When the call to prayer is made on the day of congregation, hurry towards the reminder of God and leave off your trading” (Qur’an 62:9). Jummah strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together as a community each week.

Key Fact

Sunni and Shi’a Muslims both perform the five daily prayers, but Shi’a Muslims often combine them into three sessions. Shi’a Muslims may also place a small clay tablet called a turbah on the ground to prostrate upon, as they believe the forehead should touch natural earth rather than carpet.

Sawm — Fasting During Ramadan

Sawm is the fourth pillar of Islam. During the holy month of Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn (Fajr) to sunset (Maghrib). They abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations during daylight hours. The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar, often shared with family and community.

Origins and Significance

Ramadan is the month in which the Qur’an was first revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril. The Qur’an commands: “It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast” (Qur’an 2:185). Fasting teaches self-discipline, empathy for the poor, and gratitude to Allah for His provision.

Benefits of fasting: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness), strengthens willpower, creates empathy with those who go hungry, and brings the community together through shared iftar meals and increased mosque attendance. Muslims believe fasting purifies the soul and brings them closer to Allah.

Exceptions: Certain people are exempt from fasting: young children, the elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding women, people who are ill, travellers, and those menstruating. Most of these people are expected to make up the missed days later or feed a poor person for each day missed.

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power): This falls within the last ten nights of Ramadan and commemorates the night the Qur’an was first revealed. The Qur’an says: “The Night of Power is better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the entire night in prayer, believing that worship on this night earns greater reward than a thousand months of ordinary worship.

Key Fact

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an and is described as “better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the night in prayer and reflection.
islam-practices.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on Salah, always mention both the physical preparations (wudu, facing Makkah) and the spiritual purpose (submission to God, maintaining God-consciousness). For Sawm questions, link the practice back to the Qur’an (2:185 and 97:3) and explain both the personal benefits (self-discipline, empathy) and the communal benefits (shared iftar, increased worship). In “Explain Similarities & Differences” questions, the Sunni/Shi’a prayer differences (combining prayers, turbah) are excellent points to develop.
islam-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Salah involves praying five times daily after performing wudu, facing Makkah, and completing rak’ah. Jummah on Friday is a compulsory congregational prayer. Shi’a Muslims may combine prayers into three sessions.
  • Sawm during Ramadan means fasting from dawn to sunset. It commemorates the revelation of the Qur’an, teaches self-discipline and empathy, and brings the community together.
  • Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) in the last ten nights of Ramadan is considered more valuable than a thousand months of worship.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Sawm during Ramadan is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.

Reason 2: Fasting creates empathy with the poor and hungry. By experiencing hunger first-hand, Muslims develop compassion and are motivated to give charity (Zakah). This strengthens social bonds within the ummah. (1–2 marks)

Arguments for:
• Muhammad said prayer in congregation is ‘twenty-seven times more rewarding than prayer performed individually’ (Hadith), showing the Prophet valued mosque prayer.
• Mosque prayer strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together, creating a sense of community and shared worship.
• Jummah (Friday prayer) is compulsory in congregation — the Qur’an says ‘hurry towards the reminder of God’ (62:9).
• The imam’s leadership ensures prayers are performed correctly.

Arguments against:
• Islam teaches that the entire earth is a place of prayer — Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean, showing location is less important than sincerity.
• Some Muslims (e.g. women, the elderly, those with disabilities) may find it difficult to attend a mosque regularly. Their prayers at home are equally valid.
• What matters most is the intention (niyyah) behind the prayer, not the location. A sincere prayer at home is better than a distracted one in a mosque.
• In countries where Muslims are a minority, there may not be a nearby mosque.

islam-practices.title: Zakah & Hajj
islam-practices.description: The role and significance of Zakah, Khums in Shi'a Islam, and the pilgrimage to Makkah (Hajj).
islam-practices.content_html:
Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah is the third pillar of Islam and means “purification” or “growth.” By giving away a portion of their wealth, Muslims purify what remains and acknowledge that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah. It is not considered charity in the voluntary sense — it is a compulsory duty for every Muslim whose savings exceed a minimum threshold called the nisab.

Key Fact

Muslims must give 2.5% of their annual savings above the nisab threshold. The Qur’an specifies eight categories of people who may receive Zakah, including the poor, the needy, those in debt, and travellers in difficulty (Qur’an 9:60).

Origins and Purpose

Zakah has its origins in the Qur’an and the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. The Qur’an links prayer and charity repeatedly: “Establish prayer and pay Zakah” (Qur’an 2:43). This shows that worship of God and care for others are inseparable in Islam. The purpose of Zakah is threefold: it purifies the giver from greed and selfishness, it supports those in genuine need, and it reduces inequality within the ummah.

For the giver: Zakah purifies wealth by removing attachment to material possessions. It reminds Muslims that everything they own is a trust from Allah and develops generosity and compassion. Muslims believe that giving Zakah brings spiritual reward and protects them on the Day of Judgement.

For the recipient: Zakah provides essential support for the poor, the sick, travellers in need and those in debt. It helps prevent extreme poverty and ensures basic needs are met. The Qur’an identifies eight specific categories of recipient (9:60), ensuring money reaches those who need it most.

For the community: Zakah reduces the gap between rich and poor, creating a more just and equal society. It strengthens social bonds within the ummah because the wealthy are directly responsible for supporting the vulnerable. In some Muslim-majority countries, Zakah is collected and distributed by the state.

Khums means “one fifth” and is an additional financial duty unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims pay 20% of their surplus income (after living expenses) each year. Half of the Khums goes to Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) and half to religious scholars and institutions. Khums is one of the Ten Obligatory Acts and reflects the Shi’a emphasis on supporting the Prophet’s family and the religious leadership.

Key Fact

Zakah (2.5% of savings) is paid by all Muslims, while Khums (20% of surplus income) is an additional duty for Shi’a Muslims. Both serve the purpose of social justice and redistributing wealth, but Khums also supports the Prophet’s descendants and Shi’a religious institutions.

Hajj — Pilgrimage to Makkah

Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in their lifetime. Hajj takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and attracts over two million Muslims from around the world each year. The Qur’an states: “Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it” (Qur’an 3:97).

Origins

Hajj traces its origins to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). Muslims believe that Ibrahim and his son Isma’il built the Ka’aba as the first house of worship dedicated to the one true God. Many of the rituals performed during Hajj commemorate events from Ibrahim’s life — his willingness to sacrifice his son, his wife Hajar’s search for water, and his rejection of Satan’s temptations.

How Hajj is Performed

Hajj lasts five to six days and involves a series of rituals at sacred sites in and around Makkah. Before beginning, pilgrims enter a state of ihram — they wear simple white garments (two unstitched cloths for men), symbolising equality before God. All distinctions of wealth, status and nationality are stripped away.

Tawaf: Pilgrims walk around the Ka’aba seven times in an anti-clockwise direction. This represents the unity of Muslims in worshipping one God. The Ka’aba is believed to be directly below God’s throne in heaven.

Sa’i: Pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting Hajar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma’il. This commemorates God’s provision of the Zamzam well.

Arafat: Pilgrims travel to the plain of Arafat and stand in prayer and reflection from noon to sunset. This is considered the most important ritual of Hajj — the Prophet Muhammad said: “Hajj is Arafat.” It represents standing before God on the Day of Judgement.

Muzdalifah: After sunset at Arafat, pilgrims travel to Muzdalifah where they pray, rest under the open sky, and collect pebbles for the next day’s ritual.

Mina — Stoning the Pillars: At Mina, pilgrims throw pebbles at three stone pillars representing the places where Ibrahim rejected Satan’s temptations. This symbolises the Muslim’s rejection of evil and temptation in their own life.

Sacrifice: An animal (usually a sheep or goat) is sacrificed at Mina, commemorating Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. The meat is distributed to the poor. This coincides with the festival of Id-ul-Adha celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

Key Fact

The key stages of Hajj include Tawaf (circling the Ka’aba), Sa’i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing at Arafat, collecting pebbles at Muzdalifah, stoning the pillars at Mina, and animal sacrifice. Each ritual commemorates events from the life of Ibrahim and symbolises key aspects of Muslim faith.
islam-practices.exam_tip_html: For questions on Zakah, explain both the spiritual purpose (purification of wealth, obedience to God) and the social purpose (reducing poverty, strengthening the ummah). For Hajj questions, be specific about the rituals and their significance — examiners reward students who can explain why each ritual is performed, not just what happens. Always link rituals back to Ibrahim. In “Explain Similarities & Differences” questions, Zakah vs Khums is an excellent comparison point.
islam-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Zakah requires Muslims to give 2.5% of their savings above the nisab threshold to those in need. It purifies wealth, supports the poor, and reduces inequality. Shi’a Muslims also pay Khums (20% of surplus income).
  • Hajj is a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage to Makkah involving rituals at the Ka’aba, Safa and Marwa, Arafat, Muzdalifah and Mina — each commemorating events from Ibrahim’s life.
  • Both Zakah and Hajj demonstrate submission to Allah, strengthen the global ummah, and connect Muslims to the origins of their faith.

practice_questions.text:
‘Zakah is more important than Hajj because it helps other people.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Zakah directly helps those in need — the poor, the sick, those in debt, and travellers. It addresses real-world suffering and social inequality.
• The Qur’an repeatedly links prayer and Zakah together (‘Establish prayer and pay Zakah’ — 2:43), showing that worship without social responsibility is incomplete.
• Zakah is annual and ongoing, while Hajj is a one-time obligation. Its cumulative impact on society is therefore greater.
• Helping others reflects Allah’s attribute of mercy and compassion.

Arguments against:
• Hajj is a direct command from God: ‘a duty owed to God by people who are able’ (Qur’an 3:97). Obeying God’s command is the highest priority for a Muslim.
• Hajj commemorates Ibrahim’s obedience and connects Muslims to the origins of their faith in a way Zakah cannot.
• Hajj is a transformative personal experience — standing at Arafat represents the Day of Judgement and inspires Muslims to live better lives afterwards.
• All five pillars are equally important because they form a complete framework for Islamic life. Removing any one weakens the whole.

islam-practices.title: Jihad & Islamic Festivals
islam-practices.description: Greater and lesser jihad, conditions for lesser jihad, and Islamic festivals.
islam-practices.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith). Scholars note that this hadith is graded as weak by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, and it does not appear in the six authoritative collections (Kutub al-Sittah); it traces to al-Khatib al-Baghdadi's 11th-century History of Baghdad. Despite its uncertain chain of transmission, it remains widely quoted in discussions of jihad.

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.
islam-practices.exam_tip_html: For jihad questions, always distinguish between greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) and lesser jihad (physical/military struggle). Examiners specifically look for the conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared — learn at least three with Qur’anic support (e.g. 2:190 and 8:61). For festivals, Ashura is the best topic for “Explain Similarities & Differences” questions because Sunni and Shi’a observances are completely different. Always reference the specific events each tradition commemorates.
islam-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greater jihad (the inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than lesser jihad (military defence). Lesser jihad is permitted only under strict conditions: it must be defensive, a last resort, proportionate, and declared by a legitimate authority.
  • Id-ul-Adha celebrates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son and coincides with Hajj. Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan with communal prayer, charity and celebration.
  • Ashura on 10th Muharram is observed very differently: Sunni Muslims fast (commemorating Musa), while Shi’a Muslims mourn Husayn’s martyrdom at the Battle of Karbala (680 CE).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how Sunni and Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura.
practice_questions.marks:
Difference 1: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a voluntary day of fasting. It commemorates the day God saved the Prophet Musa and the Israelites by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged others to do so. (2 marks)
Difference 2: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of intense mourning for the martyrdom of Husayn, the Prophet’s grandson, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Shi’a observe it with mourning processions and re-enactments, not fasting. (2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe greater jihad is more important than lesser jihad. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reason 1: Greater jihad is a lifelong, continuous struggle that every Muslim faces every day. It includes resisting temptation, studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, and striving to become a better person. Lesser jihad is only relevant in specific circumstances of conflict. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: The Prophet Muhammad himself described the inner struggle as the ‘greater’ jihad. When soldiers returned from battle, he told them: ‘You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires.’ This shows that even the Prophet considered personal spiritual effort more important than military action. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Hadith about returning from lesser to greater jihad / The Qur’an states ‘Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits’ (2:190), showing lesser jihad is restricted while greater jihad is unlimited in scope. (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘Islamic festivals are more important for building community than for personal faith.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Id-ul-Fitr brings the whole community together after Ramadan with shared meals, gifts and prayers at the mosque. It strengthens bonds within the ummah.
• Id-ul-Adha involves sharing sacrificial meat with neighbours and the poor, directly building social connections and supporting those in need.
• Zakat-ul-Fitr ensures even the poorest can participate in Eid celebrations, showing festivals are designed to include the whole community.
• Shi’a mourning processions during Ashura are deeply communal events that reinforce shared identity and collective memory.

Arguments against:
• Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim’s personal obedience to God — the festival reminds every Muslim of the importance of individual submission to Allah.
• Ramadan and Id-ul-Fitr are fundamentally about each Muslim’s personal relationship with God through fasting, prayer and self-discipline.
• The Qur’an links festivals to worship and gratitude to God, not primarily to social bonding.
• Personal faith and community are inseparable in Islam — one strengthens the other. The Five Pillars themselves are both individual duties and communal practices.

Top band (10–12) Well-argued with developed points on both sides, religious references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned arguments on both sides with some development.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Arguments on one side or simple arguments on both sides.
Lower band (1–3) Simple statements or a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Id-ul-Adha and Id-ul-Fitr.

judaism-practices.title: The Synagogue and Public Worship
judaism-practices.description: Synagogue roles, design features, Orthodox vs Reform differences, and the Amidah.
judaism-practices.content_html:
The Synagogue: Heart of Jewish Community Life

The synagogue is the central institution of Jewish communal life. The Hebrew word for synagogue is beit knesset — “house of assembly” — and it serves multiple purposes: a place of worship, a place of Torah study, and a community hub. Since the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE, the synagogue has replaced the Temple as the focus of Jewish religious life. Synagogues can be found wherever there is a Jewish community — from the ancient Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City of London (built 1701, the oldest synagogue in continual use in the United Kingdom) to modern synagogues in Manchester, Leeds and every major British city.

Synagogues serve three broad functions that echo the three Hebrew terms beit knesset (assembly), beit tefillah (house of prayer) and beit midrash (house of study). Prayer services are held daily in many communities; Torah classes and adult learning take place throughout the week; life-cycle events — Bar and Bat Mitzvah, weddings, memorial services — are celebrated and marked at the synagogue. In smaller communities, the synagogue is often the sole gathering point for the entire Jewish population of a town.

Key Fact

The synagogue has three functions in Jewish life: beit knesset (house of assembly — community gathering), beit tefillah (house of prayer — worship services), and beit midrash (house of study — Torah learning). Bevis Marks Synagogue in London, established 1701, is the oldest synagogue in continuous use in the United Kingdom.

Key Features of the Synagogue

Three features of the synagogue are especially significant in Jewish worship. The bimah is the raised reading platform from which the Torah scroll is read publicly. In traditional Orthodox synagogues, the bimah stands in the centre of the main hall, reflecting the ancient Temple's design and ensuring that the congregation surrounds the reader. In most Reform synagogues, the bimah is positioned at the front of the hall, closer to the ark, emphasising the unity of the service and the rabbi’s leadership role.

The aron hakodesh — the holy ark — is the most sacred object in the synagogue. It is placed on the wall facing Jerusalem (in the UK, this means the east wall), so that the congregation faces Jerusalem when they pray. The ark houses the Torah scrolls, which are dressed in embroidered covers and adorned with silver ornaments. Opening the ark is a solemn moment in the service; the congregation rises.

Above the ark burns the ner tamid — the eternal light. This light is never extinguished, symbolising God’s constant, eternal presence. It recalls the menorah (the seven-branched lamp) which burned continuously in the ancient Temple. The ner tamid is found in both Orthodox and Reform synagogues, making it one of the universal features of Jewish worship spaces.

Orthodox and Reform Synagogues: Key Differences

The two most significant differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogues are the role of women and the language of prayer. In Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately: the main floor is typically reserved for men, while women sit in a separate section — either an upper gallery (a mechitza) or a partitioned area to the side. Only men may lead services and read from the Torah in Orthodox practice. Reform synagogues are fully mixed: women sit alongside men, women may be ordained as rabbis, and both men and women lead services. The West London Synagogue (opened 1840) and the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in St John’s Wood are prominent UK Reform and Liberal institutions.

Orthodox synagogue services use Hebrew almost exclusively; many prayers have been unchanged for centuries. Reform services in the UK use a mixture of Hebrew and English, with translations and explanations integrated into the service to make worship accessible to all. Reform communities also tend to have shorter services. Despite these differences, both Orthodox and Reform synagogues affirm the same central beliefs — God’s oneness, the covenant, the mitzvot — and both face Jerusalem during prayer.

Orthodox men cover their heads at all times in the synagogue (and many do so throughout the day); in Reform settings, head covering is encouraged but not always required, and women sometimes choose to wear a kippah. Orthodox services use traditional chazanut (cantorial singing) without musical instruments on Shabbat, as playing instruments is not permitted on the day of rest. Many Reform synagogues use organs or other instruments during services. The rabbi’s role differs too: Orthodox rabbis are always male and serve primarily as legal authorities and preachers; Reform communities have ordained women as rabbis since the early twentieth century in America and since the late twentieth century in the UK.

The Amidah: The Standing Prayer

The central prayer of every Jewish service is the Amidah (literally “the standing one”). It is recited three times daily — morning, afternoon and evening. During the Amidah, the worshipper stands with feet together, facing Jerusalem, and prays silently. The Amidah is divided into three sections: praise of God (three opening blessings), petitions (thirteen blessings asking for understanding, forgiveness, healing, redemption and more), and thanksgiving (three closing blessings).

The Amidah is one of the oldest prayers in Judaism, with roots in the time of the Second Temple. On Shabbat and festivals, the thirteen petitions are replaced with a single blessing for the special holiness of the day, shortening the service. The Amidah is found in both Orthodox and Reform prayer books, although Reform versions may use more inclusive language and include Hebrew alongside English translation. Its presence at the heart of every service makes it the most important regular prayer in Jewish worship.

Jewish tradition teaches that prayer should be directed towards Jerusalem and, specifically, towards the site of the Temple Mount. This is based on the prayer of Solomon at the dedication of the First Temple, which describes God as hearing prayers offered in the direction of the Temple (1 Kings 8:38-39). Even after the Temple’s destruction, the orientation towards Jerusalem expresses the Jewish longing for restoration and the continued connection to the spiritual centre of Jewish life. It also unites all Jews in prayer: wherever they are in the world, they pray in the same direction.

Key Fact

Three essential features: bimah (raised reading platform — centre in Orthodox, front in Reform); aron hakodesh (holy ark — houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem); ner tamid (eternal light — above the ark, never extinguished, symbolises God’s constant presence). The Amidah is the standing prayer recited three times daily at the heart of synagogue worship.
judaism-practices.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about the synagogue or Jewish public worship, you must name a source of authority. Good options: the significance of the ner tamid recalling the Temple menorah (1 Kings 8); the Amidah’s roots in Second Temple worship; the orientation towards Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:38). For contrasting practices, always name the sub-tradition: ‘In Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately because...’ versus ‘In Reform synagogues, mixed seating reflects the belief that...’ This naming of the sub-tradition is exactly what the mark scheme rewards.

On 12-mark Evaluate questions about whether the synagogue is the most important place for Jewish worship, prepare both sides: arguments FOR (community, Torah reading, Amidah, Rabbi teaching) and arguments AGAINST (home worship, Shabbat observance, private prayer are equally central; in the diaspora the home has often been described as a ‘mikdash me’at’ — a little sanctuary). Reach a justified conclusion.
judaism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The synagogue (beit knesset, beit tefillah, beit midrash) serves as the centre of Jewish communal, prayerful and educational life; its three key features are the bimah (reading platform), aron hakodesh (ark) and ner tamid (eternal light above the ark).
  • Orthodox synagogues have separated seating (mechitza), Hebrew-only prayers and male-only leadership; Reform synagogues are mixed-gender, blend Hebrew and English, and ordain women as rabbis.
  • The Amidah — the standing prayer — is the central prayer of every Jewish service, recited three times daily while standing and facing Jerusalem.

'The most important feature of a synagogue is the aron hakodesh.'

- refer to Jewish teaching

- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view

practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The aron hakodesh houses the Torah scrolls — the most sacred objects in Judaism, the written word of God. The congregation rises when the ark is opened, and all prayer is oriented towards it. Without the Torah, there is no Jewish worship. The ark's position facing Jerusalem connects every service to the Temple and to the covenant. Arguments against: The bimah might be considered more central, as it is where the Torah is publicly read — the reading of Torah is the climax of the Shabbat service. The ner tamid symbolises God's eternal presence; without God's presence, the ark is merely a container. The Amidah (the standing prayer) might be considered the most important practice, as it occurs three times daily even when no ark is present (e.g. in home prayer). Non-religious view: A non-believer might argue that none of these objects is important in itself — what matters is the community that gathers around them. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source present. Developing: One side developed. Emerging: Listing, no conclusion.

judaism-practices.title: Shabbat, Home Worship and Sacred Texts
judaism-practices.description: Shabbat in the home and synagogue; private prayer; the Tenakh and Talmud and their significance in daily Jewish life.
judaism-practices.content_html:
Shabbat: The Weekly Gift of Rest

Shabbat is the holiest day of the Jewish week and is described in the Torah as a foretaste of the world to come. It begins at sunset on Friday evening and ends at nightfall on Saturday — the appearance of three stars in the sky. The basis for Shabbat is found in the creation narrative: God rested on the seventh day and declared it holy (Genesis 2:2-3), and the fourth of the Ten Commandments instructs the Jewish people to “remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8).

The observance of Shabbat in the home begins on Friday evening with the lighting of at least two candles by the woman of the household, accompanied by a blessing. The candles symbolise the two aspects of Shabbat — remembering (zachor) and keeping (shamor). The family then attends synagogue for the Friday evening service (Kabbalat Shabbat), returns home, and celebrates Kiddush — the blessing over wine — and a special Shabbat meal. Two plaited loaves of bread (challah) are placed on the table, recalling the double portion of manna the Israelites received in the desert.

Key Fact

The key elements of Shabbat home observance: candle lighting (Friday at sunset — symbolises the holiness of the day); Kiddush (blessing over wine — sanctifies the day); challah (two braided loaves); synagogue service (Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday evening, Shacharit on Saturday morning); Havdalah (the closing ceremony separating Shabbat from the rest of the week).

Shabbat Restrictions and Their Meaning

Traditional Jewish law (Halakha) prohibits 39 categories of creative work on Shabbat — the melachot — derived from the types of work required to build the Tabernacle in the desert. These include writing, cooking, lighting fires, and (in modern applications) using electricity, driving or using a telephone. For observant Orthodox Jews in Britain, Shabbat means walking to synagogue, spending time with family, studying Torah, eating special meals and resting completely from work.

Shabbat closes with a ceremony called Havdalah (“separation”), which uses a braided candle, fragrant spices and wine. The spices are smelled to carry the sweetness of Shabbat into the week; the candle’s flame distinguishes between holy and ordinary; the wine marks the end of the sacred time.

Orthodox Jews observe Shabbat strictly, adhering to the traditional 39 prohibitions, walking to synagogue (no driving), and abstaining from electronic devices throughout the day. Reform and Liberal Jews also value Shabbat highly but interpret the prohibitions more individually; many will drive to synagogue if it is far, and some will use electricity for family gatherings or meals. Both traditions affirm that Shabbat is holy and that the day should be set apart from the rest of the week. The difference lies in how that sanctity is expressed: through halakhic restriction (Orthodox) or through personal intention and meaning-making (Reform/Liberal).

Worship in the Home: Private Prayer

Jewish religious life is not confined to the synagogue. The home is described in Jewish tradition as a mikdash me’at — a “little sanctuary” — and many of the most significant religious practices take place there. The mezuzah — a small parchment scroll containing the Shema, fixed to the doorpost — is a constant reminder of God’s presence and the covenant as one enters and leaves the house.

Observant Jews pray three times daily: the morning prayer (Shacharit), the afternoon prayer (Mincha) and the evening prayer (Ma’ariv). These prayers can be said at home when attendance at synagogue is not possible, and they maintain the rhythm of connection with God throughout the day. Before eating, a blessing (bracha) is recited; after meals, a longer grace (Birkat Hamazon) is sung. These small, frequent acts of prayer sanctify daily life and express the Jewish conviction that God’s presence is everywhere, not only in the synagogue.

The Tenakh: The Written Law

The Tenakh is the Hebrew Bible and the foundational sacred text of Judaism. Its name is an acronym: Torah (the Five Books of Moses), Nevi’im (the Prophets) and Ketuvim (the Writings, including Psalms, Proverbs and the book of Job). The Torah — the first five books — is the most authoritative section, believed to have been directly revealed by God to Moses at Sinai. It is the source of the 613 mitzvot.

In the synagogue, the Torah is stored as handwritten scrolls in the aron hakodesh. The entire Torah is read aloud in the synagogue over the course of a year (the annual Torah cycle), with a portion read each Shabbat morning. The public reading of Torah is one of the oldest forms of Jewish worship, dating back at least to the time of Ezra (5th century BCE). The Prophets section of the Tenakh (Nevi’im) contributes the haftarah — a passage read after the Torah portion each Shabbat.

The Talmud: The Oral Law

Alongside the written Torah, Jewish tradition holds that God also gave Moses an oral law — practical explanations and applications of the Torah’s commandments. This oral tradition was eventually written down in the Mishnah (compiled around 200 CE) and later expanded into the Talmud through the addition of the Gemara (rabbinic commentary). The Babylonian Talmud, completed around 500 CE, is the authoritative version in most Jewish communities today.

The Talmud is central to Jewish religious life because it shows how the Torah’s principles apply to practical situations across every era. Topics include Shabbat observance, family law, prayer, business ethics, medicine and much more. For Orthodox Jews, the Talmud is an authoritative legal guide; study of Talmud (Gemara) is considered one of the greatest mitzvot. In the UK, dedicated yeshivot (religious academies) and adult learning programmes at synagogues across London and Manchester provide structured Talmud study. Reform and Liberal Jews also value the Talmud but approach it with greater selectivity — using it as a resource for ethical reflection rather than a binding legal code.

For many British Jewish families, engagement with the Tenakh and Talmud happens at multiple levels. A Reform family in north London might read the Shabbat Torah portion together at the dinner table before discussing its meaning; an Orthodox family in Manchester might have their children attending cheder (religious school) three times a week, learning Hebrew, Torah and Mishnah alongside secular education. The Daf Yomi programme (one page of Talmud per day) has participants from across the Jewish world, completing the full cycle every seven-and-a-half years; thousands of British Jews participate. These varied forms of engagement show that sacred text study is not limited to scholars but is part of the everyday fabric of Jewish life.

Key Fact

Tenakh = written law (Torah + Nevi’im + Ketuvim). Talmud = oral law (Mishnah + Gemara). Both are authoritative in Orthodox Judaism; the Talmud shows how Torah principles apply in practice. Reform Jews use both as resources for ethical guidance rather than strictly binding legal codes.
judaism-practices.exam_tip_html:
For 6-mark Explain questions on Shabbat or sacred texts, your strongest sources are: Exodus 20:8 (“remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy”) for Shabbat; Genesis 2:2-3 (God rested on the seventh day) for Shabbat’s theological basis; the Talmud itself as a source for oral law tradition. Always name the sub-tradition when explaining differences: “Orthodox Jews observe Shabbat strictly, including the 39 prohibited categories of work, because...” versus “Reform Jews approach Shabbat observance more personally, believing that the spirit of the day matters more than the specific prohibitions...” This contrast is exactly what gains marks.

On 4-mark Explain questions about Shabbat, a common error is listing elements of the Shabbat meal (candles, wine, challah) without explaining what they mean. Each element should be followed by a development: “...because this symbolises X / this shows that Jews believe Y.”
judaism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shabbat (sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday) is the holiest day of the Jewish week; key home practices include candle lighting, Kiddush (wine blessing), challah bread, synagogue attendance and Havdalah at the close; Orthodox Jews observe 39 prohibited categories of work; Reform Jews interpret observance more individually.
  • The home is a 'little sanctuary' (mikdash me'at) in Jewish life; the mezuzah, three daily prayers and blessings over food all sanctify daily life beyond the synagogue.
  • The Tenakh (written law: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim) and the Talmud (oral law: Mishnah + Gemara) together form the foundation of Jewish belief and practice; their study is itself a central mitzvah.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with named sources.
