islam-beliefs.title: Risalah, Holy Books & Prophethood
islam-beliefs.description: Prophethood (Risalah), the authority of the Qur'an and holy books, and the Shi'a Imamate.
islam-beliefs.content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but Jibril pressed him forcefully three times and commanded him to recite. As recorded in Sahih Bukhari (Hadith 3), the Prophet returned trembling, his heart beating severely. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.
islam-beliefs.exam_tip_html: When answering a 12-mark evaluation question about the importance of prophethood or the Qur’an, remember to consider both Sunni and Shi’a perspectives. Shi’a Muslims give additional authority to the Imams as interpreters of the Qur’an. Showing awareness of both traditions demonstrates “reasoned consideration of different points of view” — essential for reaching Level 4.
islam-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Risalah (prophethood) means Allah sent prophets to guide humanity. Adam was the first, Ibrahim showed perfect submission, and Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets — the final messenger (Surah 33:40).
  • The Qur’an has supreme authority because it is the only holy book Muslims believe has never been corrupted. Previous books (Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Scrolls of Abraham) are respected but considered altered.
  • The Imamate is unique to Shi’a Islam. Twelve divinely appointed, infallible Imams succeeded Muhammad. The twelfth Imam is believed to be in hiding and will return at the end of time.

Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• The Qur'an is the direct, unchanged word of Allah — the only holy book that has not been corrupted. It is the supreme source of authority.
• It covers all aspects of life: worship, morality, law, family and social conduct.
• Surah 6:115 states: 'The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice' — suggesting the Qur'an is complete.

Arguments against:
• The Hadith and Sunnah are essential for understanding how to apply the Qur'an in practice. The Qur'an commands Muslims to pray but does not detail how — this comes from Muhammad's example.
• Shi'a Muslims also follow the teachings of the Imams, who are considered infallible interpreters of the Qur'an. The Imamate provides ongoing guidance.
• Scholarly consensus (ijma) and analogical reasoning (qiyas) are used to apply Qur'anic principles to modern issues not directly addressed in the text.
• The previous holy books (Torah, Psalms, Gospel) are also recognised as originally from Allah, even if Muslims believe they have been altered.
[12 marks]

• The belief that the twelfth Imam will return to establish justice gives Shi'a Muslims hope for the future. It influences their commitment to social justice now, as they believe they should prepare for the Imam's return by fighting oppression and injustice.
[4 marks]

islam-beliefs.title: Al-Qadr, Akhirah & the Day of Judgement
islam-beliefs.description: Predestination, human freedom, the Day of Judgement, resurrection, heaven and hell in Islam.
islam-beliefs.content_html:
Al-Qadr — Predestination

Al-Qadr is the sixth article of Sunni faith. It means predestination — the belief that Allah already knows and has determined everything that will happen. Nothing occurs by accident or chance. Surah 9:51 states: “Only what God has decreed will happen to us. He is our Master.” This includes every event in a person’s life, from birth to death.

Muslims believe Allah has complete knowledge of the past, present and future. Before a child is born, an angel records four things about their life: their provision (livelihood), their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be happy or unhappy. This is written in the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh al-Mahfuz), which contains the record of all that has been and all that will be.

Key Fact

Al-Qadr does not mean humans are puppets. Muslims believe Allah knows in advance what choices a person will make, but the person still makes those choices freely. It is this freedom that makes humans accountable on the Day of Judgement.

Predestination and Human Freedom

One of the most complex issues in Islamic theology is how predestination relates to human freedom. If Allah has already decided everything, can humans truly be free? And if they are not free, how can they be held responsible for their actions on the Day of Judgement?

Most Muslims hold that both beliefs are true simultaneously. Allah’s knowledge is absolute — He knows what every person will do before they do it. But this foreknowledge does not force people to act in a particular way. Humans have genuine freedom of choice (ikhtiyar) and are responsible for their decisions. It is like a teacher who knows a student will fail an exam — the teacher’s knowledge did not cause the failure; the student’s lack of revision did.

Sunni view: Al-Qadr is one of the Six Articles of Faith. Sunni Muslims generally emphasise that everything happens according to Allah’s will. Even suffering and hardship are part of His plan. This belief gives comfort in difficult times — if something bad happens, a Muslim can trust it is part of Allah’s greater purpose, even if they cannot understand it.

Shi’a view: Shi’a Muslims place greater emphasis on Adalat (divine justice). They argue that Allah’s justice means He would not predetermine someone to sin and then punish them for it — that would be unjust. Shi’a theology therefore gives more weight to human free will, arguing that people genuinely choose their actions and are justly accountable for them.

Belief in Al-Qadr influences Muslims in practical ways. It encourages Sabr (patience) during hardship, because Muslims trust that suffering is part of Allah’s plan. It also encourages gratitude in good times, since all blessings come from Allah. However, it does not encourage passivity — Muslims are still expected to work hard, make good choices and strive to follow Allah’s guidance.

The Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din)

Muslims believe that this life is a test, and that every person will face judgement before Allah at the end of time. The Day of Judgement is described vividly in the Qur’an as a terrifying, earth-shaking event. Surah 99:1–2 states: “When the earth is shaken with its earthquake, and the earth discharges its burdens.”

On this day, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, and all living things will die. Then a second blast will resurrect every person who has ever lived. Each person will stand before Allah and their book of deeds — recorded by the angels throughout their life — will be opened. Those who receive their book in the right hand will enter paradise; those who receive it in the left hand will face punishment.

Surah 99:7–8 states: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.” This teaches that no action — however small — escapes Allah’s notice. Every good deed and every sin will be accounted for.

Surah 23:102–103 describes the scales of judgement: “Those whose scales are heavy [with good deeds] will be the successful ones. But those whose scales are light will have lost their souls; in hell they will abide.” Good deeds are weighed against bad deeds, and the balance determines a person’s fate.

Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means life after death. Muslims believe the afterlife is eternal and that this earthly life is merely a temporary test. What a person does in this life determines their fate in the next. This belief underpins Muslim morality — every action carries consequences that extend beyond death.

Jannah (Paradise): The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of eternal peace, pleasure and closeness to Allah. Surah 47:15 describes rivers of water, milk, wine and honey, with fruits of every kind and forgiveness from Allah. Jannah has multiple levels, with the highest reserved for the most righteous. It is the ultimate reward for those who lived according to Allah’s will.

Jahannam (Hell): Jahannam is a place of torment and punishment for those who rejected Allah or lived sinfully without repentance. The Qur’an describes fire, boiling water and suffering. Surah 4:56 describes how the skin of those in hell will be replaced so they continue to feel the punishment. Most Muslims believe Jahannam can be temporary for sinful Muslims — Allah may forgive them and eventually admit them to paradise — but it is eternal for those who committed Shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah means Muslims see this life as a preparation for eternity. Every deed is recorded and will be judged. This motivates Muslims to pray, give charity, avoid sin and follow the Qur’an and Sunnah — because the stakes are not just for this life but for the life to come.

Human Responsibility and Accountability

The concepts of predestination, judgement and the afterlife work together to create a strong framework of personal accountability. Muslims believe every person is responsible for their own actions. No one can carry another’s sins (Surah 17:15). On the Day of Judgement, there are no excuses — the angels’ records are complete and Allah’s judgement is perfect.

This accountability influences how Muslims live. It encourages honesty, generosity, compassion and obedience to Allah. It discourages dishonesty, cruelty and arrogance, because Muslims know that even the smallest action — an “atom’s weight” — will be seen and judged. The belief in resurrection means there is no escape from this accountability, even in death.

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters Barzakh — a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement. In the grave, two angels (Munkar and Nakir) question the deceased about their faith: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?” A righteous person will answer correctly and experience comfort; a sinful person will struggle and experience suffering. This period lasts until the Day of Resurrection.
islam-beliefs.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark evaluation question may present a statement like “Belief in the afterlife is the most important belief in Islam.” To reach Level 4 (10–12 marks), you must argue both sides with reasoned chains of logic. Use Qur’anic references (Surah 99:7–8 on the atom’s weight of deeds, Surah 9:51 on predestination) and explain how beliefs influence Muslim behaviour. Always reach a personal conclusion supported by evidence.
islam-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Al-Qadr (predestination) means Allah knows everything in advance, but humans still have free will and are accountable for their choices. Shi’a Muslims emphasise Adalat (justice) to explain why free will is genuine.
  • On the Day of Judgement, every person will be resurrected and judged by Allah. Their book of deeds will determine whether they enter Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell).
  • Akhirah (life after death) is central to Muslim morality. This life is seen as a test, and every action — no matter how small — carries eternal consequences.

• Belief in the afterlife gives Muslims comfort when facing death or bereavement. They trust that righteous people will enter Jannah (paradise), which is a place of eternal peace and happiness. This hope reduces the fear of death and encourages patience during suffering.
• Akhirah discourages sinful behaviour because Muslims know that wrongdoing will be punished, either in Jahannam or through the questioning in the grave (Barzakh). This acts as a moral deterrent.

• Despite this foreknowledge, Muslims believe humans have genuine free will. They are responsible for their choices and will be held accountable on the Day of Judgement. Predestination does not remove personal responsibility.
• Source: Surah 9:51 — 'Only what God has decreed will happen to us. He is our Master' — affirms that all events are part of Allah's decree.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the afterlife is the most important belief in Islam.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Max Level 2 if no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• Akhirah gives purpose to this life — without belief in the afterlife, there would be less motivation to follow Allah's commands. This life is a test for the next.
• Surah 99:7–8 teaches that every deed, no matter how small, will be accounted for. This underpins all Muslim morality and worship.
• The Day of Judgement is when all other beliefs (Tawhid, prophethood, angels) culminate — it is the ultimate test of faith.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is the most fundamental belief — it is the first part of the Shahadah and the basis of all other beliefs. Without God, there would be no afterlife.
• Belief in the Qur'an and prophethood could be seen as more important because they provide the guidance Muslims need to pass the test of this life.
• All beliefs are interconnected — the Six Articles and Five Roots work as a complete system. Isolating one as 'most important' misses how they reinforce each other.
• Some Muslims might argue that practical obedience (the Five Pillars) matters more than any single doctrinal belief.
[12 marks]

• Al-Qadr encourages gratitude in good times. Muslims attribute all blessings to Allah rather than to luck or personal achievement. This influences them to say 'Alhamdulillah' (praise be to Allah) when something good happens and to share their blessings through charity.
[4 marks]

theme-a-relationships.title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
theme-a-relationships.description: Christian and Islamic teachings on marriage, divorce, cohabitation and sexual relationships.
theme-a-relationships.content_html:
Human Sexuality

Human sexuality refers to how people experience and express sexual attraction. People may be heterosexual (attracted to the opposite sex), homosexual (attracted to the same sex), or bisexual (attracted to both sexes). In contemporary British society, all three orientations are widely accepted and protected by law.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that sexual relationships should take place within marriage. However, there is a range of views within Christianity on homosexuality — from conservative opposition to liberal acceptance.

Sexual Relationships Before & Outside Marriage

In modern Britain, sex before marriage is common and widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sexual intimacy belongs within the commitment of marriage.

The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Pope Pius XI declared in 1930 that “every sexual act must be within a framework of marriage.” The Church of England generally agrees but is more lenient towards committed couples. Liberal Protestants tend to accept sex in loving, stable relationships even without marriage.

Islam is clear that sex must only happen within marriage. The Qur’an forbids zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex before marriage is a serious offence. Abdul Wahid Hamid wrote: “The only way to protect all within society is to maintain a society where only a man and his wife share the act of sex.”

Both Christianity and Islam also condemn adultery. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). The Qur’an (17:32) warns: “Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage, and an evil path.”

The Nature & Purpose of Marriage

Marriage is a formal, legal union between two people. For religious believers, it is more than a legal contract — it is a sacred commitment before God. Christians call marriage a sacrament (Catholics and some Anglicans) or a covenant before God.

Key Fact

The purposes of marriage include: lifelong companionship, a stable environment for children, sexual intimacy within a committed relationship, and (for religious believers) following God’s plan. Genesis 2:24 says a man shall “be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.” The Qur’an (30:21) describes marriage as a source of “love and mercy.”

Same-Sex Marriage & Cohabitation

In a Christian marriage ceremony, couples exchange vows before God, promising to love and cherish each other “for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, till death do us part.” In Islam, the marriage contract is called a nikah. It includes a mahr (financial gift from groom to bride), and both parties must freely consent. The ceremony is often simple, witnessed by family and an imam.

Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2013. Many liberal Christians support it, arguing that love and commitment matter more than the gender of the partners. However, the Catholic Church and many evangelical Christians oppose same-sex marriage, teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman as God intended.

Islam does not recognise same-sex marriage. Traditional Islamic teaching holds that marriage can only be between a man and a woman, based on the Qur’an’s teachings about the natural order of creation.

Cohabitation (living together without marriage) is increasingly common in Britain. Most Christians prefer marriage but liberal denominations accept cohabitation in committed relationships. Islam does not accept cohabitation because sexual relationships outside marriage are forbidden.

Divorce & Remarriage

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. In Britain, divorce is common — roughly 42% of marriages end in divorce. Common reasons include adultery, unreasonable behaviour, growing apart, financial problems and domestic abuse. Religious attitudes to divorce vary significantly, and the question of whether remarriage should be permitted after divorce is closely linked to beliefs about the permanence of marriage vows.

The Catholic Church does not allow divorce because marriage is a sacrament. Jesus taught: “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). Catholics may obtain an annulment if the marriage was not valid. The Church of England permits divorce and some clergy will remarry divorced people. Most Protestant churches accept divorce as a last resort, showing compassion for those in unhappy or abusive marriages.

Islam permits divorce but discourages it. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Of all the lawful things, divorce is the most hated by Allah.” There is a waiting period called iddah (three months) to allow time for reconciliation and to check if the wife is pregnant. Both men and women can initiate divorce in Islam, and remarriage is permitted after the iddah period.

Key Fact

The ethical tension around divorce centres on two principles: the sanctity of marriage vows (marriage is sacred and permanent) versus compassion (it is cruel to force people to stay in harmful or loveless marriages). Different religious traditions balance these principles differently.
theme-a-relationships.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark “Explain similarities and differences” question on Themes, you need to compare two religious perspectives. Always name both religions clearly, give a specific teaching or scripture for each, and explain why they hold that view. For example, compare Catholic and Islamic views on divorce — both value marriage highly but differ on whether divorce is ever permitted.
theme-a-relationships.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Both Christianity and Islam teach that sexual relationships belong within marriage, though liberal Christians are more accepting of sex in committed relationships and same-sex partnerships.
  • Marriage serves purposes of companionship, procreation and following God’s plan. Same-sex marriage is accepted by some Christians but rejected by Catholics, evangelicals and Islam.
  • Divorce involves a tension between the sanctity of vows (Catholic view: no divorce) and compassion (Protestant and Islamic views: divorce as a last resort).

• Divorce can harm children and break up families.
• Couples should work harder to resolve their problems rather than give up.
Arguments against:
• Islam permits divorce as a last resort / Muhammad said it is 'the most hated of lawful things' but still allowed.
• Protestant Christians show compassion — forcing someone to stay in an abusive or loveless marriage causes suffering.
• The Church of England allows divorce and some clergy will remarry divorced people.
• Jesus showed compassion to sinners, suggesting he would not want people to suffer in bad marriages.

• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs, e.g. Catholic vs liberal Protestant views.

theme-a-relationships.title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
theme-a-relationships.description: Religious teachings on family structures, the purpose of families, and gender equality.
theme-a-relationships.content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people connected by blood, marriage or adoption. Families come in many forms in modern Britain. A nuclear family consists of two parents and their children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Other family types include single-parent families, blended (step) families, and same-sex parent families.

Both Christianity and Islam place great importance on family life. Families are seen as the foundation of society and the place where children learn right from wrong, receive love and security, and are raised in a faith. In Christianity, the Holy Family (Jesus, Mary and Joseph) is often presented as a model for family life. In Islam, the family is considered the cornerstone of the ummah and maintaining strong family ties is a religious duty.

Key Fact

The role of parents is to provide for their children physically, emotionally and spiritually. The role of children is to respect and obey their parents. The Bible says: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The Qur’an teaches: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to parents” (17:23).

The Purpose of Families

Religious teachings identify several key purposes of family life:

Procreation — Both Christianity and Islam teach that one purpose of marriage and family is to have children. Genesis 1:28 says: “Be fruitful and increase in number.” In Islam, children are seen as a blessing from Allah.

Stability and protection — Families provide a safe, stable environment where children are protected and nurtured. Christians believe the family unit reflects God’s love. Muslims see the family as the building block of the ummah (Muslim community).

Educating children in a faith — Religious families pass on their beliefs and values to the next generation. Christian parents often have children baptised and take them to church. Muslim parents teach children to pray and read the Qur’an from a young age.

Contemporary Family Issues

In modern Britain, same-sex couples can adopt children or have them through surrogacy or IVF. Some Christians accept same-sex parenting, arguing that a loving, stable home is what matters most. Liberal churches emphasise Jesus’s teaching of unconditional love. However, conservative Christians and the Catholic Church oppose same-sex parenting, believing children should be raised by a mother and a father as God intended. Islam does not accept same-sex parenting because homosexual relationships are considered haram (forbidden).

Polygamy means having more than one spouse. It is illegal in the UK. Christianity teaches that marriage is between one man and one woman. However, Islam permits a man to have up to four wives (Qur’an 4:3), provided he treats each wife equally. In practice, most British Muslims are monogamous. The Qur’an itself acknowledges this is difficult: “You will never be able to be equal between wives, even if it is your ardent desire” (4:129).

The Roles of Men & Women

Traditionally, men and women had distinct roles — men as providers and protectors, women as homemakers and carers. Many religious teachings reflect these traditional roles. St Paul wrote: “Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands” (Ephesians 5:22). In Islam, the Qur’an (4:34) states: “Men are the protectors and maintainers of women.”

Key Fact

However, many modern Christians argue for full equality between men and women. Galatians 3:28 says: “There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Similarly, the Qur’an (33:35) promises equal spiritual rewards for believing men and women. Many Muslims argue that Islam gave women rights to own property, inherit and divorce centuries before Western law did.

Gender Equality, Prejudice & Discrimination

Gender equality means treating men and women with equal rights and opportunities. Discrimination based on gender is illegal in the UK under the Equality Act 2010.

Examples of gender discrimination in religion include the Catholic Church only allowing men to be priests, and some mosques having separate (sometimes smaller) areas for women. However, many denominations now ordain women — the Church of England has had female priests since 1994 and female bishops since 2015. Many Christians and Muslims actively campaign for gender equality as part of their faith’s commitment to justice.

For equality: Both men and women are created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Galatians 3:28 teaches spiritual equality. The Qur’an (33:35) promises equal rewards. Jesus treated women with respect and included them among his followers (e.g. Mary Magdalene).

Against full equality of roles: Some believe God gave men and women different but complementary roles. St Paul said women should not teach or have authority over men (1 Timothy 2:12). In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide financially while women manage the household, though both roles are valued.

Key Fact

Prejudice means holding unfair opinions about someone based on their gender (or other characteristics). Discrimination is acting on those prejudices. Both Christianity and Islam teach that prejudice is wrong because all people are equal before God.
theme-a-relationships.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark evaluate question on gender equality, make sure you present arguments from both sides. Use specific scripture — Galatians 3:28 for equality and 1 Timothy 2:12 or Ephesians 5:22 for traditional roles. Always include both Christian and Islamic perspectives and reach a clear, justified conclusion at the end.
theme-a-relationships.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Families serve the purposes of procreation, stability and protection, and educating children in faith. Both Christianity and Islam see the family as the foundation of society.
  • Contemporary issues include same-sex parents (accepted by some Christians, rejected by Islam) and polygamy (illegal in the UK, permitted in Islam under conditions).
  • Gender equality is supported by scripture (Galatians 3:28, Qur’an 33:35) but some religious traditions maintain distinct roles for men and women. Gender discrimination is illegal in the UK.

theme-a-relationships.title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
theme-a-relationships.description: Contrasting Christian and Islamic beliefs on contraception and same-sex relationships.
theme-a-relationships.content_html:
Contraception & Family Planning

Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy. In modern Britain, contraception is widely available and accepted as a normal part of family planning. However, religious views on contraception vary significantly.

Key Fact

The Catholic Church is the only major Christian denomination that opposes all artificial contraception. Pope Paul VI’s encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968) taught that every sexual act must be open to the possibility of creating life. Catholics may only use natural family planning (tracking fertility cycles).

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept the use of artificial contraception. They argue that responsible family planning allows couples to provide better for the children they do have. The Methodist Church stated that “responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.” Contraception can also help prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Protestants see family planning as a practical way to show love and responsibility.

Islamic views on contraception are divided. Many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage, particularly if pregnancy would harm the mother’s health, the family cannot afford more children, or it would protect existing children’s welfare. The Hadith records that some companions of the Prophet practised withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and he did not forbid it. However, some scholars oppose contraception because children are a blessing from Allah and humans should not interfere with God’s will. Methods that are permanent (such as sterilisation) are generally considered haram unless medically necessary.

Sexual Relationships Before Marriage

The specification requires you to explain contrasting beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In contemporary British society, pre-marital sex is widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sex should be reserved for marriage.

Christianity: The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). However, liberal Protestants tend to accept sex within committed, loving relationships even without marriage.

Islam: Sex before marriage is strictly forbidden. The Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence. There is no liberal/conservative divide on this issue in Islam — the teaching is clear and universal.

Same-Sex Relationships

Same-sex relationships are legally protected in the UK. The Equality Act 2010 makes discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal. Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2013. However, religious views on same-sex relationships vary widely.

Key Fact

AQA requires you to explain contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships with reference to Christianity and at least one other religion. Christianity has a wide range of views, from strong opposition to full acceptance. Islam is more uniformly opposed to same-sex relationships.

Christian Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Conservative Christians oppose same-sex relationships. They cite Leviticus 18:22: “Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable.” The Catholic Church teaches that homosexual orientation is not sinful, but homosexual acts are. The Catechism states that homosexual people “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity” but should remain chaste.

Liberal Christians support same-sex relationships. They argue that the Bible must be interpreted in its historical context. Jesus never spoke about homosexuality but taught love for all people. Some denominations, such as the Quakers and United Reformed Church, perform same-sex marriages. They point to Jesus’s commandment: “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31).

The Church of England occupies a middle ground. It welcomes homosexual people and recognises civil partnerships and same-sex marriages performed in civil ceremonies. However, it does not currently allow same-sex marriages to take place in its churches. In 2023, the Church of England voted to allow blessings for same-sex couples but stopped short of allowing full church weddings. This ongoing debate shows how religious organisations can evolve on social issues.

Islamic Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Traditional Islamic teaching opposes all same-sex relationships. The Qur’an (7:80–81) tells the story of the Prophet Lut (Lot), whose people were punished for homosexual behaviour. Homosexual acts are classified as zinah under Shari’ah law.

However, some progressive Muslim organisations in Britain argue for greater acceptance. Groups like the Inclusive Mosque Initiative welcome LGBTQ+ Muslims. Many British Muslims also acknowledge that while they may personally disagree with homosexuality on religious grounds, they respect the laws of the country they live in and oppose discrimination against anyone.

Humanists and atheists generally support same-sex relationships and full equality for LGBTQ+ people. They argue that moral decisions should be based on human rights, happiness and the harm principle — not on ancient religious texts. Since same-sex relationships between consenting adults cause no harm, there is no ethical reason to oppose them. The British Humanist Association actively campaigns for LGBTQ+ rights.

Key Fact

The three contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships required by AQA are: (1) conservative Christians oppose them (Leviticus 18:22), (2) liberal Christians accept them (love is most important), and (3) Islam opposes them (Qur’an 7:80–81, story of Lut). You must be able to explain why each group holds its view.
theme-a-relationships.exam_tip_html: For “Explain contrasting beliefs” questions (4 marks), the examiner wants two different religious perspectives with development. A common mistake is giving two views from the same religion without enough contrast. For same-sex relationships, compare a liberal Christian view with an Islamic view for maximum marks. Always include a specific scripture reference to push into the top marks.
theme-a-relationships.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Catholic Church opposes artificial contraception (Humanae Vitae), while most Protestants and many Muslims accept it within marriage for responsible family planning.
  • Both Christianity and Islam teach that sex belongs within marriage, though liberal Christians are more accepting of pre-marital sex in committed relationships.
  • Christian views on same-sex relationships range from conservative opposition (Leviticus 18:22) to liberal acceptance (love is most important). Islam traditionally opposes same-sex relationships (Qur’an 7:80–81).

christianity-beliefs.title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
christianity-beliefs.description: How Christians understand God as omnipotent, loving and just, and the mystery of the Trinity.
christianity-beliefs.content_html:
The Nature of God

Christians are monotheistic — they believe in one God who created and sustains everything. Although God is called “Father,” Christians do not believe God has a physical body or a gender. God is a spirit, beyond human understanding, and is considered holy — completely pure, set apart and worthy of worship.

The Nicene Creed, recited by Christians worldwide, opens with the words: “We believe in One God.” Christians believe this one God has several key qualities that together make God perfect. Three of these qualities are central to the AQA specification: God as omnipotent, God as loving (benevolent), and God as just.

God as Omnipotent

Omnipotent means all-powerful. Christians believe God has unlimited power and authority — nothing is beyond what God can do. God demonstrated this power by creating the entire universe from nothing and continues to sustain all life.

Key Fact

“Nothing is impossible with God.” (Luke 1:37) — These words were spoken by the Angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary. Christians use this verse to show that God’s power has absolutely no limits.

Belief in God’s omnipotence influences Christians in several ways. When they see the complexity of nature, they see evidence of a powerful creator. It also means they trust that God can perform miracles, and it gives them confidence when they pray that God has the power to answer.

God as Loving (Benevolent)

Benevolent means all-loving and all-good. Christians believe God loves every human being unconditionally. God created humans out of love and wants to share that love with all creation.

Key Fact

“God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) — Christians see sending Jesus as the greatest act of God’s love.

This belief helps Christians feel valued and gives them a purpose — to share God’s love with others through kindness, charity and forgiveness. Because God is all-loving, Christians believe God forgives those who are truly sorry for their sins.

God as Just

Christians believe God is a just (fair) judge of all humanity. Because God is all-powerful and all-loving, God is the perfect giver of justice. This means God will never support injustice, oppression, prejudice or cruelty.

“God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) — This teaches Christians that God sees all actions and will judge everyone fairly. No wrongdoing will go unnoticed. Because of this, Christians are motivated to fight against injustice wherever they encounter it.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent, loving and just, why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil, and it is one of the biggest challenges to Christian belief.

The problem can be stated simply: if God is loving, he would want to stop suffering; if God is powerful, he could stop suffering; if God is just, he would not allow injustice. Yet suffering clearly exists. The philosopher David Hume called this the “inconsistent triad” — the three ideas seem to contradict each other.

Christians distinguish between two types of evil. Moral evil is caused by human actions — murder, theft, war and cruelty. Natural evil is caused by the natural world — earthquakes, disease, floods and famine.

Free will: God gave humans the freedom to choose how to live. Some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil. Christians argue that genuine free will is better than being puppets, even if some misuse it.

Life as a test: Some Christians believe suffering tests faith. The story of Job shows that God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful — and rewards those who do.

Part of God’s plan: Humans cannot fully understand God’s reasons. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) suggests God has a purpose for every person, even if suffering seems unfair.

The Devil: Some Christians believe Satan tempts people into sin. Evil is caused by the Devil, not by God — though this raises the question of why God allows the Devil to operate.

The Oneness of God and the Trinity

Although Christians believe in one God, they understand God as existing in three persons: Father, Son (Jesus Christ) and Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity. It does not mean there are three separate gods — the three persons are all fully God, sharing one divine nature.

Key Fact

The Trinity is one God in three persons: the Father (creator and sustainer), the Son (Jesus Christ, who became human to save humanity), and the Holy Spirit (God’s presence active in the world today). All three are equal and eternal.

God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all life. He is the source of all things and the one to whom Christians direct their prayers. Jesus taught his followers to pray “Our Father.”

God the Son is Jesus Christ. Christians believe the Son has always existed with the Father but took human form (the incarnation) to live among people, teach them about God, and die on the cross to save humanity from sin.

God the Holy Spirit is the unseen power of God at work in the world. Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides, comforts and strengthens believers. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire (Acts 2), empowering them to spread the Christian message.

The Nicene Creed affirms the Trinity: “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty… And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God… And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life.” The Trinity is central to Christian worship — Christians are baptised “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Some Christians find the Trinity difficult to understand. Common analogies include water existing as ice, liquid and steam (three forms, one substance), or the sun giving light, heat and energy. However, these analogies are imperfect — the Trinity is considered a mystery that humans can only partly grasp.
christianity-beliefs.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark “Explain Influence” question, you need to show how a belief affects the way Christians live. For example, believing God is just influences Christians to fight injustice and treat others fairly. Always make the link between the belief and its practical impact — do not just describe the belief on its own.
christianity-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe God is omnipotent (all-powerful), benevolent (all-loving) and just (fair) — three qualities that together make God perfect.
  • The problem of evil asks why suffering exists if God has these qualities. Christian responses include free will, suffering as a test of faith, and God’s plan being beyond human understanding.
  • The Trinity means one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit — all equal and eternal, sharing one divine nature.

• Christians are motivated to share God’s love with others through practical acts of kindness, charity work and forgiveness — imitating the unconditional love God shows them.
• Because God is all-loving, Christians believe in forgiveness. This influences them to forgive others who wrong them, just as God forgives those who repent.

practice_questions.text:
‘The problem of evil and suffering proves that God does not exist.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• If God is all-powerful and all-loving, he would want to and be able to stop suffering — yet suffering exists.
• David Hume’s inconsistent triad: God cannot be omnipotent, benevolent and allow evil to exist simultaneously.
• Natural evil (earthquakes, disease) cannot be blamed on human free will, making it harder to explain.
Arguments against the statement:
• Moral evil is explained by free will — God gave humans genuine choice, and some misuse it. This is not God’s fault.
• Suffering may be a test of faith. The story of Job shows God rewards those who remain faithful through suffering.
• God’s plan is beyond human understanding — ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you’ (Jeremiah 1:5).
• Belief in God brings hope and comfort through suffering, especially the promise of eternal life.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view. Logical chains of reasoning supported by knowledge. References to religion applied to the issue.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration of different points of view with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view. OR Recognition of different points of view. Max Level 2 if no reference to religion.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s) stated.
[12 marks]

Students may include:

• Belief in the Holy Spirit gives Christians confidence that God is active in the world today — guiding, comforting and strengthening them in daily life and decision-making.
• The Trinity helps Christians understand God’s relationship with humanity: the Father as creator, the Son as saviour, and the Spirit as ongoing guide.
• Christians recite the Nicene Creed which affirms the Trinity, uniting believers across different denominations in a shared statement of faith.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

christianity-beliefs.title: Creation, the Afterlife & Judgement
christianity-beliefs.description: Christian beliefs about how and why God created the world, and what happens after death.
christianity-beliefs.content_html:
Christian Beliefs About Creation

Christians believe God created the entire universe. The two main biblical accounts of creation are found in Genesis 1 and John 1:1–3. Both are important For the exam , and students must understand different Christian interpretations of these texts.

Genesis 1:1–3 — The Creation Account

The book of Genesis describes God creating the world in six days and resting on the seventh. “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:1–3)

Key Fact

Genesis 1 shows the role of both the Word and the Spirit in creation. God’s Spirit hovered over the waters (the Holy Spirit was present), and God spoke creation into existence (“God said”) — this is the Word (Logos) at work. Christians see this as evidence that the Trinity was active at creation.

John 1:1–3 — The Word (Logos)

The Gospel of John opens with a different perspective on creation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.” (John 1:1–3)

Christians understand “the Word” as referring to Jesus Christ (God the Son). This passage teaches that Jesus was not just a human teacher — he existed with God from the very beginning and played an active role in creating everything. Nothing that exists was made without him.

Taken together, Genesis 1 and John 1 show that all three persons of the Trinity were involved in creation. God the Father initiated creation. God the Son (the Word) was the agent through whom everything was made. God the Holy Spirit was present, hovering over the waters. This is significant because it shows the Trinity working together from the very beginning of time.

Different Interpretations of Creation

Christians disagree about how to interpret the creation accounts. The AQA exam expects you to understand these different views:

Literalist (fundamentalist) view: Some Christians believe the Genesis account is literally true — God created the world in six 24-hour days exactly as described. They reject the theory of evolution and believe the Earth is only a few thousand years old. They see the Bible as the direct word of God, without error.

Liberal (non-literal) view: Many Christians interpret the creation story as a myth or metaphor — it communicates important truths (that God is the creator, that creation is good, that humans are special) without being a scientific account. They accept the theory of evolution and the Big Bang as the mechanism God used. The “six days” may represent long periods of time.

Catholic view: The Catholic Church teaches that faith and science are not in conflict. Pope Francis has said that the Big Bang and evolution are real, but God is behind them. The creation stories reveal why God created (out of love), not how the physical process worked.

Key Fact

All Christians agree that God is the ultimate creator of everything. They disagree about how to interpret the Genesis account — literally (six 24-hour days) or non-literally (metaphorical, compatible with science). The exam often tests these “common and divergent views.”

Christian Beliefs About the Afterlife

Christians believe that physical death is not the end. What happens after death is a central part of Christian faith, and different Christians hold different views about the details.

Resurrection and Life After Death

Resurrection is the belief that the dead will be raised to new life. Christians believe this because Jesus himself was resurrected three days after his crucifixion. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17) — showing that resurrection is absolutely central to Christianity.

Some Christians believe in bodily resurrection — that the physical body will be raised and transformed. Others believe in spiritual resurrection — that the soul lives on in a new spiritual form. Catholics believe the body and soul are reunited at the resurrection on the last day.

Judgement

Christians believe God will judge every person after death. Some Christians distinguish between two types of judgement:

Particular judgement: This happens immediately after a person dies. Their soul is judged by God and sent to heaven, hell or (in Catholic belief) purgatory.

Final (Last) judgement: At the end of time, Jesus will return and judge all people — both the living and the dead. This is described in Matthew 25:31–46, the parable of the sheep and the goats, where those who helped others are welcomed into God’s kingdom and those who did not are sent away.

Heaven and Hell

Heaven is understood as a state of eternal happiness and peace in the presence of God. It is the ultimate reward for those who have lived according to God’s will. Jesus told the criminal crucified beside him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Hell is understood as eternal separation from God. Some Christians believe hell is a literal place of fire and torment. Others interpret it as the absence of God’s love and presence — a spiritual suffering rather than a physical one. Some liberal Christians question whether a loving God would condemn anyone to eternal suffering.

Key Fact

Beliefs about the afterlife influence how Christians live. Because they believe in judgement, they try to live morally, follow Jesus’s teachings, help others and avoid sin. The hope of heaven brings comfort in times of suffering, and the possibility of hell motivates them to stay on the right path.

Catholics also believe in purgatory — a state of purification after death where souls are cleansed of their sins before entering heaven. This is not a Protestant belief. Catholics pray for the dead, asking God to release souls from purgatory sooner.
christianity-beliefs.exam_tip_html: For the 6-mark “Explain with Sources” question, you must name and explain two beliefs AND support each with a specific source of authority (a Bible verse, creed or official teaching). Simply describing a belief without a source will limit you to a maximum of 4 marks. Write the quote, name the source, and then explain how it supports the belief.
christianity-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genesis 1 and John 1:1–3 show all three persons of the Trinity were involved in creation — the Father initiated, the Word (Son) was the agent, and the Spirit was present.
  • Christians disagree about whether Genesis should be taken literally (six days) or non-literally (metaphor compatible with science), but all agree God is the ultimate creator.
  • Christians believe in resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell — these beliefs shape how they live by motivating moral behaviour and offering hope beyond death.

• Belief in judgement motivates Christians to live morally and follow God’s teachings, because they believe their actions will be assessed by God after death. This influences daily decisions about honesty, kindness and helping others.
• The hope of heaven brings comfort during suffering or bereavement. Christians believe death is not the end, which helps them cope with grief and gives them something positive to look forward to.
• Belief in hell acts as a deterrent — Christians try to avoid sin because they believe persistent rejection of God leads to eternal separation from him.
• Catholics pray for the dead, believing prayers can help souls in purgatory reach heaven sooner. This influences their worship practices.

• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• Scientific evidence (Big Bang, evolution) contradicts a literal six-day creation. Most scientists accept the Earth is billions of years old, not thousands.
• Some argue Genesis was written for an ancient audience and reflects their understanding of the world, not modern scientific knowledge.
• The creation accounts in Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 appear to contradict each other, suggesting they are not literal historical records.
Arguments against the statement:
• Literalist Christians believe the Bible is the direct word of God and therefore without error. Genesis describes exactly what happened.
• Liberal Christians argue the creation accounts are not meant to be scientific — they teach important truths about WHY God created (out of love) and humanity’s special place in creation.
• Many Christians accept science and faith together — Pope Francis said the Big Bang and evolution are real but God is behind them. The accounts are not ‘outdated’ because their purpose is theological, not scientific.
• John 1:1–3 reinforces the importance of the Word in creation, giving it theological depth beyond a simple historical account.

• Some Christians are motivated to evangelise (spread the faith) because they believe accepting Jesus is necessary for a favourable judgement.

christianity-beliefs.title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection
christianity-beliefs.description: Why Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, and the significance of his death and rising.
christianity-beliefs.content_html:
The Incarnation

The incarnation is the Christian belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. The word literally means “made flesh.” Christians believe that Jesus was not just a good teacher or prophet — he was God the Son taking on a human body to live among people on Earth.

John 1:14 states: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” This connects directly to John 1:1, which says the Word was God. So the Word (God the Son) who created all things became a human being — Jesus of Nazareth. This is one of the most important beliefs in Christianity.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus is both fully God and fully human. He was not half-God and half-human, nor God pretending to be human. He experienced everything humans experience — hunger, tiredness, pain, temptation — while also being divine. This is affirmed in the Nicene Creed: “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.”

Jesus as the Son of God

Christians call Jesus the Son of God, meaning he has a unique relationship with God the Father. This is not meant literally — God did not have a child in the human sense. Rather, it means Jesus shares God’s divine nature and has existed with the Father for all eternity.

Several events in the Gospels confirm Jesus as the Son of God:

  • At Jesus’s baptism, a voice from heaven said: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).
  • At the transfiguration, God’s voice again declared: “This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!” (Mark 9:7).
  • Jesus performed miracles — healing the sick, calming storms, raising the dead — demonstrating divine power.

The incarnation is significant for several reasons. It shows that God loves humanity enough to become one of us. It means God understands human suffering from personal experience. It also means that Jesus’s teachings carry the full authority of God — when Jesus speaks, God speaks. Finally, it was necessary for salvation: only someone who was both God and human could bridge the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity.

The Crucifixion

The crucifixion refers to the death of Jesus on a Roman cross. Jesus was arrested, tried, and sentenced to death by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. He was nailed to a cross and died on a Friday, now commemorated as Good Friday.

Christians believe the crucifixion was not simply a tragic execution — it was part of God’s plan to save humanity from sin. Jesus willingly gave up his life as a sacrifice. Before his arrest, Jesus prayed: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42), showing he accepted his suffering as the Father’s will.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus’s death on the cross paid the price for human sin. Because Jesus was sinless, his death was a perfect sacrifice that restored the relationship between God and humanity. This is why the cross is the most important symbol in Christianity.

The Resurrection

The resurrection is the belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after his crucifixion. On Easter Sunday, women visiting Jesus’s tomb found it empty. An angel told them: “He is not here; he has risen!” (Matthew 28:6). Jesus then appeared to his disciples over 40 days.

The resurrection is the most important event in Christianity. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christianity falls apart.

It proves Jesus is the Son of God. Only God could conquer death. The resurrection confirms that Jesus truly was divine.

It shows God’s power over death. Death is not the end — God has the power to raise the dead. This gives Christians hope that they too will be resurrected.

It confirms the promise of eternal life. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25).

It is the basis of Christian worship. Christians worship on Sunday because it is the day Jesus rose. Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar.

The Ascension

Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus ascended (went up) to heaven. Acts 1:9 describes how “he was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid him from their sight.” Two angels then told the disciples that Jesus would return in the same way.

The ascension is significant because it shows Jesus’s mission on Earth was complete. He returned to the Father, where Christians believe he sits “at the right hand of God” (the Nicene Creed) — a position of honour and authority. The ascension also prepared the way for the Holy Spirit to come at Pentecost, empowering the disciples to spread the Christian message. Christians believe Jesus will return from heaven at the end of time to judge the living and the dead.

Key Fact

The events of Jesus’s life form a connected sequence: the incarnation (God becomes human), the crucifixion (Jesus dies for sin), the resurrection (Jesus conquers death), and the ascension (Jesus returns to heaven). Each event is essential to the Christian understanding of salvation.
christianity-beliefs.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the crucifixion and resurrection, always explain the significance — not just what happened, but why it matters to Christians. For example, don’t just say “Jesus died on the cross” — explain that his death paid the price for human sin and restored the relationship between God and humanity. The exam rewards understanding of meaning and importance, not just retelling the story.
christianity-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The incarnation means God became human in Jesus Christ. Jesus is both fully God and fully human, as affirmed in John 1:14 and the Nicene Creed.
  • The crucifixion was not just a tragic death but a sacrifice for human sin. The resurrection proved Jesus was the Son of God and gives Christians hope of eternal life.
  • The ascension completed Jesus’s earthly mission and prepared the way for the Holy Spirit to guide believers.

• Christians worship on Sunday because it is the day Jesus rose from the dead. The resurrection shapes the pattern of Christian worship and makes Easter the most important festival in the Christian calendar.
• The resurrection confirms that Jesus is the Son of God, which strengthens Christians’ faith and commitment to following his teachings.

Students may include:

• Jesus is both fully God and fully human. The Nicene Creed affirms Jesus as ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.’ He was not half-God or God pretending to be human, but genuinely both. This was necessary for salvation — only someone who was both could bridge the gap between God and humanity. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied for additional marks. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources of authority. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The resurrection of Jesus is the most important Christian belief.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• St Paul wrote ‘If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile’ (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christianity would have no foundation.
• The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God. Only God could conquer death, confirming Jesus’s divine nature.
• It gives Christians the promise of eternal life — ‘I am the resurrection and the life’ (John 11:25). Without this hope, the Christian message loses its power.
• It is the reason Christians worship on Sundays and celebrate Easter as their most important festival.
Arguments against the statement:
• The incarnation could be seen as more important — without God becoming human, none of the other events (crucifixion, resurrection) would have happened.
• The crucifixion is when salvation actually happened — Jesus’s death paid the price for sin. Without the sacrifice, the resurrection would have less meaning.
• Some Christians might argue that the teachings of Jesus are most important — the Sermon on the Mount and the parables guide how Christians live daily.
• Others argue that all the events are interconnected and equally important — you cannot separate incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension.

• Because Jesus was God in human form, his teachings carry divine authority. Christians follow his moral teachings (love your neighbour, forgive others) because they believe these come directly from God.
• The incarnation shows God values human life enough to become part of it. This influences Christians to respect and care for all human beings, seeing every person as precious to God.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

christianity-beliefs.title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement
christianity-beliefs.description: How Christians understand sin, original sin, and the different ways salvation is achieved.
christianity-beliefs.content_html:
What Is Sin?

Sin is any thought or action that goes against God’s will. Christians believe sin damages the relationship between humans and God. Every time a person sins, they move further away from God. Sin can take many forms — lying, stealing, hatred, selfishness, envy and many others.

Christians believe all humans are sinful. Nobody is perfect, and everyone falls short of God’s standards. St Paul wrote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). This is a problem because God is holy and just — sin cannot exist in God’s presence. Humans therefore need to be saved from the consequences of their sin.

Original Sin

Original sin is the belief that all humans are born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. This idea comes from the story of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3. God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and told them not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate the fruit, and Adam followed.

Key Fact

Adam and Eve’s disobedience is called the Fall. Christians believe this act of disobedience broke the perfect relationship between God and humanity. As a result, all humans are born with a tendency to sin — this is original sin. It is not a specific sin a person commits, but a condition inherited from the first humans.

Catholic view: Original sin is washed away through the sacrament of baptism. This is one reason Catholics baptise infants — to free the baby from original sin as early as possible. Even after baptism, humans still have a tendency to sin (called concupiscence).

Protestant view: Most Protestants accept the concept of original sin but emphasise that salvation comes through faith in Jesus rather than through sacraments. Some Protestants do not practise infant baptism, believing a person must choose to follow Christ for themselves.

Liberal view: Some liberal Christians see the story of Adam and Eve as a myth that teaches an important truth — humans have a natural tendency to do wrong — rather than a literal historical event. The lesson is the same: humans need God’s help to overcome sin.

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences — ultimately, being granted eternal life with God rather than eternal separation from God. Christians believe humans cannot save themselves because all are sinful. They need God’s help.

the specification identifies three means of salvation: law, grace and Spirit. Different Christian traditions emphasise these differently.

Salvation Through Law

Some Christians believe that following God’s laws — the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus — is essential for salvation. By obeying God’s commands, a person shows they are devoted to God and deserving of eternal life. Catholics especially emphasise the importance of good works alongside faith — the Epistle of James states: “Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead” (James 2:17).

Salvation Through Grace

Grace is the free, undeserved gift of God’s love. Christians believe God offers salvation not because humans deserve it, but because God loves them. Ephesians 2:8–9 states: “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast.”

Key Fact

Protestants, especially those in the Reformed tradition, emphasise salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Humans cannot earn salvation by doing good deeds — it is a free gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Catholics believe both faith and works are necessary — grace enables good works, and both contribute to salvation.

Salvation Through the Holy Spirit

Christians believe the Holy Spirit plays an active role in salvation. The Spirit works within believers to help them recognise their sin, turn towards God, and live a holy life. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians particularly emphasise the role of the Holy Spirit, believing it gives spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing.

The Holy Spirit guides Christians in daily life, helping them make good decisions and resist temptation. Jesus promised: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Spirit also brings comfort in suffering, strengthens faith in difficult times, and empowers Christians to share the gospel with others.

The Role of Christ in Salvation

All Christians agree that Jesus Christ is central to salvation. Without Jesus, humans would remain trapped in sin with no way back to God. Jesus’s death and resurrection made salvation possible.

Atonement

Atonement literally means “at-one-ment” — making God and humanity “at one” again. It is the belief that Jesus’s death on the cross restored the broken relationship between God and humans caused by sin. Through his sacrifice, Jesus took the punishment that humans deserved.

Key Fact

Isaiah 53:5 prophesied the atonement: “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Christians believe this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus on the cross.

Substitutionary atonement: Jesus took the place of sinful humans and bore the punishment they deserved. He was a substitute — dying instead of humanity. This view is common among evangelical Protestants.

Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is the foundational Catholic/Thomistic atonement model. Note: the penal substitution view described above is a distinctly Protestant teaching, rooted in Luther and Calvin; Anselm's satisfaction theory differs in mechanism (paying an honour-debt, not a penal penalty).

Moral example: Some liberal Christians see Jesus’s death less as a payment for sin and more as a supreme example of self-sacrificing love. His willingness to die inspires Christians to live selflessly and sacrificially for others.

Regardless of which understanding they hold, all Christians agree that the atonement makes salvation available. Jesus’s sacrifice opened the door for humans to be reconciled with God, forgiven for their sins, and given the promise of eternal life.
christianity-beliefs.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark evaluation questions on salvation, you will often need to discuss whether faith or works (or both) are more important. A strong answer will show you understand the Protestant view (grace alone through faith alone, Ephesians 2:8–9) and the Catholic view (faith and works together, James 2:17). Always include specific Bible references or teachings to support each side — this is what moves you from Level 2 to Level 3 and above.
christianity-beliefs.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sin separates humans from God. Original sin means all humans are born with a tendency to do wrong, inherited from Adam and Eve’s disobedience (the Fall).
  • Salvation comes through law (obedience), grace (God’s free gift) and the Holy Spirit. Protestants emphasise grace alone; Catholics emphasise faith and works together.
  • Atonement means Jesus’s death reconciled God and humanity. Different Christians understand this as substitution, satisfaction of justice, or a moral example of self-sacrifice.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in salvation influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians try to follow God’s laws and the teachings of Jesus because they believe obedience to God is part of how they achieve salvation. This motivates moral behaviour and charitable actions in daily life.
• Belief that salvation is a free gift of grace gives Christians a sense of gratitude and humility. They feel they do not deserve God’s love but receive it anyway, which motivates them to show the same grace and forgiveness to others.
• Christians who emphasise the Holy Spirit’s role seek a personal relationship with God through prayer and worship, believing the Spirit guides them towards salvation.
• The belief that Jesus died for their sins gives Christians confidence that they can be forgiven, encouraging them to repent when they do wrong rather than giving up.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about atonement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.

Students may include:
• Jesus’s death on the cross restored the relationship between God and humanity. Isaiah 53:5 states: ‘He was pierced for our transgressions… by his wounds we are healed.’ Christians believe Jesus took the punishment humans deserved for their sins, making reconciliation with God possible. (1–2 marks)
• Jesus was a substitute for sinful humanity — he died in our place. Romans 5:8 states: ‘God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.’ This shows atonement is an act of God’s love, not something humans earned. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to support each belief. (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘Good works are more important than faith for achieving salvation.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• James 2:17 states ‘Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.’ This suggests that believing in God is not enough — Christians must also act on their beliefs.
• Catholics teach that good works are essential alongside faith. The sacraments (baptism, Eucharist) and acts of charity contribute to salvation.
• In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25), those who helped the hungry, thirsty and sick were saved. This seems to prioritise actions over beliefs.
Arguments against the statement:
• Ephesians 2:8–9 states salvation is ‘by grace… through faith — not by works, so that no one can boast.’ Protestants argue salvation is a free gift that cannot be earned.
• The criminal crucified next to Jesus was promised paradise despite having no time for good works (Luke 23:43). This shows faith alone is sufficient.
• Martin Luther argued that humans are saved by faith alone (sola fide). Good works are a natural result of faith, not a condition for salvation.
• Some argue faith and works cannot be separated — genuine faith naturally produces good actions.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued, multiple viewpoints, religion references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration with religion references.
