practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in original sin influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Catholics practise infant baptism to wash away original sin. They believe it is important to baptise babies as soon as possible so the child is freed from this inherited condition and welcomed into the Church.
• Belief in original sin reminds Christians that they are not perfect and will always be tempted to do wrong. This influences them to be humble, to regularly confess their sins, and to depend on God’s grace rather than their own efforts.
• Original sin explains why the world is imperfect and why humans need a saviour. This strengthens Christians’ belief in the necessity of Jesus and motivates them to follow his teachings.

hinduism-practices.title: Worship at Home and the Mandir
hinduism-practices.description: Places of Hindu worship — home, mandir, outdoors — and forms including puja, arati, bhajan and japa.
hinduism-practices.content_html:
Where Do Hindus Worship?

Hindu teaching holds that the divine is present everywhere — in the home, the temple, the natural world and, most profoundly, within the heart of every individual. This understanding means that worship (puja in its broadest sense) is not limited to a special building or a weekly appointment, but is woven into daily life.

The four places of worship are: the home, the temple (mandir), outdoors (including natural shrines), and the space of the heart. Each has its own character and importance, and in British Hindu life all four are actively used.

The Home Shrine

For most Hindu families in Britain, the home is the primary place of daily worship. Almost every Hindu home has a dedicated sacred space — a shelf, a cabinet or a whole room — known as the puja room or home shrine. Here, images or statues of deities (murtis) are kept, along with incense, oil lamps (diyas), flowers and other offerings.

Nalini, a 52-year-old Vaishnavite Hindu in Coventry, begins every day at 6am at her home shrine. She offers flowers to a murti of Krishna, lights a diya, recites a mantra and performs a short arati. “It sets the tone for the whole day,” she says. “I am reminding myself of what is truly real before the busy world begins.” This daily domestic ritual is a central expression of Hindu devotion in Britain today.

The Mandir: Temple Worship

The mandir (temple) is understood as the house of God. The most prominent Hindu temple in the UK is the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden, London — the largest Hindu temple in Europe — built entirely from hand-carved limestone and marble by craftsmen following ancient temple-building principles. When a worshipper enters the mandir, they remove their shoes as a sign of respect, signalling that they are entering sacred ground.

Central to temple worship is darshan: the auspicious sight of the divine through the murti. Hindus come to the mandir not primarily to hear a sermon but to “see and be seen by” the deity. The gaze of the murti is considered a living transmission of divine blessing. In a large mandir, worshippers will queue to stand before the consecrated image and receive darshan.

Key Fact

Four places: home shrine, mandir (temple), outdoors/natural shrines, the space of the heart. Key forms of worship: puja, arati, darshan, havan, bhajan/kirtan, japa/mantra.

Key Fact

The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden, London, is the largest Hindu temple in Europe. It was built entirely from hand-carved Bulgarian limestone and marble (including Carrara marble from Italy and Ambaji marble from Gujarat), without the use of steel, following ancient Vedic Shilpa Shastra building principles. Over 3,000 volunteers helped during its construction, illustrating how the mandir functions as a community expression of devotion as well as a place of worship.

Forms of Worship: Puja, Arati and Havan

Puja is the central act of Hindu worship. At home or in the mandir, puja involves a sequence of offerings to the deity: water for washing, flowers, incense, food (prasad), a flame and sometimes cloth. Each offering honours a different aspect of the deity and the worshipper’s relationship with the divine. Puja creates a sacred transaction — the devotee offers love and honour; the deity offers blessing and presence in return.

Arati is the waving of a flame (typically in a multi-wicked lamp called a thali or aarti dish) before a murti. It is accompanied by the singing of devotional hymns. The flame symbolises divine light illuminating the worshipper’s life. After arati, worshippers bring their hands over the flame and then to their face — symbolically receiving the divine light.

Havan (also called yajna) is a fire ritual. Offerings of ghee (clarified butter), grains and sometimes specific herbs are made into a consecrated fire while Sanskrit mantras are recited. Havan is one of the oldest forms of Hindu worship, rooted in the Vedic tradition. It is performed at key life events (weddings, naming ceremonies, housewarmings) and at special temple occasions.

Bhajan, Kirtan, Japa and Mantra

Bhajan and kirtan are devotional singing. Bhajans are devotional songs praising a deity; kirtan is the communal, call-and-response chanting of divine names or scripture. Both are considered acts of bhakti (devotion) and are especially beloved in Vaishnavite communities. The ISKCON community at Bhaktivedanta Manor (near Watford) is well known for its joyful public kirtan.

Japa is the meditative repetition of a divine name or mantra. It is typically counted on a mala (a string of 108 beads, corresponding to the 108 names of God). The most famous japa in Vaishnavite tradition is the Hare Krishna maha-mantra; Shaivite Hindus may repeat the name of Shiva (“Om Namah Shivaya”). A mantra is a sacred sound or phrase believed to carry spiritual potency. Mantras may be in Sanskrit and are received from a teacher (guru).

While the forms of worship — puja, arati, bhajan, japa — are broadly shared, the focus of devotion differs between Hindu sub-traditions. Vaishnavite worship centres on Vishnu, Krishna or Rama. The Bhagavad Gita’s emphasis on loving devotion to a personal God makes bhakti the heart of Vaishnavite practice. Vaishnavite mandirs display images of Krishna, Rama, Lakshmi and Vishnu; the maha-mantra (“Hare Krishna”) is central to japa. Shaivite worship centres on Shiva. The Shiva lingam — an abstract form representing Shiva’s divine energy — is the central sacred object in Shaivite temples. Shaivite puja may involve the ritual bathing (abhisheka) of the lingam with water, milk and honey. The mantra “Om Namah Shivaya” is widely used for japa. Both traditions use the same forms of worship (puja, arati, mantra), but their specific prayers, images and theological emphasis differ significantly.

Outdoor worship takes many forms. Natural features — rivers (especially the Ganges in India), hilltops, sacred trees and rocks — are recognised as places where the divine is particularly present. In Britain, some Hindus gather at outdoor events for festivals such as Holi. The Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishads both speak of the divine as present in every element of nature. The “space of the heart” refers to the innermost place of consciousness where, according to Hindu teaching, God dwells within every individual. Advanced meditation is understood as entering this inner sanctuary — the most immediate encounter with the divine possible.
hinduism-practices.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on Hindu worship, a common stem is “Explain two different forms of Hindu worship and their importance.” The mark scheme requires you to name a sacred writing or source of authority. For worship, you can refer to the Bhagavad Gita’s teaching on bhakti devotion as a path to God, or to the Upanishadic teaching that God dwells within the heart. Name the source, state what it teaches, and develop two reasons. Without a source, you are capped below Mastering.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, a common statement is “Worship at a mandir is more important than home worship.” Make sure you present both sides (communal darshan and temple tradition vs. daily domestic puja as the heart of Hindu practice), include relevant teachings, and reach a justified conclusion. Remember: Vaishnavism and Shaivism offer different emphases — naming sub-traditions earns marks.
hinduism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hindus worship in four places: the home shrine, the mandir, outdoors and within the heart. All are valid expressions of devotion to Brahman in its many forms.
  • Key forms of worship: puja (ritual offering), arati (lamp waving), havan (fire ritual), darshan (sacred sight of the deity), bhajan/kirtan (devotional song), japa/mantra (repetition of divine names). Each expresses love for God in a different mode.
  • Vaishnavism and Shaivism share the same forms of worship but focus on different deities — Vishnu/Krishna/Rama in Vaishnavism, Shiva in Shaivism — with different specific prayers, images and mantras.

practice_questions.text:
'Worship at a mandir is more important for Hindus than worship at home.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The mandir is the consecrated house of God, where the murti has been installed through religious ceremonies (prana-pratishtha) and the presence of the divine is especially intense. Darshan — receiving the auspicious gaze of the divine — is only fully available in the mandir. The communal dimension of mandir worship (singing bhajans together, celebrating festivals, receiving teachings) strengthens the Hindu community and provides support that home worship alone cannot. The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden represents the significance Hindus place on the temple as a sacred institution. Arguments against: Hindu teaching holds that the divine is present everywhere — in the home, in nature and within the heart. For most British Hindus, daily puja at the home shrine is the primary and most consistent act of worship; the mandir is visited less frequently. The Upanishads teach that God dwells within the heart — the most direct encounter with the divine does not require a special building. The Bhagavad Gita's teaching on japa (repetition of God's name) and bhakti (devotion) emphasises an inward, personal relationship with God that can be practised anywhere. Non-religious view: A humanist would likely argue that communal gathering has social and emotional benefits regardless of its metaphysical claims — and might value the mandir's community function while remaining agnostic about its religious significance. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that most Hindu teaching would suggest both are important and complementary — the mandir as a sacred communal space, and the home shrine as the daily foundation of devotion. Neither is more important in absolute terms; different life stages, traditions and temperaments will emphasise different settings. Mastering: Full range, sources, sub-tradition contrast, conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

hinduism-practices.title: Focuses of Worship and the Murti
hinduism-practices.description: Focuses and representations of the divine: many deities, one God, the guru, holy land, sacred plants and the murti.
hinduism-practices.content_html:
The Diversity of Hindu Worship

One of the most striking features of Hinduism is the variety of what believers focus their worship on. A Hindu might worship a personal God in the form of a beautifully sculpted image; another might meditate on the formless absolute; another might honour the divine through the Ganges river or the sacred tulsi plant. The tradition holds that all of these are valid expressions of devotion to the one Brahman, approached from different angles and through different paths.

The GCSE specification identifies five main focuses of Hindu worship, which this lesson covers: the many deities; one God (personal or non-personal); the guru and elders; holy land, hills and rivers; sacred plants and animals; and the murti as a representation of God.

The Many Deities

As covered in the Beliefs unit, Hindu practice includes worship of a vast range of deities, each embodying different aspects of Brahman. For many Hindus, the particular deity they worship most devotedly is called their ishta-devata (chosen deity). A Vaishnavite Hindu might have Krishna as their ishta-devata; a Shaivite Hindu might choose Shiva; another Hindu might be most drawn to the mother goddess.

Worshipping many deities is not considered contradictory in Hindu thought because the tradition teaches that all deities are ultimately manifestations of the one Brahman. An ancient Hindu saying — “Truth is one; the wise call it by many names” (Rig Veda 1.164.46) — captures this inclusive approach to divine diversity.

One God: Personal and Non-Personal

Some Hindus — especially in bhakti (devotional) sub-traditions — focus their worship on one personal God with whom they seek a loving relationship. For Vaishnavite Hindus, this is Vishnu or Krishna; for Shaivites, it is Shiva. The Bhagavad Gita teaches that loving devotion to a personal God (bhakti yoga) is one of the highest paths to liberation.

Other Hindus, particularly those influenced by Advaita Vedanta, focus on the non-personal aspect of the divine — the formless Brahman beyond all qualities. Their “worship” may take the form of meditation and inquiry into the nature of the self (jnana yoga) rather than devotion to an image. Both approaches are honoured within the tradition.

The Guru and Elders

The guru holds a central place in Hindu religious life. The word guru means “one who removes darkness”. A guru is not simply a teacher of religious facts but is understood as a transmitter of spiritual realisation — in many Hindu traditions, the guru’s blessing (guru-kripa) is essential for the disciple’s spiritual progress.

Some Hindu sub-traditions teach that the guru is to be honoured as a living representative of God. “Guru Brahma, Guru Vishnu, Guru Devo Maheshwara” is a well-known Sanskrit verse: “The guru is Brahma, the guru is Vishnu, the guru is Shiva — to the guru I bow.” Elders in the family and community are also honoured as expressions of divine wisdom and as channels of the tradition across generations.

Key Fact

Five focuses: (1) the many deities; (2) one God (personal or non-personal); (3) the guru and elders; (4) holy land, hills and rivers; (5) sacred plants and animals. The murti — the sacred image — is the central focus of temple worship.

Key Fact

Kumbh Mela attracts the largest peaceful human gathering on Earth — over 40 million pilgrims attended a single day of the 2019 gathering at Prayagraj. The pilgrimage focuses on bathing at sacred river confluences, believed to wash away sin and assist the atman’s journey toward liberation. This scale of devotion illustrates how sacred geography is not peripheral but central to Hindu practice.

Holy Land, Hills and Rivers

Hindu teaching holds that the divine is present in the natural world in concentrated form at certain sacred places. The Ganges (Ganga) is the most sacred river — bathing in it is believed to wash away sins and assist the atman’s journey. Varanasi (also known as Kashi or Benares) on the banks of the Ganges is the most sacred city in Hinduism; dying in Varanasi is believed to bring moksha. Pilgrimage sites like Vrindavan (associated with Krishna), Tirupati, Rameshwaram and Puri are all understood as places where the divine is especially accessible.

Mountains — especially the Himalayas — are associated with Shiva and with ascetic spiritual practice. The concept of the entire Indian subcontinent as sacred land (bharatvarsha) is important in some Hindu nationalist thought, though British Hindu communities emphasise the spiritual rather than political dimensions of sacred geography.

Sacred Plants and Animals

Certain plants and animals are considered sacred in Hindu belief because they are associated with specific deities or carry spiritual significance. The tulsi (holy basil) plant is perhaps the most important: it is associated with Vishnu and Lakshmi and is commonly grown in Hindu homes, where it is watered and honoured daily. The peepal (fig) tree is also considered sacred — the Buddha attained enlightenment under a peepal tree, and Hindus use the tree in certain rituals.

The cow holds a uniquely sacred status in Hinduism. The cow is associated with abundance, non-harm (ahimsa) and the goddess Kamadhenu. Most Hindus are vegetarian, in part because of ahimsa and in part because of the cow’s sacred status. Cow protection (go-raksha) is practised by many Hindu organisations, including ISKCON, which runs farm sanctuaries where cows are cared for throughout their natural lives. This practice will be explored further in the lesson on Hindu charities.

A common misconception is that Hindus worship a piece of stone or metal. Hindu teaching explains that the murti is not the deity itself but a vehicle through which the divine becomes accessible to human perception. When a murti is installed in a temple, it undergoes a sacred ceremony (prana-pratishtha) during which the priest invites the divine to be present in and through the image. From that point, the murti is treated as a living divine presence — bathed, clothed, fed and honoured.

The murti provides a focus for bhakti (devotion). Just as a photograph of a loved one helps focus feelings of love even though the person is not literally in the photograph, the murti helps the devotee focus love, attention and intention on the divine. Top-band exam answers distinguish between popular misconceptions about “idol worship” and the theological understanding that the murti is a representation and a vehicle for the divine presence.

The specification distinguishes between personal and non-personal focuses of worship. Personal focuses include deities (Vishnu, Shiva, Ganesha), the guru, the murti, and sacred places associated with a particular deity’s story. Non-personal focuses include the formless Brahman approached through meditation, the sacred power present in the Ganges or the Himalayas, and the divine as present in all of nature. Both types of focus are valid in Hindu theology. The Bhagavad Gita explicitly teaches that God accepts sincere devotion offered through any sincere path: “In whatever way people are devoted to me, in that same way I fulfil their desires.” This inclusivity is characteristic of Hindu thought.
hinduism-practices.exam_tip_html:
For a 6-mark Explain question asking about the importance of different focuses of Hindu worship, you must name a source. The Rig Veda (“Truth is one; the wise call it by many names” — Rig Veda 1.164.46) explains why Hindus can worship many deities while believing in one Brahman. The Bhagavad Gita on bhakti (devotion to a personal God) and on the guru’s role are also reliable sources. Name the source, state what it says, and develop your reason.

Common error: students describe the murti as an “idol” that Hindus worship as if it were the deity. The top-band response distinguishes between the popular misconception and the theological reality: the murti is a consecrated representation through which the divine is made accessible to human perception. Use the term “representation” not “idol”.
hinduism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hindu worship focuses on the many deities, one God (personal or non-personal), the guru and elders, holy land, hills and rivers, and sacred plants and animals. All are understood as ways of approaching the one Brahman.
  • The murti is a sacred representation of God through which the divine is made accessible to human perception — not an idol, but a consecrated vehicle for divine presence. The ceremony of prana-pratishtha invites God to be present in the image.
  • The tulsi plant and the cow are especially sacred in Hindu practice — the tulsi associated with Lakshmi and Vishnu, the cow with ahimsa and divine abundance. Cow protection (go-raksha) is practised by Hindu organisations including ISKCON.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the murti is important in Hindu worship.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons with named source. Reason 1: the murti provides a focus for bhakti devotion — the Bhagavad Gita teaches that sincere devotion offered through any path is accepted by God; the murti makes the formless divine accessible to human perception and emotion. Reason 2: the murti is a consecrated vehicle for divine presence (prana-pratishtha ceremony invites God to dwell in the image) — receiving darshan through the murti is one of the most important moments in Hindu temple worship. Sub-tradition contrast: Vaishnavite temples use images of Krishna/Vishnu; Shaivite temples centre on the Shiva lingam — showing how even the focus of the murti differs. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: One reason without development. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text:
'Worshipping the murti is the most important form of Hindu devotion.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: For the majority of practising Hindus, the murti is the central focus of daily puja — both at home and in the mandir. Darshan through the murti is widely understood as the most direct encounter with the personal God. The ceremony of prana-pratishtha makes the murti a living divine presence. The Bhagavad Gita's emphasis on bhakti (devotion to a personal God) supports the importance of the murti as a focus for that devotion. Arguments against: Many Hindu traditions, especially Advaita Vedanta, teach that the highest form of devotion is meditation on the formless Brahman — the murti is a helpful aid for those not yet able to contemplate the formless, but it is not the highest path. The Upanishads emphasise the divine within the heart as the most direct presence of God — this requires no murti. Japa (repetition of God's name) and bhajan (devotional song) are also important forms of devotion that do not depend on a physical image. Non-religious view: A humanist might observe that humans benefit from having physical anchors for focused attention, but would not accept the theological claim that the murti is a vehicle for a divine presence. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that the murti is important for most Hindus but not the most important form of devotion for all — different paths (bhakti, jnana, karma yoga) suit different practitioners. The tradition is explicitly inclusive on this point. Mastering: Full range, sources, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

hinduism-practices.title: Festivals: Diwali and Holi
hinduism-practices.description: The origins, meaning and importance of Diwali and Holi for Hindus in Great Britain today.
hinduism-practices.content_html:
Hindu Festivals in British Life

Festivals are central to Hindu religious life. They mark time by sacred stories, bring communities together, renew devotion and express joy in the divine. Two of the most widely celebrated Hindu festivals in Britain are Diwali and Holi. Both are celebrated by millions of Hindus across the UK and both have meanings that reach deep into Hindu scripture and devotional life.

It is important to note that Diwali is also celebrated by Sikhs (as Bandi Chhor Divas, marking the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment) and by Jains. The festival’s meaning differs across traditions. In this lesson, the focus is on its meaning for Hindus specifically.

Diwali: Origins and Meaning

Diwali (also spelled Divali) is a five-day festival celebrated in late October or November, according to the Hindu lunar calendar. The word diwali comes from the Sanskrit dipavali, meaning “row of lights.” The festival is known as the Festival of Lights.

The most widely known origin story is from the Ramayana: after Rama’s victory over the demon Ravana and his 14-year exile, he and Sita returned to their kingdom of Ayodhya. The people of Ayodhya lit rows of clay lamps (diyas) to welcome them home and to light their way through the dark. This story celebrates the triumph of righteousness over evil and the return of the divine king.

In Vaishnavite communities, Diwali is also associated with the worship of Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity. On the main Diwali night, homes are lit with lamps and decorated with rangoli (intricate patterns made from coloured powder) to welcome Lakshmi in. Worshippers perform puja to Lakshmi and pray for prosperity and wellbeing in the coming year.

In South India, Diwali is associated with Krishna’s defeat of the demon Narakasura — showing that even within Hinduism, the same festival can have different origin stories in different regional traditions.

Key Fact

Diwali primary meanings: (1) Rama’s return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — triumph of righteousness over evil; (2) worship of Lakshmi, goddess of wealth and prosperity. The lighting of diyas symbolises the triumph of light over darkness.

Diwali in Great Britain Today

The Hindu community in Britain celebrates Diwali with great enthusiasm. In Leicester, which has one of the largest Hindu populations outside India, the Diwali celebrations on Belgrave Road attract hundreds of thousands of visitors each year and include one of the largest Diwali parades outside Asia. The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden holds special puja and events throughout the festival period.

Meena, a 72-year-old grandmother who came from Gujarat to Leicester in the 1970s, describes Diwali as “the time when our whole family comes together. The children help make rangoli at the door; we do arati together; we share sweets with the neighbours. It keeps us Hindu even in England.” For the British Hindu community, Diwali is both a religious festival and a powerful expression of cultural identity and continuity.

The festival includes: lighting of diyas and candles in the home; performance of Lakshmi puja on the main night; exchange of gifts and sweets; fireworks; and in larger communities, public processions and light displays. The lighting of the home symbolises the divine light entering and blessing the household.

Each of the five days of Diwali has its own significance. Day 1 (Dhanteras) — prayers for prosperity and wealth, associated with Lakshmi and Kubera (the god of wealth). Day 2 (Choti Diwali / Naraka Chaturdashi) — associated with Krishna’s defeat of Narakasura in South Indian tradition; symbolic cleansing. Day 3 (Diwali / Lakshmi Puja) — the main night, with Lakshmi puja, diyas and fireworks; the most important day of the festival. Day 4 (Govardhan Puja / Padwa) — associated with Krishna lifting the Govardhan hill; celebrations of new year in some regions. Day 5 (Bhai Dooj) — celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

Holi: Origins and Meaning

Holi is celebrated in late February or March, at the full moon that marks the end of winter and the arrival of spring. It is known as the Festival of Colours. The name Holi comes from Holika, a demoness who features in one of the festival’s origin stories.

The main origin story involves the demon king Hiranyakashipu, who demanded that everyone worship him instead of God. His own son, Prahlada, refused — he was a devoted worshipper of Vishnu. Hiranyakashipu tried many times to kill Prahlada, but Vishnu protected him each time. Finally, Holika (the demon king’s sister) tried to burn Prahlada in a fire, but Holika herself was burned while Prahlada emerged unharmed. This is the theological meaning of the bonfire (Holika Dahan) lit on the eve of Holi: the destruction of evil and the protection of the devoted.

A second strand of Holi’s meaning comes from the story of Krishna and Radha. Krishna, as a young man in Vrindavan, playfully sprayed coloured water on Radha and the gopis (cowherd women). This playfulness became the tradition of throwing coloured powder and water at Holi — a joyful, egalitarian celebration in which social distinctions are temporarily dissolved.

Key Fact

Holi has two main meanings: (1) the triumph of devotion over evil — Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu protecting him from Holika; (2) the joyful, playful love of Krishna and Radha — the throwing of colours expresses the exuberance of bhakti devotion.

Holi in Great Britain Today

Holi has grown significantly in visibility in Britain. Hindu communities gather for Holika Dahan (the bonfire on the eve of Holi) and then the colour celebration the following day. University Hindu Societies across the UK hold Holi events that attract both Hindu and non-Hindu students. The Bhaktivedanta Manor in Hertfordshire holds a celebrated Holi festival.

Dev, a 19-year-old student at a UK university, describes Holi as “the one festival where being Hindu feels completely joyful and free. The colours, the music — it feels like the tradition is saying: God loves joy.” For many young British Hindus, Holi’s themes of renewal, joy and the equality of all people give it particular resonance in a multicultural society.

The theological significance of Holi includes: renewal and the transition from winter to spring; the triumph of dharma (right conduct and devotion) over adharma (evil); the equality of all people before God — during Holi, social hierarchies are temporarily set aside and all play together as equals.

Both Diwali and Holi celebrate the triumph of good over evil and are rooted in stories of Vishnu’s protective power (through his avatars Rama and Krishna, or directly in the case of Prahlada). Both are community celebrations with strong family dimensions. However, they differ in character: Diwali is primarily a devotional festival with puja, lamps and prayers for prosperity — it has a more formal religious character. Holi is primarily a festival of joy and social renewal, with its emphasis on colour, play and equality — its religious dimension (Holika Dahan) sits alongside a more exuberant, popular celebration. This contrast is worth noting in any exam question that asks you to compare two Hindu festivals.
hinduism-practices.exam_tip_html:
For a 6-mark Explain question on Hindu festivals, a typical stem is “Explain two reasons why Diwali is important for Hindus in Britain today.” You must name a source — the Ramayana is the primary textual source for Diwali (Rama’s return to Ayodhya). Name the Ramayana, state what it says (Rama returned after defeating Ravana and the people lit lamps), and develop two reasons (e.g. community worship and Lakshmi puja for prosperity; cultural identity for British Hindus). Without a named source, you are capped below Mastering.

Common error: students describe Holi only as “a festival where Hindus throw coloured powder.” The top-band response explains the theological meaning: the destruction of evil (Holika Dahan), the victory of Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu, and the joyful bhakti associated with Krishna and Radha. Describe the practice and its meaning.
hinduism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diwali is the Festival of Lights, celebrated in autumn. Its primary Hindu meanings are: the return of Rama to Ayodhya (Ramayana) and the worship of Lakshmi for prosperity. Lamps, rangoli and puja mark the festival; in Leicester, it is a major public celebration.
  • Holi is the spring Festival of Colours. Its theological meanings are: the triumph of Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu over the evil of Holika (Holika Dahan), and the joyful love of Krishna and Radha. The throwing of colours expresses equality and the exuberance of bhakti.
  • Both festivals reinforce core Hindu themes: the triumph of dharma over adharma, the power of bhakti devotion, and the importance of community and family. For British Hindus, they are also expressions of cultural identity and continuity.

Parveen is a 15-year-old Hindu girl preparing for Holi with her family in Birmingham. She asks her grandmother why the festival involves throwing coloured powder.

practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable reasons: the colours recall the playful story of Krishna and Radha at Vrindavan — the joyful expression of bhakti love; the throwing of colours on all people equally symbolises that before God all are equal — social distinctions are dissolved during Holi; the festival celebrates the arrival of spring and the renewal of the natural world, which Hindus understand as God's creation; the colour represents the exuberance and joy of devotion.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Diwali is an important festival for Hindus.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with a named source integrated. Primary source: the Ramayana (Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — the lighting of lamps celebrated his return and the triumph of righteousness). Reason 1: Diwali reaffirms core Hindu beliefs about dharma — Rama's story teaches that truth and righteousness will ultimately triumph over evil, giving worshippers confidence in the cosmic moral order. Reason 2: Lakshmi puja connects the festival to daily Hindu life — the prayers for prosperity and wellbeing at Diwali reflect the purushartha of artha (material wellbeing as a legitimate aim of life), and the lighting of the home symbolises inviting divine grace into everyday existence. Sub-tradition contrast (different Diwali stories in Vaishnavite/South Indian traditions) earns further credit. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: One reason without development. Emerging: Basic description of practices.

practice_questions.text:
'Holi is a more important festival than Diwali for Hindus in Britain today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Holi's themes of equality, joy and the renewal of community may be especially resonant for British Hindus living in a multicultural society where social divisions are a daily reality. Holi has grown significantly in public visibility in Britain — university events, Bhaktivedanta Manor's Holi celebration. Holi's joyful, accessible character may appeal to younger generations and bridge Hindu and non-Hindu communities in a way that Diwali's domestic puja does not. Arguments against: Diwali is far more widely recognised as a Hindu festival in British public life and has greater public impact (Leicester's celebrations, public lighting events, Diwali cards). The religious depth of Diwali — Lakshmi puja, the return of Rama — gives it a more explicitly devotional character. For most Hindu families in Britain, Diwali is the festival at which the whole family gathers and which most directly expresses devotion to God through puja. The Ramayana's story of Rama's return is one of the most beloved narratives in the Hindu tradition and gives Diwali deep theological grounding. Non-religious view: A humanist might value both festivals for their community-building functions and the joy they bring, without accepting their theological claims. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that both festivals serve important but different functions — Diwali is more central to formal devotional practice and cultural identity in Britain, while Holi is increasingly important for community integration and for younger Hindus. The statement is therefore an overstatement — both are important, serving different needs. Mastering: Full range, named sources, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

hinduism-practices.title: The Four Yogas, Pilgrimage and Hindu Charities
hinduism-practices.description: The four yogas, pilgrimage to Varanasi and Kumbh Mela, and Hindu charitable and environmental work.
hinduism-practices.content_html:
The Four Paths of Yoga

The word yoga does not simply mean physical exercise. From the Sanskrit root meaning “to yoke” or “to unite”, yoga in its Hindu theological sense is any path that leads the individual towards union with the divine (Brahman). The Bhagavad Gita — particularly chapters 3, 4, 6 and 12 — identifies four main paths of yoga, each suited to a different human temperament.

The Bhagavad Gita teaches that no single path is the only valid one. Different people are suited to different paths; all four lead ultimately to the same destination: moksha. The tradition’s inclusivity on the question of how to reach God is one of its characteristic features.

Key Fact

Four yogas: karma yoga (action), jnana yoga (knowledge), astanga yoga (meditation), bhakti yoga (devotion). All lead to moksha. Primary sources: the Bhagavad Gita (karma, jnana, bhakti yoga) and the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (astanga yoga).

Key Fact

The Char Dham (“four abodes”) are four sacred pilgrimage sites in India — Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameshwaram — traditionally associated with the four directions and considered the most important pilgrimage circuit in Hinduism. Visiting all four is believed to wash away all sin and assist the soul’s liberation. Sewa International UK is a leading British Hindu charity that coordinates disaster relief and community projects globally, rooted in the principle of selfless service (seva) as an expression of karma yoga.

Karma Yoga: The Path of Action

Karma yoga is the path of selfless action. The Bhagavad Gita’s core teaching is that a person should perform their duties and serve others without attachment to the fruits of their actions. When work is done as an offering to God — with no desire for personal reward or recognition — it becomes a spiritual practice. This path is particularly suited to active, socially engaged personalities.

Karma yoga is the theological basis for much Hindu charitable and social action. Hindu organisations that run food banks, support the elderly or care for animals are often described as practising karma yoga — serving the divine in all beings.

Jnana Yoga: The Path of Knowledge

Jnana yoga is the path of wisdom and self-inquiry. It involves the deep study of Hindu scripture — especially the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita — and the use of philosophical reasoning to understand the true nature of the self (atman) and ultimate reality (Brahman). The practitioner of jnana yoga seeks to see through the illusion of maya and realise that atman and Brahman are one or intimately related.

This path is associated with the Advaita Vedanta school (Shankara’s tradition) and requires sharp intellectual ability and a capacity for sustained meditation on abstract truths. The Upanishads’ method of “neti, neti” (not this, not this) — systematically negating everything that is not Brahman until only Brahman remains — is a classic jnana yoga technique.

Astanga Yoga: The Path of Meditation

Astanga yoga (ashtanga yoga) is the eight-limbed path described by the sage Patanjali in the Yoga Sutras. The eight limbs move progressively from ethical conduct (yama and niyama), through physical posture (asana) and breath control (pranayama), to meditation (dharana and dhyana) and ultimately to samadhi — a state of complete absorption in the divine. This is the source of what in the West is often called “yoga” — though the full path is much broader than the physical practice alone.

The aim of astanga yoga is to still the mind and purify the body and spirit so that the practitioner can experience the divine directly. It requires sustained daily practice and is particularly suited to those who benefit from a structured, gradual path.

Bhakti Yoga: The Path of Devotion

Bhakti yoga is widely considered the most accessible and popular path. It involves intense, loving devotion to a personal deity — Vishnu, Krishna, Shiva or another form of God. Through puja, prayer, bhajan, japa and pilgrimage, the devotee draws the mind and heart towards God until their love becomes the overwhelming reality of their life.

The Bhagavad Gita (chapter 12) presents bhakti as the highest path for most people: “Those who fix their minds on me and worship me with constant devotion — I consider them to be the best yogis.” The Vaishnavite tradition (including ISKCON at Bhaktivedanta Manor) centres its practice on bhakti yoga. Many Hindu saints and mystics — such as Mirabai and Tukaram — have expressed their realisation through intense devotional love.

Different Hindu sub-traditions emphasise different yogas. The Advaita Vedanta tradition often favours jnana yoga as the highest path; the bhakti traditions of Vaishnavism and Shaivism emphasise bhakti yoga. Many modern Hindu teachers (such as Swami Vivekananda in the 19th century) advocated combining all four paths — this approach is sometimes called “integral yoga.” For the GCSE exam, the key is to describe each path accurately, explain its difference, and (for top-band answers) note that different Hindu sub-traditions have different views on which is most important.

Pilgrimage: Varanasi and Kumbh Mela

Varanasi (also known as Kashi or Benares) is the holiest city in Hinduism. Situated on the western bank of the Ganges, it has been a centre of Hindu worship and learning for thousands of years. The Vishwanath Temple, dedicated to Shiva, is one of its most important sites. Pilgrims come to bathe in the Ganges, to cremate the dead (the ghats or riverbank steps are used for cremations), and to seek moksha. Hindu tradition teaches that any person who dies in Varanasi receives liberation — Shiva himself is said to whisper the “liberation mantra” (taraka mantra) in the ear of the dying.

The Kumbh Mela is the world’s largest religious gathering. Held at four rotating sacred river sites in India (Prayagraj/Allahabad at the confluence of the Ganges, Yamuna and the mythical Saraswati; Haridwar on the Ganges; Nashik on the Godavari; Ujjain on the Shipra) at regular intervals, the Kumbh Mela can attract tens of millions of pilgrims. Bathing at the sacred confluence at the auspicious time is believed to wash away all sin and assist the atman’s journey towards liberation.

Hindu Environmental Projects and Charities

Hindu organisations in Britain and globally are actively engaged in environmental and social welfare work, motivated by Hindu theological principles. Three areas are particularly relevant to the GCSE specification:

Cow protection (go-raksha): The cow is sacred in Hinduism, associated with abundance, Lakshmi and the principle of ahimsa (non-harm). ISKCON runs farm sanctuaries in Britain (including at Bhaktivedanta Manor) where cows are cared for throughout their natural lives and never slaughtered. The practice is understood as both ahimsa and karma yoga — service to sacred beings as an expression of devotion.

Environmental projects: Several Hindu organisations frame environmental care as a religious duty. The Isha Foundation, founded by the teacher Sadhguru, has led large-scale tree-planting campaigns in India. The Hindu Climate Declaration (2015), to which many British Hindu organisations are signatories, draws on the Hindu principle that the natural world is sacred — embedded with divine consciousness — and therefore deserves care and protection. The Bhagavad Gita’s teaching on non-attachment (not exploiting the world for selfish gain) provides theological grounding for environmental ethics.

Charities promoting well-being and women’s rights: The Sewa UK charity, inspired directly by the Vedic principle of service (seva/sewa), runs food banks, befriending services for the elderly and community healthcare projects across Britain. On women’s rights, the position of women within Hinduism is complex: classical texts contain both egalitarian statements (the Upanishads describe female sages such as Gargi and Maitreyi as great spiritual teachers) and more restrictive social norms (as reflected in parts of the Laws of Manu). Many British Hindu communities actively promote women’s equality, and organisations such as the Hindu Forum of Britain work to address domestic violence and gender inequality within and beyond the Hindu community.

Hindu charitable action is theologically grounded in karma yoga — the understanding that selfless service to others is service to God. The Bhagavad Gita teaches: “Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.” Service is not merely philanthropy in the Western sense; it is understood as a form of worship, performed without attachment to recognition or reward. This distinguishes Hindu seva from purely secular charity: the act of service is itself a spiritual practice, purifying the karma of the giver while helping the recipient.
hinduism-practices.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on the four yogas, the required source is the Bhagavad Gita. A reliable approach: name the Gita, state what it teaches about one specific yoga (e.g. “The Bhagavad Gita teaches that performing duty without attachment to results is the path of karma yoga”), then develop your two reasons. Sub-tradition contrast earns marks: Vaishnavism prioritises bhakti yoga; Advaita Vedanta tends to emphasise jnana yoga.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, if the statement concerns pilgrimage (e.g. “Pilgrimage to Varanasi is the most important Hindu practice”), make sure your conclusion genuinely weighs the arguments. A top-band answer will note that different Hindu sub-traditions emphasise different practices — for a Vaishnavite, bhakti yoga and temple worship may be more central than pilgrimage to Varanasi (which is especially associated with Shaivism). Diversity of practice is a mark-scheme reward.
hinduism-practices.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four yogas — karma (action), jnana (knowledge), astanga (meditation) and bhakti (devotion) — are four paths to moksha described in the Bhagavad Gita. Each suits a different temperament. Different sub-traditions emphasise different yogas.
  • Pilgrimage is an important Hindu practice. Varanasi on the Ganges is the holiest Hindu city; dying there is believed to bring moksha. Kumbh Mela is the world’s largest religious gathering, held at four sacred river sites in India.
  • Hindu charitable and environmental work is rooted in karma yoga and ahimsa. Cow protection, environmental campaigns and organisations like Sewa UK express the Hindu principle that selfless service to others is service to God.

practice_questions.text:
'Bhakti yoga is the most important of the four yogas for Hindus today.'

In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Bhagavad Gita (chapter 12) explicitly states that those who fix their minds on God with constant devotion are the best yogis, suggesting bhakti is the highest path. Bhakti yoga is by far the most widely practised path among Hindus today — in Vaishnavite and Shaivite traditions, devotion through puja, bhajan and pilgrimage is the primary form of practice. Bhakti yoga is accessible to all regardless of education or physical ability; it requires only sincere love for God. ISKCON at Bhaktivedanta Manor represents the global reach of bhakti yoga practice. Arguments against: The Bhagavad Gita also states that all four paths are valid and that God accepts sincere devotion through any path. Jnana yoga, as the path of knowledge, is held by Advaita Vedanta teachers (such as Shankara and, later, Ramana Maharshi) to be the most direct route to liberation. Karma yoga is arguably the most practically relevant path for modern Hindus in working and family life — social action, ethical business and community service are all expressions of karma yoga. Astanga yoga (through practices like daily meditation) has gained millions of practitioners globally, including among British Hindus. Non-religious view: A humanist might value the ethical and social dimensions of karma yoga (selfless service) while remaining sceptical of the metaphysical claims of any of the paths. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that for the majority of practising Hindus today, especially in bhakti-centred Vaishnavite and Shaivite communities, bhakti yoga is indeed the most central practice; but the tradition itself is explicit that all four paths are valid. The statement is partly true but overstates a single path in a tradition that celebrates diversity of approach. Mastering: Full range, named sources, sub-tradition contrasts, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

theme-d-peace-conflict.title: Peace, Justice & Forgiveness
theme-d-peace-conflict.description: Peace, justice, forgiveness, reconciliation, and religious views on violence.
theme-d-peace-conflict.content_html:
The Meaning and Significance of Peace

Peace is more than simply the absence of war. For religious believers, peace refers to a deep sense of harmony — between individuals, communities and nations. Both Christianity and Islam teach that peace is a central goal of human life and that believers have a duty to work towards it.

Christians believe that Jesus taught a message of peace throughout his ministry. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). This teaching shows that God values those who actively work to create peace, not simply those who avoid conflict.

In Islam, one of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam, meaning “the source of peace.” Muslims greet each other with “salaam alaikum” — “peace be upon you” — reinforcing the idea that peace is woven into everyday Muslim life. The Qur’an teaches that Allah created humanity to live in peace and harmony.

Key Fact

Christianity: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Islam: One of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam (“the source of peace”). Both religions teach that peace is a central value and that believers should work actively to promote it.

Justice, Forgiveness and Reconciliation

Justice means ensuring fairness and upholding what is morally right. Religious believers see justice as a divine quality — God is just, and humans should reflect this in their treatment of others. Christians believe that God commands justice: “Act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). In Islam, the Qur’an repeatedly instructs Muslims to act justly, even towards those they dislike: “Be just; that is nearer to righteousness” (Qur’an 5:8).

Forgiveness is the act of pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment. Christianity places forgiveness at the heart of its teaching. Jesus said: “If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). On the cross, Jesus prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described as “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman) and “the most forgiving” (Al-Ghaffar). Muslims are encouraged to forgive others because Allah forgives those who forgive. The Qur’an teaches: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40).

Key Fact

Reconciliation goes beyond forgiveness — it means restoring a broken relationship and rebuilding trust. While forgiveness is a personal decision, reconciliation requires both sides to work together. Christians see reconciliation as central to their faith: God reconciled humanity to himself through Jesus’s death on the cross (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

Violence means using physical force to cause harm. Some people use violent protest to try to bring about political or social change — for example, fighting with police, destroying property or setting off explosives. UK law allows peaceful protest but prohibits violent protest.

Christianity teaches non-violence. Jesus instructed his followers: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also” (Matthew 5:39). However, some Christians accept that violence may sometimes be a last resort when all peaceful options have failed. In Islam, violence is generally forbidden, but the Qur’an permits self-defence: “Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms” (Qur’an 22:39).

Terrorism is the use of violence against innocent people to create fear and force political change. It is condemned by all mainstream religious traditions. Christianity teaches that every human life is sacred (“sanctity of life”), and Islam states: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (Qur’an 6:151).

Some extremist groups claim religious justification for terrorism, but the vast majority of religious believers reject this. Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim education activist shot by the Taliban, demonstrated that faith inspires peace, not violence: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Nelson Mandela, a Christian, spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid through protest rather than terrorism.

Contrasting Beliefs on Violence

Christians and Muslims share many views on violence, but there are important differences in emphasis. Most Christians follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” and believe violence should be avoided wherever possible. The Quaker tradition (Society of Friends) takes an absolute pacifist stance, rejecting all forms of violence.

In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle in defence of Islam, but only under strict conditions — it must be declared by a legitimate authority, be proportionate, and be a last resort. The majority of Muslims reject violence as a tool for spreading faith, emphasising that “there is no compulsion in religion” (Qur’an 2:256). The key contrast is that Christianity has a stronger tradition of absolute pacifism (through groups like the Quakers), while Islam more explicitly permits defensive violence under strict conditions — but both religions agree that peace should always be the primary goal.
theme-d-peace-conflict.exam_tip_html: For Theme D questions, always include contrasting beliefs from both Christianity and Islam with specific scripture references. In the 4-mark “Explain similarities and differences” question, make sure you identify a genuine point of similarity or difference — do not simply describe two beliefs. For the 12-mark evaluation, present arguments on both sides, use religious teachings as evidence, and reach a clear personal conclusion.
theme-d-peace-conflict.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation are central values in both Christianity and Islam, supported by specific teachings and scripture.
  • Both religions condemn terrorism and unjustified violence, though they accept that force may sometimes be necessary in self-defence as a last resort.
  • Reconciliation goes beyond forgiveness — it requires both sides to actively work towards restoring a broken relationship.

• Islam — the Qur'an teaches 'Do not take life, which God has made sacred' (6:151), showing that Muslims believe human life has a God-given value that violence violates. While self-defence is permitted, unprovoked violence is forbidden.

• Both condemn terrorism and the targeting of innocent civilians.
• Both accept that violence may be justified in extreme circumstances, such as self-defence or as a last resort.
• Both teach the sanctity of life — violence against innocent people is always wrong.

Arguments against:
• Christianity has a stronger pacifist tradition — Jesus taught 'turn the other cheek' and the Quakers reject all violence absolutely.
• Islam permits armed struggle (lesser jihad) under strict conditions, which goes further than most Christian traditions in accepting the use of force.
• The concept of lesser jihad has no direct equivalent in mainstream Christianity.
• Some Christians argue that the Old Testament shows God supporting violence, while others reject this as outdated.

Conclusion: While there are significant similarities in their commitment to peace and condemnation of unjustified violence, there are genuine differences in how each religion frames the conditions under which force may be acceptable.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

theme-d-peace-conflict.title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism
theme-d-peace-conflict.description: Just war criteria, holy war, pacifism, and contrasting Christian and Islamic beliefs about warfare.
theme-d-peace-conflict.content_html:
Reasons for War

War is an armed conflict between two or more sides, usually nations or organised groups. There are many reasons why wars begin, but the three main reasons studied in GCSE Religious Studies are greed, self-defence and retaliation.

Greed drives wars fought for power, territory or resources. Many governments disguise greed as other motivations, but religious believers generally consider greed an unjust reason for war. Self-defence is widely accepted as a legitimate reason for fighting — both Christians and Muslims agree that protecting yourself and others from harm is justified. Retaliation means fighting back as revenge for a previous attack. While it can deter future aggression, religious believers warn that retaliation often creates a cycle of violence.

Just War Theory

The just war theory draws on the work of St Thomas Aquinas, who in the 13th century (Summa Theologiae II-II Q40) gave three conditions: just cause, right intention, and legitimate authority. The fuller seven-criteria version used today comes from the 1992 Catholic Catechism (CCC 2309), which added last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportional force, and civilian protection. It recognises that while peace is always preferable, there are circumstances where war may be the lesser evil.

Key Fact

The criteria for a just war include: (1) it must be fought for a just cause, such as self-defence; (2) it must be declared by a legitimate authority, such as a government; (3) the intention must be to promote good and overcome evil; (4) war must be a last resort, after all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted; (5) there must be a reasonable chance of success; (6) proportional force must be used — no more violence than is necessary; (7) civilians must not be deliberately targeted.

Most mainstream Christian denominations accept the just war theory. The Catholic Church teaches that governments have a right and duty to defend their citizens, provided the strict conditions of a just war are met. The Church of England also supports the just war approach, arguing that there are times when failing to act would cause greater suffering.

However, Jesus’s own teaching emphasises peace and non-violence. He said: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44) and “All who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). This creates a tension within Christianity between the ideal of peace and the practical reality that war may sometimes be necessary.

Holy War

A holy war is a war fought for a religious cause or believed to be commanded by God. In Christianity, the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) are the most well-known example — European Christians fought to recapture the Holy Land from Muslim control. In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but only under strict conditions.

For a holy war to be legitimate in Islam, it must be declared by a recognised religious authority, be fought in self-defence (not aggression), use proportionate force, and not target civilians, the elderly, women or children. The Qur’an states: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors” (2:190).

Key Fact

Just war vs holy war: A just war uses moral criteria to decide if a war is acceptable — it does not have to be religious. A holy war is fought specifically for a religious cause. Today, most Christian and Muslim leaders reject the idea of holy war, arguing that religion should not be used to justify violence.

Pacifism

Pacifism is the belief that all violence and war is wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Pacifists argue that conflicts should always be resolved through dialogue, negotiation and peaceful protest.

The strongest pacifist tradition in Christianity comes from the Quakers (Society of Friends), who believe that all war is wrong. They follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any conflict. Many Quakers served as conscientious objectors during the World Wars, working as ambulance drivers or in hospitals instead.

Islam does not have a strong pacifist tradition in the same way. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad himself participated in battles to protect the early Muslim community. However, many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace” and that the greater jihad — the internal struggle to be a good Muslim — is more important than any physical conflict.

Religion as a Cause of War

Religion has been cited as a cause of conflict throughout history — from the Crusades to modern-day conflicts in the Middle East. However, many scholars argue that religion is rarely the sole cause of war. Most conflicts involve a complex mix of political, economic and territorial factors, with religion sometimes used to justify violence rather than being its root cause.

Both Christians and Muslims argue that their faith promotes peace, not war. Where religious violence occurs, leaders from both traditions condemn it. Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,” and Muslim scholars worldwide have signed declarations condemning violence carried out in the name of Islam.

Christianity: Quakers take an absolute pacifist position, rejecting all violence. Most other Christian denominations accept that war may sometimes be necessary (just war theory) but should always be a last resort. All Christians agree that Jesus taught peace and non-violence as the ideal.

Islam: Most Muslims are not pacifists in the absolute sense. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad fought to protect the Muslim community. However, peace is the preferred state, and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict). Some individual Muslims, such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan, have adopted pacifist positions inspired by their faith.
theme-d-peace-conflict.exam_tip_html: When writing about just war theory, do not simply list the criteria — explain how they apply in practice. For the 12-mark evaluation question, consider whether just war theory works in the modern world (with nuclear weapons and drone strikes) or whether it was designed for a different era. Always include contrasting Christian and Islamic perspectives with specific teachings.
theme-d-peace-conflict.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Just war theory sets strict criteria for when war may be morally acceptable, including just cause, legitimate authority, last resort and proportional force.
  • Holy war is fought for a religious cause; both Christianity (Crusades) and Islam (lesser jihad) have historical examples, but most modern religious leaders reject the concept.
  • Pacifism rejects all violence — Quakers are the strongest Christian pacifist tradition, while Islam permits self-defence but prioritises peace.

Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Quakers (Society of Friends) believe in absolute pacifism. They follow Jesus's teaching to 'turn the other cheek' (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any war. This shows a tradition within Christianity that rejects all violence.
• Islam — most Muslims are not absolute pacifists. The Qur'an permits self-defence: 'Fight in the way of God those who fight you' (2:190). Muhammad participated in battles to defend the Muslim community. However, peace is always preferred.
• Most mainstream Christian denominations (Catholic, Anglican) accept just war theory, which means they are not absolute pacifists either, but accept war only as a last resort.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — the just war theory, developed by St Thomas Aquinas, states that war is justified if it meets strict criteria such as just cause, legitimate authority and proportional force. Jesus also said 'All who draw the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52), warning against unnecessary violence, but the Church accepts that self-defence may be necessary.
• Islam — the Qur'an states 'Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms' (22:39), showing that self-defence is a legitimate reason for war. The lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but the response must be proportionate: 'If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate' (Qur'an).
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious believers should always be pacifists.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers' and 'turn the other cheek' — these teachings suggest Christians should always choose peace over violence.
• Quakers demonstrate that it is possible to be an absolute pacifist and still serve others during wartime (ambulance drivers, hospital workers).
• One meaning of Islam is 'peace', and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict).
• Violence creates cycles of retaliation — pacifism breaks this cycle.

Arguments against:
• Most Christian denominations accept just war theory, recognising that sometimes failing to fight causes more suffering (e.g. allowing genocide).
• Islam permits self-defence — the Qur'an says 'Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms.' Refusing to defend yourself goes against this teaching.
• Pacifism may be unrealistic when faced with threats like terrorism or invasion.
• Some argue that fighting to protect the innocent is itself a moral duty, not a failure of faith.

Conclusion: While religious teachings clearly value peace, most believers accept that absolute pacifism is difficult to maintain when faced with extreme threats. The just war tradition offers a middle ground.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

• Islam — the lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, which some consider a form of holy war. The Qur'an states: 'Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress' (2:190). However, this is strictly defensive and must be proportionate. Most Muslim leaders reject the term 'holy war' as a misrepresentation of jihad.
[6 marks]

theme-d-peace-conflict.title: Weapons of Mass Destruction & Peacemaking
theme-d-peace-conflict.description: Nuclear weapons, WMDs, nuclear deterrence, and religious peacemaking efforts.
theme-d-peace-conflict.content_html:
Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

Weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) are weapons that can kill huge numbers of people and cause devastation over a wide area. The three main types are nuclear weapons, biological weapons (using disease) and chemical weapons (using poisonous substances). The use of WMDs is one of the most controversial moral issues in modern warfare.

Nuclear weapons are the most powerful WMDs ever created. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 killed over 200,000 people, many of them civilians. The long-term effects included radiation sickness, birth defects and environmental destruction that lasted for decades. Today, several countries possess nuclear arsenals, and the threat of nuclear war remains a global concern.

Key Fact

Nuclear weapons violate several criteria of the just war theory: they cannot be used proportionately (their destructive power is too great), they inevitably target civilians (blast radius is indiscriminate), and their long-term effects (radiation, environmental damage) extend far beyond the battlefield. For these reasons, most religious believers oppose their use.

Nuclear Deterrence

Nuclear deterrence is the idea that possessing nuclear weapons prevents war because no nation would risk attacking a country that could retaliate with nuclear force. This was the basis of the Cold War strategy of “mutually assured destruction” (MAD) — if both sides would be destroyed, neither side would start a war.

Arguments for deterrence: Nuclear weapons have arguably prevented major wars between nuclear powers since 1945. The threat of mutual destruction makes war too costly to consider. Some argue that giving up nuclear weapons unilaterally would leave a country vulnerable to attack or nuclear blackmail.

Arguments against deterrence: The threat to use weapons that would kill millions of civilians is itself immoral. Deterrence relies on the willingness to commit mass murder, which contradicts the sanctity of life. Accidents, miscalculations or rogue states could lead to nuclear war regardless of deterrence. The money spent on nuclear weapons could be used to address poverty and suffering.

Contrasting Beliefs on WMDs

Christianity: Most Christian denominations oppose the use of nuclear weapons. The Catholic Church has called for complete nuclear disarmament, and Pope Francis has stated that even the possession of nuclear weapons is “to be condemned.” Jesus’s teaching to “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44) and the principle of sanctity of life make the mass killing caused by nuclear weapons incompatible with Christian ethics. However, some Christians support nuclear deterrence as a way of preventing war, arguing that the intention is peace, not destruction.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that war must be proportionate — “If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate” (Qur’an). Nuclear weapons are inherently disproportionate and indiscriminate, violating this principle. Islam also forbids the killing of innocent civilians, which makes the use of WMDs incompatible with Islamic teachings. However, some Muslim-majority countries possess nuclear weapons, arguing that deterrence protects their people from aggression.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction. The key area of debate is possession for deterrence. Some believers argue that possessing nuclear weapons prevents greater harm; others argue that even the threat of using them is morally wrong because it relies on the willingness to kill millions of innocent people.

Peacemaking and the Work of Individuals

Religious teachings have inspired many individuals and organisations to work for peace. Peacemaking involves actively working to resolve conflicts, support victims and prevent future violence. Both Christianity and Islam teach that believers have a duty to pursue peace.

Desmond Tutu was an Anglican archbishop in South Africa who led the fight against apartheid through peaceful means. Inspired by Jesus’s teachings on love and reconciliation, he chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid ended, helping victims and perpetrators to find a path to forgiveness. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.

Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim from Pakistan, campaigned for girls’ right to education despite death threats from the Taliban. After being shot in the head in 2012, she continued her work, saying: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Her faith in Allah’s plan sustained her through her recovery. She became the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2014.

Religious Responses to Victims of War

Religious organisations play a vital role in supporting victims of war around the world. They provide humanitarian aid, shelter, medical care, education and emotional support to refugees and displaced people.

Islamic Relief Worldwide was founded in Birmingham, UK, in 1984. Inspired by the Islamic principle of zakah (charitable giving), it provides emergency relief and long-term development support to victims of war and conflict worldwide. In recent years, it has responded to crises in Syria, Yemen, Gaza and Afghanistan, providing food, clean water, medical care and shelter to millions of displaced people.

Islamic Relief’s work is motivated by the Qur’anic teaching: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved the whole of humanity” (5:32). The organisation works across religious boundaries, helping people of all faiths and none. This reflects the Islamic belief in the universal value of human life and the duty to help those in need, regardless of their background.

Other religious organisations involved in supporting victims of war include Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), and the Red Cross (founded on Christian principles of compassion). These organisations demonstrate that religious teachings on peace, justice and compassion are not just theoretical — they inspire practical action to help those suffering from the effects of conflict.
theme-d-peace-conflict.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on WMDs, always link your answer to specific religious teachings and the just war criteria. For the 12-mark evaluation, consider both the moral arguments about using WMDs and the separate debate about possessing them for deterrence. For questions about religious responses to victims of war, you need to know the name and work of at least one present-day religious organisation (such as Islamic Relief Worldwide).
theme-d-peace-conflict.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Both Christianity and Islam oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction because they violate proportionality, target civilians and contradict the sanctity of life.
  • Nuclear deterrence is debated — some argue it prevents war, while others believe even the threat of mass destruction is immoral.
  • Religious teachings inspire individuals (such as Desmond Tutu and Malala Yousafzai) and organisations (such as Islamic Relief Worldwide) to work for peace and support victims of conflict.

• Christianity — Jesus taught the Parable of the Good Samaritan, showing that believers should help anyone in need regardless of their background. practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:

• The Qur'an teaches that any response to attack must be proportionate — nuclear weapons are the ultimate disproportionate response.
• Pope Francis has stated that even possession of nuclear weapons is 'to be condemned.'

Arguments against:
• Nuclear deterrence has arguably prevented major wars since 1945 — if possessing weapons prevents their use, this could be seen as promoting peace.

• Unilateral disarmament could leave a country vulnerable to nuclear blackmail from hostile states.
• Some religious believers argue that the intention behind deterrence is peace, not destruction.

Conclusion: While the use of nuclear weapons is almost universally condemned on religious and ethical grounds, the debate around possession for deterrence remains complex. Most religious teaching supports disarmament, but pragmatic concerns about security make this a difficult issue.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

• Christian organisations like CAFOD and Christian Aid provide long-term development support and emergency relief to refugees and displaced people. This follows Jesus's teaching in the Parable of the Good Samaritan — helping those in need regardless of their background.
